items.title: A pristine Palm Springs 'fortress' with a surprising mob connection asks $6.4 million
items.summary: The Factor Residence at 1255 E Via Estrella comes with untouched midcentury interiors –and colourful ties to a Prohibition-era con artist
items.text: (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter It might be time to make an offer they can’t refuse. The price of an imposing midcentury modern ‘fortress’ in Palm Springs, California has just been slashed, and – in addition to a swimming pool and groovy original ‘60s-era interiors– the property comes with an astonishing connection to the Chicago mob. (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) The Factor Residence at 1255 E Via Estrella in the midcentury desert mecca was built in 1969 for Jerome Factor, a financier and relative of the pioneering Hollywood makeup artist, Max Factor. More famously, however, Jerome was the son of notorious Windy City con artist, John ‘Jake the Barber’ Factor, whose crimes included rigged casino tables and an $8 million stock scam in England. The scandals came to a head in 1933 when Jerome, then just 19, was kidnapped and held for ransom; his father, improbably, was also kidnapped just weeks later. (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) The elder Factor served six years in federal prison for mail fraud before turning over a new leaf as the operator of the Stardust Hotel in Las Vegas and, eventually, as a political donor. The new career paid off: in 1962, John Factor received a presidential pardon from John F. Kennedy. Jerome Factor cast aside his family’s sordid history and found success as a venture capitalist. He tapped Los Angeles architects Hank Webber and Don Staska to design a modern – and intensely private – Palm Springs retreat. The three-bedroom, five-bathroom house is surrounded by a 12-foot-tall wall, giving the home an intimidating street presence, no doubt due to Jerome’s kidnapping and family past (The Desert Sun reported that he also had a robust security camera network). But once inside, the home prioritises light and sightlines to a central courtyard and pool. (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) The interiors were designed by Richard Himmel, Chicago’s top decorator at the time, whose clients also included Hugh Hefner. The Factor Residence is similarly flamboyant with glossy finishes, lucite furnishings, mirrored finishes, shimmering wallpaper and collection of pop and op art by Alexander Calder, Victor Vasarely and more. The home even earned a spread in House Beautiful. Remarkably, more than 50 years later, much of the original design remains untouched, even though the home has passed through a few different hands since Jerome died in 1998. The kitchen is a ‘60s-era time capsule; even the cocktail napkins at the bar are reportedly original to the home. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) The Factor Residence hit the market this summer for $6.75 million, but has been reduced to $6.4 million. Eric Lavey of Eric Lavey + Partners holds the listing. The home is an entertainer’s paradise, and will likely draw a buyer to suit, with party-ready spaces that include indoor-outdoor living areas, a recently-restored pool terrace, a sunken granite bar and even a built-in hibachi – perhaps proof that you should keep your friends close, and your enemies closer. (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) (Image credit: © Andrew Bramasco & Melissa Bramasco) TOPICS Anna Fixsen U.S. Editor Anna Fixsen is a Brooklyn-based editor and journalist with 13 years of experience reporting on architecture, design, and the way we live. Before joining the Wallpaper* team as the US Editor, she was the Deputy Digital Editor of ELLE DECOR, where she oversaw all aspects of the magazine’s digital footprint.

items.title: Gustaf Westman’s brilliantly bonkers Disney homeware is now available online
items.summary: From bar carts to keychains, Gustaf Westman has built a surreal cartoon world with his Disney homeware collection. Here, he explains how he brought it to life
items.text: ‘Donald’ candelabra, £640 (Image credit: Disney) Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Last month, Wallpaper* previewed the first three products from Gustaf Westman's 35-piece homeware collection with Disney . Over the past three weeks, alongside an immersive pop-up in Tokyo , Westman has been gradually revealing more of the glossy designs on social media. As of today (15 November 2026), the full collection is available to shop on his website . Ranging from large furniture to keychains, each piece is an inventive abstraction or simplification of the familiar features of the Mickey & Friends characters. Larger pieces from the collection, such as this 'Mickey' dresser are made to order (Image credit: Disney) Goofy Vase They include a mirror (€390) with a chrome tubular steel frame tracing Mickey's head and outsized ears, and a pink ceramic 'Minnie' cup (€75) to match the 'Mickey' one revealed last month. Goofy's hat has been transformed into a side table while his legs and feet have been fashioned into a playful coffee table. There is a Mickey plate (€80) and jewellery box (€1,190), a cup based on Donald's hat (€85), a ceramic vase in the shape of Mickey's trousers (€225) and a glass one based on Goofy's hat (€440). 'Mickey' bar cart (Image credit: Disney) 'Mickey' plate While many of the rounded, high-gloss ceramic pieces are available off the shelf, larger designs and those in more unusual materials and finishes are made to order. These include a freestanding 'Donald' shelf, where Donald Duck's hat, arms, belly and feet serve as display surfaces, and a 'Mickey' bar cart with a circular frame and swooping, ear-shaped handles. The 'Pluto' lamp strikes an almost gothic note, with a yellow satin shade and long black beaded fringing, while the 'Donald' candelabra leans towards Memphis Milano with its geometric forms in enamelled cast iron. Together, the pieces make up a slightly bonkers cartoon world, with enough variety to tempt Disney devotees and Westman collectors back for more. The 'Pluto' lamp (Image credit: Disney) 'Minnie' glass We sat down with Westman to find out more about the design process, his research trip to Disneyland Paris and why he thinks playfulness is important at every age. 'Mickey’s Shorts' keychain Goofy's hat is transformed into a soft upholstered stool (Image credit: Disney) Gustaf Westman relaxes on the 'Mickey' sofa (Image credit: Disney) Wallpaper*: How did the collaboration with Disney begin? Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Gustaf Westman: I was introduced to Disney by my friend and collaborator, Harry Lambert. We first connected through another project and what started as a smaller idea developed very naturally into something much bigger. I didn’t really have to think about it. Disney felt like a dream collaboration because there was already such a natural connection between their world and mine. The joy, playfulness and colour felt very intuitive, so from the first sketches there was never a sense of having to force the two together. The 'Mickey Pipe' mirror will be made to order (Image credit: Disney) 'Mickey' cup W*: What was your brief? GW: It was very open, which gave me a lot of freedom to explore Mickey & Friends in different ways. I started by looking at the characters almost as a collection of shapes, colours and silhouettes. An ear, a bow or a particular combination of colours can be so recognisable on its own, so I kept asking how those details could become something else. Rather than simply putting a character onto an existing product, I wanted to deconstruct them and turn those elements into the object itself. With something like the Mickey cup, the reference is immediate, whereas some pieces take a moment to realise the character references I liked having both approaches within the collection. ‘An ear, a bow or a particular combination of colours can be so recognisable on its own, so I kept asking how those details could become something else’ Gustaf Westman 'Mickey' jewellery box 'Mickey' mirror W*: Can you tell us about the design process? GW: My process isn’t very methodical. I sketch a lot, I always carry a pen and paper. The first pieces I worked on were the cup and plate. It was almost as simple as looking at forms I already use in my work and asking: how do we make this recognisable as a character? From there I could go deeper. I started looking at pictures of the characters and breaking them down into individual elements: an ear, a shape, a colour. Because Mickey & Friends have such a clear visual language, you can take those elements quite far and they remain recognisable. That gave me a lot of creative freedom, particularly with the bigger furniture pieces. 'Minnie' cup 'Donald´s Hat' keychain W*: You visited Disneyland Paris before designing the collection. Did anything surprise you or spark anything that found its way into the collection? GW: I get inspired by shapes wherever I am, so of course there is an incredible amount to look at at Disneyland Paris. In some ways there is almost too much because the whole environment is so immersive. I don’t think there was one detail in the park that I saw and then directly turned into an object. It was more about experiencing the Disney

items.title: The niche art of bauble-making, according to hospitality’s go-to baublier
items.summary: We speak with baublier Tom Martin about his new ‘Pursuits’ collection inspired by the quiet pleasures of everyday life, hand-painted using a traditional technique
items.text: Tom Martin’s new ‘Pursuits’ bauble collection (Image credit: Courtesy of Tom Martin) Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter For Tom Martin, a bauble is so much more than a seasonal decoration; it’s a little memento, each carrying a meaning that's entirely personal to its owner. ‘There's something particularly lovely about the ritual of unpacking decorations each year,’ says Martin. ‘An object that's been carefully stored away for 11 months suddenly brings back memories and emotions that might otherwise have been forgotten.’ Working from his namesake studio, which he founded in 2010, Martin designs intricate, inside-painted glass baubles and has created bespoke pieces for clients including Claridge’s, Rosewood London , and Belmond. Now, he launches The Pursuits Collection, a new series inspired by the quiet pleasures of daily life. Discover The Pursuit Collection For the Love of Evenings For the Love of a Classic Martin sketches out each design, which is then passed on to artisans who use the centuries-old Chinese art of inside painting to bring the design to life. His collections span two distinct styles: more traditional pieces, which are scenic, often depicting atmospheric, almost Dickensian Christmas settings but in the modern world; and a more contemporary, still-life style, as seen in the latest collection, which leans into a new visual language for the brand. The seven baubles of the new collection feature little rituals, such as sharing wine and cheese, enjoying a morning coffee, or playing cards. Artisan painter at the Tom Martin studio (Image credit: Courtesy of Tom Martin) ‘My love of baubles began with a family tradition,’ says Martin. ‘Every Christmas, my mum would buy my brother and me an inside-painted glass bauble, and over the years they became a treasured part of our celebrations. My parents always made Christmas feel incredibly magical, so those decorations held a particular significance.’ (Image credit: Courtesy of Tom Martin) He continues, ‘Having studied art at school and always enjoyed painting, I eventually decided to turn the tradition on its head and design a bauble myself. I created the artwork and found an extraordinarily talented artist who could bring it to life using the intricate, centuries-old technique of painting in reverse, inside glass. The minimum quantity was 100 to justify her time, so I kept three, one each for my mother, my brother, and me, and sold the rest through a website I'd built myself.’ For the Love of the Match For the Love of a Game What began as a small project swiftly took off. Martin notes that although clients include the world's leading hotels and retailers, the philosophy remains exactly as it was when he started: creating beautiful objects that become lasting mementos. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Courtesy of Tom Martin) But what makes for a good bauble? For Martin, it is one that feels personal. ‘The most treasured decorations are rarely just beautiful objects; they have a story behind them. Many of our customers choose our baubles to commemorate a particular moment, celebrate an occasion or simply reflect something they love,’ he explains. ‘Choosing a favourite is rather like choosing between children, particularly after so many years of designing them. However, I do enjoy a martini on a Friday evening, so I think our new martini bauble probably has to be my favourite from this year's collection!’ (Image credit: Courtesy of Tom Martin) For the other ‘pursuits’ that inform the collection, Martin didn’t have to look far. ‘Much of the Pursuits collection was inspired by my own friends and family. My brother-in-law is particularly fond of card games, we enjoy playing tennis, and I have friends who are passionate golfers. These are the little interests and rituals that make people who they are, and I thought there was something rather charming about celebrating them through Christmas decorations. ‘The idea was to create a collection that felt personal without necessarily being personalised,’ he adds. ‘Something you could give to a friend and they'd immediately recognise why you'd chosen it for them.’ For the Love of the Course For the Love of Mornings Martin says that much like decorating an interior, creating a beautiful tree is all about layering, contrast and depth. Lighting is key, and he also notes that when it comes to decorations, it is important to introduce a variation of sizes, shapes and hanging positions. ‘People often make the mistake of decorating only the outermost branches, but some of the most beautiful effects come from placing baubles deeper within the tree, where they catch the light and create a sense of dimension.’ For the Love of the Garden The baublier concludes, ‘It's incredibly rewarding to think that something we've created might become part of another family's Christmas for generations. Ultimately, I hope our baubles become treasured possessions, not simply because of how they're made, but because of what they come to represent.’ Discover all of Tom Martin's collections at tommartin.co.uk Tianna Williams Staff Writer Tianna Williams is Wallpaper’s staff writer. items.title: All things sweet and colourful helped shape this unconventional superyacht interior
items.summary: All aboard the good ship Lollipop, a 37.4m superyacht from Vripack with a distinctive candy-coloured interior design scheme
items.text: Lollipop, Moonen Yachts with Vripack Design (Image credit: YachtShot) Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter One of the privileges of building your own superyacht is having a vast creative arsenal at your disposal, a team whose role is to ensure that every facet of your aesthetic vision is fully realised. When the design process for this particular superyacht kicked off, were the creatives involved surprised to be asked to shape an aesthetic vision based on the ‘owner's affection for Shirley Temple's classic song “On the Good Ship Lollipop”’? Lollipop with its twin tenders, BonBon and Cracker Jack (Image credit: YachtShot) It’s unconventional, to say the least, but perhaps it’s also a bracing change from the monochrome austerity and maudlin modernism that passes for so much contemporary yacht design. The studio responsible is Dutch designer Vripack , founded in 1961 and adept at working across a variety of scales and styles with some of the world’s leading shipyards. In the case of Lollipop , the collaboration was with Moonen Yachts, Dutch specialist in ‘mid-sized’ steel-hulled superyachts since 1981. Lollipop superyacht, with interiors by Vripack (Image credit: YachtShot) This was the first time Vripack had worked on Moonen’s 122 Martinique range, a 37.4m (345 gross tonnage) vessel with sleeping accommodation for 12 guests. The first 122 Martinique was delivered in 2018; Lollipop is the eighth in the series. So how does a confectionary-inspired interior actually make it into reality? Image 1 of 2 (Image credit: YachtShot) The main salon and dining area, with custom Delft mural (Image credit: YachtShot) The main salon and dining area, with custom Delft mural Image 1 of 2 View Original Image 2 of 2 View Original ‘When I was young working as a skipper, I always said, if I ever have a big power boat, it'll be The Good Ship Lollipop ,’ the American owner says, adding that ‘it was important to us that Lollipop didn't take herself too seriously. The candy theme is fun, but underneath is an elegant yacht that feels comfortable and completely ours.’ The sweet references are playful but not exactly subtle, from the swirling patterned leather ceiling in the owner’s suite to the themed guest cabins on the lower deck. Image 1 of 4 (Image credit: YachtShot) The lemon drop-themed guest cabin (Image credit: YachtShot) The peppermint-themed guest cabin (Image credit: YachtShot) The Swedish fish-themed guest cabin (Image credit: YachtShot) The Gummy Bear-themed guest cabin Image 1 of 4 View Original Image 2 of 4 View Original Image 3 of 4 View Original Image 4 of 4 View Original Each of these cabins takes its cue from a particular favourite sweet, with Vripack listing a pick’n’mix smorgasbord that includes peppermints, Gummy Bears, Swedish fish and lemon drops, each lending a colour scheme. In the main salon, the theme is more traditional, with blue and white accents and a custom Delft pottery-inspired mural as a focal point. Look closely, and you’ll see that this apparently classical scene actually incorporates swirling lollipops, lemon drops, Tootsie Rolls and bonbons. Image 1 of 2 (Image credit: YachtShot) Guest cabin details (Image credit: YachtShot) Guest cabin details Image 1 of 2 View Original Image 2 of 2 View Original The theme doesn’t stop there. Around the hot tub on the deck there are scatterings of sweets formed from Murano glass, while the sun-deck bar top and surround also have a candy-striped glow. Lollipop’s twin tenders have candy-inspired names, BonBon for the main tender (a Vripack-designed Wajer 38 day boat) and a crew tender named Cracker Jack (‘As well as being a sweet treat, the definition of crackerjack is someone who is skilful at what they're doing, which we felt was more than fitting for the crew,’ the owner notes). Image 1 of 3 (Image credit: YachtShot) Owner's cabin views (Image credit: YachtShot) Owner's en-suite (Image credit: YachtShot) Owner's cabin detail Image 1 of 3 View Original Image 2 of 3 View Original Image 3 of 3 View Original Amidst of all this sugary splendour it’s easy to overlook the fact that this is a very much a working boat, a serious home-from-home for owners who are looking to spend two thirds of the year at sea (along with their dogs). That means pairing whimsical details with practical interiors that can stand up to extended time at sea. Lollipop makes great use of the 122 Martinique’s large windows and generous decks, with the full beam main salon serving as a natural focal point. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Image 1 of 3 (Image credit: YachtShot) Dining and seating on deck (Image credit: YachtShot) Dining and seating on deck (Image credit: YachtShot) The hot tub, with Murano glass surround Image 1 of 3 View Original Image 2 of 3 View Original Image 3 of 3 View Original ‘This project was a lot of fun,’ admits Vripack's co-creative director, Marnix J Hoekstra, ‘Ultimately, yachting is about enjoying time on the water with the people you love, and Lollipop captures that spirit perfectly. The playful touches are deeply personal to the owner, yet the interior remains both comfortable and practical for long periods of time at sea.’ Image 1 of 3 (Image credit: YachtShot) Design details aboard L

items.title: Can Public West Hollywood bring buzz back to the Sunset Strip?
items.summary: Ian Schrager brings his signature mix of theatrical design, buzzy bars and boutique-hotel polish to the Sunset Strip, as Public West Hollywood makes a spirited bid to revive the area’s after-dark appeal
items.text: Inside Public West Hollywood (Image credit: Courtesy of Ian Shraeger) Jump to category: What’s on your doorstep? Who is behind the design? The room to book Staying for drinks and dinner? Where to switch off The Verdict Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Ian Schrager has spent decades creating legendary entertainment and hospitality spaces, from New York City’s renowned nightclub Studio 54 to lifestyle hotels like Delano Miami Beach and Edition Hotels. His latest venture brings that same verve and vision to West Hollywood’s Sunset Strip. Demonstrating his well-honed skill for writing (and continually rewriting) the playbook on boutique hotels that are often imitated, never duplicated, Public West Hollywood opens as an alluring, exciting and theatrical addition to the scene, full of drama and delight. Because, as Schrager puts it, ‘if it’s not unique, why bother?’ What’s on your doorstep? (Image credit: Courtesy of Public West Hollywood) Located in West Hollywood – an autonomous city within Greater Los Angeles that’s synonymous with boozy brunches, nightlife and Pride parades – Public West Hollywood sits on the Sunset Strip, bringing fresh energy to an area defined by iconic Hollywood haunts such as Chateau Marmont and The Tower Bar . The hotel is also well placed for exploring the Westside. Sushi Park, a favourite among Hollywood’s A-list, is a ten-minute walk away, while Rodeo Drive’s luxury boutiques and Melrose Avenue’s independent shops are around a 15-minute drive. Architecture enthusiasts can head into the hills to catch a glimpse of two very different LA landmarks: Pierre Koenig’s midcentury modernist masterpiece, the Stahl House , and Frank Lloyd Wright ’s Mayan Revival Storer House. Who is behind the design? (Image credit: Courtesy of Ian Shraeger) The aesthetic narrative for Public West Hollywood is a collaboration between Schrager and his ISC design team, architects John Pawson and Alan Bell, and interior designers François Champsaur and Aurore Rouillay. The result is cohesive yet dynamic, surprising and sophisticated. Every detail feels thoughtful and intentional, but there’s still a sense of levity and playfulness, a slight subversive edge. Three commissioned metallic magenta sculptures by artist Anselm Reyle replace a check-in desk in the glossy lobby, which also features a custom Bianco Neve marble billiard table, a 19th-century mahogany grandfather clock lacquered white with an Yves Klein-blue tassel and Salvador Dalí-designed ‘Muletas’ floor lamps . The pool bar flaunts bespoke François Champsaur sofas and lounge chairs in solid oiled teak with pink cotton fabric imported from Italy , a 51ft-long mural inspired by Fernand Leger’s original work, Les Danseuses at La Colombe d’Or in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, France, and lush foliage. At Studio, a custom-designed John Pawson black scalloped nightclub, black velvet curtains and digital screens displaying subtly moving operetta portraits set the mood. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Truly, no moment to make an impression is missed. Even the hallways leading to the guest rooms are illuminated in red, blue or green, depending on the floor. (Image credit: Courtesy of Ian Shraeger) The room to book (Image credit: Courtesy of Ian Shraeger) When it’s time to call it a night, the rooms are a crisp white refuge from the colour and curated chaos. All the accommodations are minimally minded, kitted with plush beds, blackout drapery, a projection screen and laser-display projector for film screenings (should you go all out on the after-dark antics and need some recovery time). The pool-facing room categories have private terraces with seating for enjoying daytime views and nightly poolside programming. There is no in-room mini -bar, but there are tea- and coffee-making facilities. Staying for drinks and dinner? (Image credit: Courtesy of Ian Shraeger) Ian Schrager is quick to tell you what Public West Hollywood doesn’t have – and that’s a fancy restaurant with a big-name chef. Much like the New York outpost, there’s an all-day cafe for fresh-baked pastries, daytime fare (salads, sandwiches and bowls) and coffee. Ultimately, the property is conceived as a destination for drinking and dancing. When hunger hits after the sun goes down, the colourful pool bar serves seasonal sustenance such as little gem salads and mezze plates to pair with margaritas, martinis and signature sips like the Luna Luna (a mezcal, passion fruit and blue spirulina elixir). The open-air rooftop terrace comes alive with well-dressed patrons sipping wine and cocktails, alongside panoramic vistas of Los Angeles. And if the mood takes you, you'll find a DJ spinning tunes in on-site nightclub Studio, a playful nod to Schrager's legendary New York nightlife roots. Where to switch off At first glance, Public West Hollywood feels more like a place where you’d turn things up rather than switch off, but beneath the shiny façade of revelry is a less obvious, though no less well-thought-out, undercurrent of relaxation. Rather than a dedicated spa, the hotel offers a full roster of in-room treatments, including deep-tissue lymphatic drainage, sports and prenatal massages, facials, manicures and pedicures, hair and make-up

items.title: Aman's next big move is a 1,049ft wellness tower in Miami
items.summary: The luxury hospitality group is launching ATMA, a new brand centred on sport, longevity and performance, with a vast wellness centre and private residences planned for Miami's waterfront
items.text: (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Aman has found a new way to raise the stakes in luxury hospitality. The hotel group is joining forces with tennis champion Novak Djokovic on ATMA , a new global brand built around sport, wellness and longevity. Its first project is a 1,049ft tower on Miami 's waterfront, complete with a 120,000 sq ft wellness centre, indoor tennis and padel courts, a private marina and a collection of residences. (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) Announced this week, ATMA marks a new direction for the hotel group, bringing elite sporting expertise into its established world of design-led hospitality. Djokovic, who becomes the brand's Global Partner, will oversee its longevity, nutrition, racquet and wellness programming, drawing on the knowledge accumulated over his professional tennis career. The idea is to bring elements of an elite athlete's training and recovery regime into everyday life. Miami is the first location, with ATMA set to occupy a waterfront site in Brickell, the city's financial district. Developed by OKO Group and Oak Row Equities, the project will rise alongside the five-mile Baywalk, with far-reaching views across Biscayne Bay. The architecture comes from SHoP Architects , whose sculptural tower will feature curved balconies and floor-to-ceiling windows. Studio Paolo Ferrari is responsible for the interiors, bringing together organic forms and furniture shaped around the human body. Lighting and ambience will also be calibrated to respond to the circadian rhythms of residents and guests. (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) The real scale of the proposition becomes apparent in the wellness facilities. At 120,000 sq ft, the spa and wellness centre is set to be among Miami's largest. It will include a high-performance fitness centre, private and group training studios, mobility and conditioning labs, a medical wellness centre and dedicated recovery spaces. Away from the training schedule, ATMA Miami will have a more sociable side, with nutrition-led dining, entertainment and event spaces. The development will also include one-to-five bedroom residences, alongside six-bedroom penthouses at the top of the tower. Owners will have access to a private pool, fitness and yoga studios, thermal spa facilities, a co-working space, as well as priority nomination to the invitation-only ATMA Club. (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) For Aman, which has spent the past 38 years building a reputation around considered design and exceptional service, ATMA represents an exciting new chapter – and a serious step into the business of wellbeing. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Its first Miami outpost is scheduled for completion in 2031. Find out more at atma.com TOPICS Charlotte Gunn Director of Digital Content Charlotte Gunn is a writer and editor with 20 years experience in journalism, audience growth and content strategy. Formerly the Editor of NME, Charlotte has written for publications such as Rolling Stone, CN Traveller, The Face and Red.

items.title: Around the world in 24 chocolates with Laila Gohar’s travel-themed advent calendar
items.summary: Banana and sea salt? We’re in Waikiki. Hazelnut praline? Must be Paris. Every day, a new Casa Bosques chocolate flavour transports you to a different Luxury Collection hotel destination
items.text: (Image credit: The Luxury Collection) Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Hotel brand The Luxury Collection has unveiled an exquisite limited-edition advent calendar created in collaboration with artist and designer Laila Gohar (a former Wallpaper* guest editor) , the company’s Epicurean Global Explorer. Discerning travellers are invited to discover The Luxury Collection’s diverse portfolio of hotels and resorts through the sensory experience of very fine chocolate. The advent calendar – available in the US from The Luxury Collection and in the UK and select countries through Gohar World – presents a culinary round-the-world trip with 24 destinations. Each of its numbered drawers slides open to reveal an enticing chocolate bar, with each bar celebrating a different Luxury Collection hotel; from The Gritti Palace in Venice to The Laurus in Singapore. Gohar World The Luxury Collection x Laila Gohar advent calendar 2026 (Image credit: The Luxury Collection) The spirit and cultural identity of the locations are expressed, deliciously, through the flavour notes in the chocolate. Your journey will take you, for instance, to Waikiki with flavours of banana and sea salt. Another day, you will stop off in Los Cabos, tasting smoked mesquite and dates; arriving at The Prince de Galles in Paris , you will enjoy rich hazelnut praline. The chocolate nestled within the calendar has been created for The Luxury Collection by Casa Bosques , the acclaimed Mexican brand known for its bean-to-bar production of organic single-origin bars. It uses rare heirloom cacaos sourced from farmers across Mexico and an unconventional and exciting range of spices and flavourings from around the world. Illustrations are by Joana Avillez (Image credit: The Luxury Collection) The chocolates are by Mexican brand Casa Bosques (Image credit: The Luxury Collection) Illustrated by Joana Avillez, the calendar takes the form of a grand hotel. The façade opens to reveal a gallery of quirky, joyful, festive scenes, and the requisite 24 drawers – portals to just a selection of The Luxury Collection’s 130-plus hotels and resorts in 42 countries. Bruce Rohr, vice president and global brand leader of The Luxury Collection, says: ‘This imaginative collaboration celebrates the destination-inspired flavours and culinary traditions found across our global portfolio, offering a transportive journey through the cultures and stories that make each place distinct.’ The calendars in the making (Image credit: The Luxury Collection) There’s a different flavoured chocolate for each day (Image credit: The Luxury Collection) Gohar’s creative vision for the calendar is extended to a series of pop-up chocolate shops located in key Luxury Collection destinations, including Paris, Nashville, Singapore and Los Cabos. Their design was inspired by traditional Parisian chocolatiers and Milanese apothecaries and features glass vitrines with chocolate-hued swags of drapery and banks of wooden drawers. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Gohar comments: ‘Each drawer is a small world of its own, inspired by the flavours, traditions, and details that make destinations so special at this time of year. I hope each discovery sparks curiosity and joy.’ The Paris pop-up, one of a series to promote the partnership (Image credit: The Luxury Collection) The advent calendar can be purchased through The Luxury Collection in the US, Gohar World in select countries internationally, and at select hotel pop-ups. Melina Keays Melina Keays is the entertaining director of Wallpaper*. She has been part of the brand since the magazine’s launch in 1996, and is responsible for entertaining content across the print and digital platforms, and for Wallpaper’s creative agency Bespoke. A native Londoner, Melina takes inspiration from the whole spectrum of art and design – including film, literature, and fashion. Her work for the brand involves curating content, writing, and creative direction – conceiving luxury interior landscapes with a focus on food, drinks, and entertaining in all its forms

items.title: Amanvari is a study in desert minimalism on Mexico’s Baja California coast
items.summary: Set between the desert, mountains and Sea of Cortez, Amanvari brings nature-led architecture, exceptional dining and the signature serenity of Aman to Baja California’s East Cape
items.text: (Image credit: Courtesy of Amanvari) Jump to category: What's on your doorstep? Who is behind the design? The room to book Staying for drinks and dinner? Where to switch off The service The verdict Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Amanvari means 'peace' and 'water' in Sanskrit. An ethos of seaside tranquility is woven into every aspect of the intimate, 18-key property. Unlike the sprawling resorts in nearby Cabo San Lucas, Aman’s exclusive new Baja California retreat is intentionally small, with privacy, serenity and connection to nature of equal importance. The landscape drives the design, acting as both the inspiration and the backdrop for a place so at home in its surroundings it feels as though the land and sea might have given permission to build it. What's on your doorstep? (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) Set within the exclusive Costa Palmas community on Baja California’s East Cape, Amanvari is positioned to escape it all. Aside from Four Seasons Resort Los Cabos at Costa Palmas , a 10-minute drive away, there’s not much around. And that’s exactly the point. The property is wrapped in nature, removed from tourist-trodden Cabo San Lucas, but accessible enough to venture to a buzzy restaurant or bar should the mood strike – though, speaking from personal experience, you’re not going to want to leave the premises, aside from, perhaps, a day trip snorkelling the ancient coral reefs of Cabo Pulmo National Marine Park or an off-road expedition into the Sierra de la Laguna. Who is behind the design? (Image credit: Courtesy of Amanvari) The Baja California landscape – soft sand extending into the deep blue Sea of Cortez, swaying palms, towering cardón cacti, arid desert, an estuary and distant mountains – inspired Elastic Architects ’ design. The award-winning firm, with initial contributions from Heah & Co., used local elements, embraced minimalism and spotlighted artistic expression – from contemporary Mexican art to ancestral crafts – to create an indoor-outdoor sanctuary with a deep sense of place. At the heart of the resort is Casa Grande, an open-plan, atrium-like structure perfectly balanced by a restrained neutral palette with views of the ever-changing sky throughout the day and night. It’s also home to one of Amanvari’s most impressive commissions: an intricate, textured dome, inspired by the spiral chambers of an extinct marine microfossil, which took artists Abi and Luisa Calvete of Extra Neutro more than 1,000 hours to create. To the left, the curved lounge bar is enveloped in earthy materials, still water and rounded edges, fostering a sense of softness and serenity that’s matched by sweeping Baja vistas. Descend the spiral staircase down to the lower level for the panoramic main pool crafted from Caledonia Black granite as well as three dining venues that follow the same nature-led principles. The room to book (Image credit: Amanvari) Amanvari has 18 stilted casitas, which almost appear to float above the trees. Contemporary rooms are anchored by white concrete, natural limestone and tropical hardwoods, complemented by bespoke furnishings, textiles in sandy hues and original works by Mexican artisans such as exclusive mixed-media pieces by Arozarena de la Fuente and sculptural ceramics by Tomás Díaz of Disciplina Studio. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. The alfresco living spaces are an extension of the interiors – generous terraces with seating areas for morning coffee, and below, heated pools and outdoor showers. While all the accommodations are striking, the most soul-stirring views are found in those facing the estuary or situated directly on the sand. I stayed in Casita #4, a short stroll down the path from Casa Grande. (Image credit: Courtesy of Amanvari) Entering through the large wooden door into the courtyard and through the floor-to-ceiling sliding glass doors, the sightlines of the inlet extend, unobstructed to the generous, second-floor terrace, an extension of the white-and-wood interiors. (Image credit: Amanvari) Below, the heated pool and outdoor shower served as a private holiday haven, an even quieter respite, devoid of other guests (not that I saw many during my stay), where the only sounds were the fish frolicking in the water and the birds chirping. Back inside, clever choices such as thoughtfully positioned beds and a television that rises and hides at the touch of a button reinforce the idea that the best thing to watch is the outdoors. The bathrooms feature dual limestone vanities on either side, Vermont Beige marble floors and walls, a spacious shower and a soaking tub for the ultimate unwinding experience. Estuary casita, at Amanvari (Image credit: Amanvari) Staying for drinks and dinner? (Image credit: Courtesy of Amanvari) The curved, open-air lounge bar, which faces the waves on one side and the Sierra de la Laguna mountains on the other, is the place for pre-dinner drinks (I recommend the Bartolo, a clarified concoction of raicilla, mango and habanero) with a soundtrack of soulful live saxophone and the gentle crash of the waves. Sesui is a sleek Japanese concept, centred around a 10-seat wood counter, illuminated by loofah lanterns the shape of sea urchins. It’s here that Chef Mas

items.title: This Belgian designer’s home is a ‘winterised’ take on California modernism
items.summary: Belgian interior architect and furniture designer Bieke Casteleyn was inspired by Palm Springs when putting together her home's interiors
items.text: (Image credit: Anaïs Lesy) Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter 'I have always been fascinated by midcentury homes in California , particularly the houses found in Palm Springs and Los Angeles ,' says Belgian interior architect and furniture designer Bieke Casteleyn . When she went to create her family home in Belgium, she knew she wanted to take cues from California midcentury modernism, yet adapt it to fit the cooler climate and darker months of Belgium. Step inside this Belgian countryside home (Image credit: Anaïs Lesy) Located in the polders in Belgium , a flat and low-lying countryside area, the residence is a 'winterised interpretation of California modernism '. Casteleyn drew from elements of the genre in both the architecture and interiors of the home, which is set on a single level, with warm wood and abundant natural light. Tweaks were made to fit the Belgian context, with exteriors in stone sourced by Casteleyn and her husband, chosen in a grey-green to better flow with the landscape. The flat roof is covered in grass, letting the home further blend with the green surroundings. For the interiors, the warm tones meet touches of cooler materials, such as stainless steel, in a nod to the local climate. (Image credit: Anaïs Lesy) Casteleyn launched her first furniture collection in 2015, featuring natural curves, tactile materials, and a sense of playful boldness. Her own home carries these same sensibilities, yet is also driven by her love of midcentury modernism. She began the project in 2018, working on the initial plans with architect Simone de Burbure, before developing it further with a site coordinator, an external architecture office, and a member of her own team. Casteleyn designed the interiors herself, creating a home that’s open, inviting, and connected to the nature around it. (Image credit: Anaïs Lesy) The main living areas are separated from the private wing of the home by a sweeping 36m corridor, with glass walls for immersion in the surrounding landscape. Curtains were added for privacy, in addition to a wooden claustra (or architectural screen) that runs along the exterior in an elongated oval pattern. This oval shape recurs throughout the home, from the door handles to the kitchen cabinetry, acting as a 'visual signature’ of the property. (Image credit: Anaïs Lesy) Casteleyn deliberately balanced the home’s open-plan areas and expansive views with a sense of warmth. 'Houses with extensive glazing and long sightlines can sometimes feel exposed or impersonal,' she says. 'By contrast, homes with smaller corners and enclosed spaces tend to feel naturally more inviting. I wanted to find a balance between the two: a home filled with light and long views that would still provide warmth, privacy, and a sense of shelter.' Rich woods and natural materials, organic curves, and tactile textures are signatures of Casteleyn’s designs, and these feature heavily within the interiors. ‘Instead of having the interior and then choosing which pieces fit, I chose to do the opposite: design the house around the furniture’ Bieke Casteleyn Over the years of designing the project, Casteleyn and her husband had collected a range of furniture and art, and they used the pieces to define the home. 'Instead of having the interior and then choosing which pieces fit, I chose to do the opposite: design the house around the furniture,' she explains. Collectible design pieces are interspersed with antiques from Casteleyn’s family, alongside select designs of her own. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Anaïs Lesy) In the living room, for example, a sofa designed by Minotti, chosen in collaboration with RR Interieur, sits alongside a coffee table prototype by Bieke Casteleyn, in high-gloss ivory lacquer and afromosia wood, and vintage Artifort armchairs. In the dining room, an inherited table, whose legs Casteleyn upholstered in burgundy, sits underneath a tiered midcentury chandelier sourced from Morentz Gallery. (Image credit: Anaïs Lesy) Around the home, thoughtful features were added to deepen the indoor-outdoor connection. On one terrace, a circular opening in the roof makes space for a tree to grow through it. Elsewhere, stairs lead to a small deck over a pond, with seating for watching the birds and taking in the bucolic landscape. biekecasteleyn.com (Image credit: Anaïs Lesy) (Image credit: Anaïs Lesy) (Image credit: Anaïs Lesy) (Image credit: Anaïs Lesy) TOPICS Charlotte Boates Charlotte Boates is a writer based in Vancouver and has lived internationally in Barcelona, New Zealand, New York and San Francisco. She writes about architecture, design and travel, while working as a communications consultant for creative firms.

items.title: This 377-Square-Foot Island Getaway in Denmark Is a Picture-Perfect Pint-Sized Retreat
items.summary: The sustainable vacation house includes a sauna and plunge pool—and boasts an emissions rate to impress any earth lover
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story A mini vacation home in Zealand, Denmark , is a particularly appealing retreat, no matter the season. With its rugged coastlines, forests, and small villages, the western side of Zealand offers an ideal setting for a break from everyday life. Nestled among trees is a tiny house that was designed to be as unobtrusive as possible. Its compact shape, natural color palette, and large windows allow it to blend almost seamlessly into the forest. Here, nature isn’t just right outside the door—it’s always present inside as well. Surrounded by trees, this small wooden house in Denmark blends seamlessly with nature. Edi Cliff A mini vacation home for all seasons Named the EcoNeo House, the home was designed by the Danish architectural firm SAGA Space Architects , both as a family home and as a prototype for tiny house-style vacation homes. Although originally conceived as a summer house, the cottage has been insulated and heated, allowing it to be used even during colder weather. At only 377 square feet, it combines the essential features of a vacation home, sleeping up to six people. The design prioritizes a thoughtful use of the available space and forward-thinking architecture that blends into the landscape. The spacious terrace is perfect for sunbathing and dining outdoors, especially in the summer. Edi Cliff Smart living in a small space Inside, the living and dining areas flow seamlessly into one another. Thanks to the large windows that offer views of the surrounding trees, there’s a connection between indoors and outdoors. The kitchen is set slightly apart, but opens up into the dining area, blending smoothly into the floor plan. Designed with functionality in mind, it’s still fully equipped with all the necessary appliances. The dining area flows seamlessly into the kitchen. Additional storage space was created below the stairs on the left, which lead to the sleeping lofts. Edi Cliff Instead of breaking up the floor plan with additional walls, the architects made use of the home’s height: Stairs next to the kitchen lead to two sleeping lofts that offer a private retreat for up to four people. Storage was also a priority in the design. Items not needed on a daily basis can be stowed under the stairs, a clever solution that again makes the most of the small space. Large windows let in plenty of natural light and create a connection between indoors and outdoors. Despite its compact size, the kitchen has all the necessary appliances. Edi Cliff There’s even a sauna , which can be converted into a sleeping space for two additional guests if needed. The generous window front offers a view of the surrounding landscape, while a cold plunge pool on the terrace is waiting for a refreshing dip afterward. Through the sauna’s large window, you can enjoy the surrounding nature even while relaxing. It’s an appealing retreat, especially on chilly days. There’s also a cold plunge pool on the terrace. Edi Cliff Wood as a unifying element The choice of materials complements the understated architecture. The floor’s wide Douglas fir planks introduce a warm color and vibrant grain. The use of wood is consistently carried through to other areas of the house, creating a visual connection between the living space and the sauna. Natural materials are also used in the bathroom, including Kolmården marble, a Swedish stone distinguished by its characteristic green hue. Wood defines the interior and lends the rooms a natural warmth. Large windows bring the surrounding nature into the home, while the dining area is spacious even within the compact layout. Edi Cliff Together with the stones and the greenery outside, the result is a design that deliberately avoids contrasts and excess. “When designing the summer house, every detail was intended to reflect the harmony between sustainable innovation and timeless craftsmanship,” explains Niklas Munk-Andersen, architect and partner at SAGA Space Architects. Beanbag chairs provide extra seating and blend harmoniously into the interior with their colors. Edi Cliff The Douglas fir floorboards also give the clean design a natural, tactile quality. The material is more than a surface design choice, instead it shapes the way that the rooms feel. The bathroom features natural materials and Swedish marble finishes. Edi Cliff The sauna can also be converted into a sleeping area for two additional guests. Edi Cliff Natural materials and small spaces form a sustainable combination The compact design also has a positive impact on the home’s carbon footprint. According to calculations by SAGA Space Architects, the EcoNeo House produces approximately 386 pounds of CO₂ annually, whereas an average vacation home for six people is estimated to emit about 2,282 pounds. This means emissions are approximately 83% lower. In addition to the small living area, bio-based materials are the primary factor contributing to this difference. The boundary between indoors and outdoors blurs, bringing nature into focus. Edi Cliff The architects also designed the construction process to be as efficient as possible by digitally planning the house, precisely prefabricating its individual components, and then assembling them on-site in a modular fashion. This approach not only simplified assembly but also minimized the impact on the site. Thanks to its small footprint, this vacation home’s emissions are 83% lower than those of the average vacation home that can accommodate six people. In addition, the modular construction minimizes the impact on the natural environment. Photo: Edi Cliff The EcoNeo House demonstrates that sustainable construction isn’t just a matter of the materials used. The size of a building and how the available space is utilized also play a crucial role. Though it may sound small, 377 square feet can be perfectly sufficient for a getaway home—provided the floor plan, storage space, and amenities are all carefully designed. Although prima

items.title: Nickey Kehoe’s New Collection With The Lacquer Company Takes Its Cues From Beloved Antiques
items.summary: The vintage-inspired coffee tables, trays, and tissue boxes are all coated and sanded by hand in Vietnam
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story In 2024, AD heralded the return of lacquer . In our April 2026 issue, cover star Athena Calderone was pictured leaning over an enormous burgundy-lacquered kitchen island, and in May, cover star Mark Grattan showed off his parrot green lacquer walls . Today’s collaboration between AD100 design firm Nickey Kehoe and The Lacquer Company brings the glossy finish down to a slightly more manageable scale, applying it to coffee tables, desks, trays, and tissue boxes. Nickey Kehoe founders Todd Nickey and Amy Kehoe designed the 30-piece collection with The Lacquer Company founder James Lowther, drawing on antique furniture and objects the three have collected over the years. SHOP THE COLLECTION The Bonne Nuit nightstand in Cassis staged among various Nickey Kehoe textiles and an upholstered headboard. The Florin Tray in Carreaux & Marine Blue is styled with all small pieces from the Nickey Kehoe collection. Many of the pieces, as is often true of Nickey Kehoe’s in-house catalog , draw on the founders’ personal vintage collections. The Pastis side table is based on a bamboo folding table that belongs to Nickey. The Hugo desk is a Louis XVI–style writing desk , with tapered, fluted legs, brass details, and three soft-close drawers in a bright red lacquer. The colorways sound like a very civilized, French late lunch: cassis and lettuce green, carreaux and marine blue, khaki and chocolate brown. The Jules catchall tray comes with a matching tissue box cover for the powder room. Lacquer trays, tissue boxes, side tables, and the collection’s coffee table are staged together here to show the full line. The Pastis side table references a vintage style with the lacquer and bamboo combination reminiscent of Regency Chinoiserie. Lowther bought his first piece of lacquer, a burnt-orange betel box , while traveling in Burma in 1999, and it’s still one of his favorite things. He later found the craftspeople he was looking for in Saigon, and every piece from The Lacquer Company is still made there in Sơn Mài lacquer, a Vietnamese art form that goes back centuries. The process is lengthy: Wood is first sealed with a resin called Sinh. It’s then coated repeatedly with natural lacquer mixed with ground mountain rock, alluvial soil, and cashew nut shell oil. Each coat is wet-sanded until it’s smooth before the next coat is applied. “There is no prescribed drying time, no set number of layers,” according to the company. That makes the eight- to 12-week lead time on larger pieces easier to forgive. Nickey Kehoe’s goal is for its furniture to feel “as if it was acquired, not purchased.” With these pieces so rooted in vintage styles and techniques, they make good on their promise. The collection is available to shop on NickeyKehoe.com. items.title: The Six Bells Madewell Collection 2026
items.summary: The contemporary clothing brand and New York hotel deliver a slice of upstate with a 28-piece fashion and home goods capsule
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Whimsical design flourishes, cozy interiors, and close proximity to upstate antiquing all make The Six Bells Countryside Inn one of the best weekend escapes in the Empire State. Now, thanks to Madewell , you never have to check out. Launching today, the two brands have joined forces on a 28-piece holiday capsule of heirloom-worthy wardrobe and home essentials inspired by The Six Bells’ vintage aesthetic. Pieces specifically pay homage to the hotel’s interiors through references to archival patterns and wallpaper prints found throughout the Inn’s rooms and communal spaces. “We fell in love with [The Six Bells’] distinct, whimsical world—the mix of patterns, the nostalgic sentiment, and the personality in every detail,” says Madewell creative director Steven Cateron. During initial planning for the clothing brand’s holiday collection, the hotel in Rosendale, New York became an unexpected source of inspiration for Cateron and his team because of the shared appreciation for heritage and storytelling. “Each piece has intention, whether it’s to wear day-to-day or for a celebration, a gifting moment for a loved one or hostess , or pajama pieces that lean into cozy season,” he says. SHOP THE COLLECTION Sock slippers from the collaboration and Madewell’s classic denim make a perfect pairing. Courtesy of Madewell Founded by Audrey Gelman in 2025, who designed the hotel in collaboration with interiors firm GrecoDeco, The Six Bells Countryside Inn has quickly risen in popularity—even earning a spot in AD ’s list of Great Design Hotels last year. “This project is so rooted in a shared love of the decorative arts and global human history,” designer Adam Greco previously told AD . Design-wise, maximalism dominates the interiors. Picture: rooms wrapped in fretwork wallpaper and deep cinnabar paint, with pistachio window shades and striped seating. The collection also builds on the fantasy of Barrow’s Green , the fictional English village dreamed up by Gelman that includes its own imaginary landmarks and distinct locals (including a town gossip and poignant editor). “It was so interesting to broaden our imaginations and think about how The Six Bells’ style could be brought to life through clothes,” says Gelman. A cheeky message makes this classic needlepoint pillow pop. Courtesy of Madewell At the same time, the collaboration was an opportunity to venture into Madwell’s less-explored categories—specifically the home space. The collection’s interior goods are a practice in curated nostalgia: There are holiday ornaments you’ll reach for year after year, scented candles and soaps to integrate into your daily winter routine, and cozy pajamas inspired by vintage sleep silhouettes. “If it’s something we don’t currently offer, we want to work with people that do the category best,” says Cateron. “The Six Bells team were the perfect partners to bring this collection’s home accessories to life.” Still, versatility isn’t lost in the assortment. In designing the clothing, Cateron made sure to include “pieces to wear upstate, in the city, or for day-to-day celebrations.” Classic denim jackets are neutral staples that you can reach for any day of the week, while Fair Isle wool knits are seasonally appropriate while still feeling adaptable enough to wear after the holidays. “There’s a real point of view behind every detail [at The Six Bells Countryside Inn], from the interiors to collected vintage pieces,” says Cateron. “This collection captures that sensibility in a way that felt authentic to both brands.” The collection is available to shop on Madewell.com and in Madewell stores starting today, November 12. “There’s so much character in every detail at The Six Bells, and we wanted to bring that sensibility into each piece,” says Madewell creative director Steven Cateron. items.title: How One Creative Couple Found Harmony in Their 1920s Los Angeles Craftsman
items.summary: Interior designer Harrison Soll and Lenny Kravitz's longtime stylist Rodney Burns balanced their minimalist and maximalist leanings in their Laurel Canyon home
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Nothing about where interior designer Harrison Soll is now was part of the plan. Five years ago, he was focused on his work, and he didn’t want any distractions. But when he met Rodney Burns, a stylist and owner of the legendary Los Angeles vintage gallery, Church Boutique , it set everything on a new path. They met in the fall; by New Year’s they were a couple. “I didn’t think it was going to be a relationship,” Soll says. He credits their shared interests for bringing them together: “We always found a throughline with design.” They now live in a 1925 craftsman house in Laurel Canyon. Soll took the lead decorating the nearly 1,400-square-foot home in a combination of his and Burns’s styles with many pieces coming from Burns’s eclectic collection of vintage art, furniture, and sculpture. Burns has worked with Lenny Kravitz as a stylist and creative collaborator for the past 15 years, and the singer says he admires what Burns and Soll have created together. “The mix of Rodney’s early- to midcentury style mixed with ethnic expression next to Harrison’s bold minimalist modern approach seamlessly blend together,” Kravitz tells AD . The backyard of Soll’s and Burns’s Laurel Canyon home is a bricolage of funky, inherited stonework and vintage pottery. The nail art above the fireplace has a cute backstory story: Burns and Soll had seen it at a vintage shop in Santa Monica and Burns regretted not buying it. When he went back to purchase the piece, it was marked as sold. But only because Soll had already covertly bought it as a Valentine’s Day gift for Burns. The giant Sergio Bustamante giraffe bust in the foyer is a delicate topic. “The giraffe was one of our biggest fights in decorating this house,” Burns explains. “I was determined to have that giraffe live some place in this house because he’s just fantastic, and the scale of him, and the rarity of him.” Except, counters Soll, that the placement of the giraffe is treacherous because the front door swings right in its path. “You just have to be careful,” Soll says. The foyer—which features a collection of masks and vintage paintings—was one of the most difficult areas to style, explains Burns. The couple was trying to be selective of what pieces to incorporate from Burns’s massive collection and at one point Burns suggested putting all of his masks in storage to save for another house down the line, or passing them onto Burns’s vintage boutique, Church. Soll dissented, saying, “No, let’s put them everywhere.” The living room features two sofas—a Joseph D’Urso for Knoll piece reupholstered in leopard fabric and a leather De Sede Terrazza. The carpet is the Antilocarpa style from Stark. A trio of fiberglass shell art was sourced through Kelly Wearstler. The art behind the sofa is a manipulated canvas garment bag by the artist Roosevelt “Rip” Woods, the first black artist to have a solo show at the Phoenix Art Museum. As renters, there were naturally limitations on what could be achieved. Soll got permission to retile a bathroom and install a new vanity. The doe-patterned wall-to-wall carpeting in the living room was an “ask for forgiveness” move, but his landladies ended up loving it. Burns, on the other hand, needed more convincing. “The carpet took many dinners of conversations between the two of us,” Soll says. Soll describes himself as more of a minimalist while Burns avows, “I’m a maximalist to the umpteenth power.” The couple attempted to strike a balance while still filling the space with character. Some rooms nod to Soll’s leanings toward minimalism like an office with a midcentury desk and a 1970s tapestry and the dining room where a Sergio Bustamante table and a Chinese Art Deco rug are the main attractions. When decorating their Laurel Canyon home, Soll and Burns had to figure out how to combine their opposing styles, with Soll being more of a minimalist and Burns being a maximalist. But, says Burns, “[Soll] has made me be able to take a pause and then also make me a little less attached to some of the things that I’ve collected and given me an opportunity to maybe show a little bit more restraint.” In the corner, a brass Maison Jansen palm tree mingles with a Sergio Bustamante monkey. Burns, who has been styling Lenny Kravitz for over a decade, says his approach to home design and fashion are one in the same: “Building an outfit, building a room: same thing in my opinion.” Kravitz offers these kind words on Burns: “What I love about Rodney is that he is limitless in his concepts and always thinks outside of the box. His visual vocabulary enables him to mix a vast stew of eras and genres. He pays tribute to our ancestors and uplifts new innovators. Always soulful, expressive, and elegant.” In the dining room, Soll placed a Sergio Bustamante table on a diagonal to make enough room for the couple’s large dog. “She’s a girthy girl,” says Soll, referring to the table, not the dog. The chairs are by Paul Evans and the Chinese Art Deco rug was sourced from Ariana Rugs. The Tom Greene chandelier was sourced from Burns’s boutique, Church. Burns’s maximalism is on display in the living room, where a couch upholstered in leopard Scalamandré mixes with zebra-hide chairs and a sinuous De Sede sofa. (That animal print couch, Soll wants you to know, also features a block of leather upholstery: “I just think it would have been too maximalist to do a full Scalamandré sofa.”) The living room is filled with brass sculptures (a Maison Jansen palm tree and a Sergio Bustamante monkey), bronze figures sourced from an estate sale in Arizona, and several pieces of sculptural artwork. The bedroom mixes patterns and textures with a stainless steel bed from TTMM, Paul Evans “Cityscape” nightstands, striped bedding, and antique bronze table lamps with African mud cloth shades. items.title: 7 Best Writing Desks That Are Furniture Chameleons (2026)
items.summary: These slender pieces easily blend in a range of interior styles
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Regardless of whether you have a home office or not, a good writing desk is a versatile piece of furniture to have on hand. Unlike a secretary desk , which is usually equipped with a drop-front panel or concealed compartments, this type of desk has a streamlined surface and open-leg construction, making it best suited for pen-and-paper tasks. In other words, it’s less intrusive style-wise since it’s not designed to have a million compartments for cable management or bulky drawers to stash old bills. The design options feel endless in this furniture category. You can try a larger, minimal silhouette with a slender drawer or two if you’re a creative like TV writer Mike Gauyo , who spends hours behind a writing desk in a Los Angeles studio. Or you can opt for a vintage desk to bring lived-in character to your interiors, like the styles in this A-frame Catskills cabin and Southampton, New York, enclave . Because the silhouettes are so adaptable, many can easily work as entryway console tables , dressing tables , and even sideboards to hold extra plates and silverware after all your dinner parties. All in all, this desk setup encourages peaceful moments rooted in intention, and it might speed up your to-do list. Now is the time to knock out those holiday cards or try your hand at writing a novel. items.title: 8 Best Hotel Mattress Picks for a Five-Star Staycation (2026)
items.summary: Bring home the beds behind some of the world's most high-end stays—no reservations required
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story The hotel mattress probably isn't on your vacation itinerary, but it can make or break the trip. A lumpy, unsupportive bed can derail even the most carefully planned getaway . A really good one, though, might become an unexpected highlight—the kind that has you looking forward to bedtime and quietly checking the mattress label before checkout. Recreating that experience at home doesn't require another plane ticket. Some of our favorite properties, including design-forward waterfront retreats and charming bed-and-breakfasts, put just as much thought into their mattresses as they do their interiors. Many turn to brands like Saatva , Ostermoor, and Casper to outfit their guest rooms; others, like the W Hotels , have signature mattresses you can purchase directly. We've rounded up our favorites, such as options with plush pillow tops, supportive coils, and pressure-relieving foam, to help you bring home the best part of your stay. The room service, unfortunately, is still up to you.
