items.title: Andy Baraghani’s New NYC Restaurant is Full of Design Surprises
items.summary: From Bauhaus to his house, we’re gobbling up all the decor ideas on display at Ditto
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story “I’ve always been obsessed with design, since I was a kid,” says Andy Baraghani. “I love how restaurant interiors can take you to a different place.” At Ditto —the all-day café he is opening in New York’s Flatiron —the chef, cookbook author, and YouTube star has given that obsession free rein. With each design decision—from the vintage glass-prism Holophane pendants in the front window to the intense blue (tinted to match Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue) of the rear dining area’s Venetian plaster walls—he asked himself: “Would I actually do this in my home?” If the answer was yes, it passed the test. The interior of Ditto, with Venetian plaster walls in a shade matching Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue, and Model S22 chairs from Galvanitas. Photo: Adrian Gaut For Andy Baraghani, design is something of a family affair. His husband, Keith Pollock , is a former AD editor and now a West Elm executive. But opening a restaurant was never part of the plan. In fact, when Michael Silber, a restaurant investor behind New York hot spots like Borgo, Penny, and Bistrot Ha, approached him with the idea of a laid-back restaurant open for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, Baraghani admits his first reaction was: “I have no interest.” It wasn’t for lack of experience. He had started his career in restaurants—from Chez Panisse in Berkeley, where he worked as a teenager, to Estela in New York—before becoming a food editor at Bon Appetit and winning a James Beard Award for his cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be . But he bonded with Silber over their shared love of greenmarket cooking and decorating deep dives. When it came to Ditto, he says, he wanted the space to convey his personal style. It helped that he and Silber were on the same page. “Andy and I talked about styles ranging from Bauhaus , de Stijl , and classic modernism to 1970s and ’80s aesthetics from places like Italy and France,” Silber says. The Bauhaus-inspired counter at Ditto. Photo: Adrian Gaut They brought in like-minded collaborators: interior designer Eric Wink and architect Alta Indelman . Wink, a close friend of Baraghani who helped with the design of his and Pollock’s home, says the partners told him that New York’s much-missed City Bakery, which was two blocks uptown from Ditto’s 16th Street location, was an inspiration. “They wanted it to feel casual and approachable, with a bit of a New York diner quality,” Wink says. Holophane pendant lamps hang in the restaurant’s front window. Photo: Adrian Gaut The space, in a 1905 former factory (its last incarnation was an agnès b. store), is divided into three zones. In the front section, visitors can shop at a market area with hand-picked groceries. A glossy white counter with Bauhaus curves anchors the middle section; this is where customers line up, take a number, and either carry the food out or dine at laminate-topped tables under a trio of oversized custom fabric pendants. The menu, handwritten on a roll of butcher’s paper and updated daily, features dishes like pomegranate spoon salad and what Baraghani calls “the Platonic ideal of granola,” with tahini, maple syrup, and yogurt drizzled with fig-leaf oil. Flaky Biscuits will be a signature dish. Photo Credit: Adrian Gaut The third zone, the one painted blue, features an open kitchen and café tables pulled up to a banquette that runs the length of the room. “There’s that good chaos in the middle and the back is a calmer moment,” says Baraghani. Indelman, a veteran collaborator with New York restaurateurs like Andrew Tarlow and Gabe Stulman, was tasked with giving the space a utilitarian, high-tech ambience. She clad the walls and the open kitchen in patinated stainless steel and preserved industrial elements like structural arches and polished concrete floors. But it was Baraghani and Silber who took the lead on honing the visual details of the interiors. “We went through 50 possibilities to find the right chair,” Silber says. The one they selected—a 1960s Dutch industrial chair, the Model S22 from Galvanitas —was sourced from Amsterdam Modern in Los Angeles. Silber also spent hours on eBay bidding on midcentury ceramic bud vases. “They were each under $20 but put them together on a shelf and you have your own little Giorgio Morandi tableau,” he says. White wall speakers and a French ceramic mask hang above the banquette, tables, and stools upholstered in Maharam’s Stripe It fabric. The no-nonsense decor also features white wall speakers, created for the space by sound artist Tom Bloxam , and programmed with playlists created by Michael Scanlon of Chandelier Creative , which oversaw Ditto’s branding. But there are quirkier moments too. When it came to choosing fabric for the custom stools, Baraghani insisted on Maharam’s Stripe It , which he felt had a “Baja California” vibe. “We needed that twist,” he says. For his part, Wink specified his favorite stainless-steel toilet for the restrooms— Neo-Metro’s wall-mounted MiniLoo . “I added a custom wood top to soften it a bit,” Wink says. Meanwhile, a pair of massive midcentury French ceramic faces that hang on a wall opposite the menu of the day are on loan from Baraghani’s own home. “They anchor the space and add a touch of craft,” he says. “I just knew they needed to be here.”

items.title: Are Zen Hotels Now Putting Us to Sleep?
items.summary: Rich, layered maximalism is the latest form of escapism—historically inspired decor spiked with creative contemporary flair. Get ready to Instagram every nook.
items.text: Above: One of the cottages at Little Saint in Healdsburg, CA. On the top floor of a Gilded Age McKim, Mead & White mansion in New York, now reincarnated as the Fifth Avenue Hotel, Martin Brudnizki recently put the finishing touches on a two-bedroom suite dubbed the Flâneur Penthouse. With his hallmark exuberance, the Elle Decor A-List designer arrayed the space with distinctive flourishes: a spirited Scalamandré wallcovering trimmed in grosgrain ribbon, bespoke furnishings mixed with French Art Deco pieces, India-inspired inlaid nightstands, Japanese-style lamps, and Murano glass ceiling lights. Each element connects to an imagined narrative that shaped Brudnizki’s vision for the hotel: “this cinematic idea of the home of a flâneur who has traveled the world, has seen and acquired a lot, and put it together here,” the designer says. “It’s a multicultural journey.” Douglas Friedman Designer Martin Brudnizki used a Scalamandré wallcovering in the entry vestibule of the Flâneur Penthouse at the Fifth Avenue Hotel in New York. Brudnizki is among a cadre of prominent designers whose approach contrasts markedly, and quite intentionally, with the school of quiet hotel luxury that has become ubiquitous over the past few decades, defined by natural woods, pale stone, organic fibers, and warm minimalist palettes. It’s a style that has a universal appeal—as practiced by Aman, say—when executed in more mundane, cookie-cutter fashion it can feel just, well, beige . “There’s a homogeneity that passes as mass luxury where you could be anywhere,” says Elle Decor A-List designer Ken Fulk, who is currently reimagining the Beverly Hills Hotel’s public spaces. “I think we all crave spaces that avoid this sameness, to feel deeply connected with a place.” Simon Brown A sitting room by Kit Kemp at New York’s Warren Street Hotel. Hotels in this vein tend to be -owner-operated properties looking to carve out a niche. One could trace a baroque family tree that links mold-breaking 1980s boutique hotels like Ian Schrager and Philippe Starck’s Royalton in New York to Jacques Garcia’s interiors for the Hôtel Costes and L’Hotel in Paris to Ilse Crawford’s Ett Hem in Stockholm to Kelly Wearstler’s Proper Hotel in Austin. “It’s Studio 54 meets your grandmother’s Soho townhouse, a disco granny kind of thing.” —Martin Brudnizki Fulk’s hospitality design, like Brudnizki’s, embraces spaces inspired by history and storytelling, with an emphasis on artistry, material richness, and character. Both men’s work is rooted in tradition, with idiosyncratic twists that feel fresh. And they have plenty of kindred spirits working in a diversity of styles, including such designers as Lorenzo Castillo, Kit Kemp, and Laura Gonzalez. While far from a coherent movement, the sumptuous, high-impact aesthetics practiced by these designers just might be today’s most zeitgeisty current. Oskar Proctor A lounge area at the Broadwick Soho in London by Martin Brudnizki. Take Fulk’s Cottages at Little Saint in Healdsburg, California, each one an elevated boho mashup of influences. “Sixties and ’70s rock and roll, and a sort of Laurel Canyon meets Northern California spirit,” explains the designer. “The cottages feel utterly like nowhere else.” And that, of course, is the point. For his part, Brudnizki doesn’t care much for maximalism as a label. In the case of his glamorously moody interiors for the Broadwick Soho in London—shimmering surfaces, lavishly upholstered furnishings, a riot of pattern—everything began with an idea he describes as “Studio 54 meets your grandmother’s Soho townhouse, a disco granny kind of thing.” Jérôme Galland A bar Laura Gonzalez designed for the Casa Monti hotel in Rome. Then there are the roughly dozen memorable properties created by Kit and Tim Kemp under their Firmdale Hotels group. The most recent is the Warren Street Hotel in New York, with the forthcoming Bedford Place Hotel slated to open next year in London next to the British Museum. “It’s about personality, a sense of arrival, and fun,” says Kit Kemp, who outfits each of her hotels with a more-is-more mix of her ebullient textiles and wallpapers in splashy colors, animated by art and craft. Kimberley Cohen, the creative director behind Maisons Pariente, says her family’s small portfolio of hôtels de charme are about creating a residential-feeling experience that is also “something you have never seen, that you would not do in your own home.” She has worked with Brudnizki on Le Grand Mazarin in Paris, with Charles Zana on two hotels in the South of France, and with Pierre Yovanovitch on a Méribel chalet. Her latest project, opening this winter, is a Courchevel retreat named Saint Roch, with interiors by Friedmann & Versace that channel the chic romanticism of traditional dachas. Next up for Brudnizki, meanwhile, is the Knox Hotel, set to open soon in Dallas, new territory for him. As for what one should expect of the decor, he sums it up as “100 percent unapologetic glamour. It won’t be boring.” This story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of ELLE Decor . SUBSCRIBE Stephen Wallis ELLE Decor features director Stephen Wallis has spent three decades covering art, design, and culture. He was previously the consulting features editor for Galerie and held top positions at Architectural Digest and Departures. His writing has appeared in numerous publications, including The New York Times, T magazine, WSJ magazine, Esquire, Town & Country, Veranda, and Cultured . He is the author of Fontainebleau, a history of the iconic Miami Beach hotel, and Jim Thompson: Beyond Silk, Beyond Thailand . items.title: The Kitchen Trends Designers Expect to See Everywhere in 2027
items.summary: The National Kitchen & Bath Association’s 2027 forecast has arrived.
items.text: 2 min read Above: the kitchen of an Athens home designed by Nashmita Rajiah. Partial walls, hidden appliances, and pantries with room for prep are among the kitchen features expected to gain ground next year, according to the National Kitchen & Bath Association’s 2027 Kitchen Trends Report . Based on a survey of 830 kitchen-industry professionals—including designers, manufacturers, remodelers, and architects—the report looks at the layouts, materials, lighting, and technology they expect to be popular over the next three years. Here are the main takeaways. Defined Layouts Gieves Anderson In a David Netto-designed apartment , linen curtains with Samuel & Sons trim divide the space between the kitchen and dining area. NKBA reports growing interest in partial walls, movable partitions, and separate kitchen zones—a shift from last year’s forecast, when open layouts were still gaining ground. Dedicated prep spaces and back kitchens are also emerging features, cited by nearly half of designers. Kitchens are still expected to get bigger, with 52 percent of designers anticipating growth. The kitchen’s surrounding rooms are growing, too. NKBA reports that mudrooms and laundry spaces are increasingly being integrated into kitchen plans. The vast majority of designers expect attached mudrooms to be popular over the next three years, with 45 percent anticipating mudrooms getting larger and 43 percent expecting laundry spaces to grow. Hidden Appliances and Enclosed Storage Appliances are increasingly being incorporated into cabinetry rather than left on display. Eighty-five percent of designers agree cabinets are being designed to hide appliances and other functional elements, and roughly two-thirds say open shelving is on its way out in favor of enclosed storage. Pantries are taking on more work, too. Nearly 90 percent agree they are becoming multifunctional extensions of the kitchen, and three-quarters expect dedicated small-appliance stations to be popular. Separate beverage areas continue to gain support, with 90 percent anticipating their popularity, up from 85 percent in the 2026 report. Martin Morrell An English Victorian manor designed by Linda Boronkay features an enclosed pantry with bespoke oak joinery. Wood Cabinets and Neutral Colors Neutrals remain the leading color of choice, followed by greens and blues. For cabinetry, light and medium tones draw equal interest, and white oak is the preferred wood for roughly half of designers. Islands don’t necessarily have to match: a little more than half expect them to feature a different color from the surrounding cabinets. Quartzite and quartz lead countertop preferences, with nearly half of designers favoring honed or matte finishes. Layers of Lighting The lighting forecast includes under-cabinet lights, illuminated cabinet interiors, nighttime path lighting, sconces, and pendants. Eighty-four percent of designers agree kitchens will incorporate multiple layers of light, and 78 percent say lighting is increasingly being used as a design feature rather than just a functional necessity. Under-cabinet lighting leads the forecast at 87 percent, followed by interior-cabinet lighting at 76 percent. Ventilation, Water Filtration, and Leak Protection NKBA identifies ventilation, water filtration, touchless faucets, and sound-absorbing materials among the report’s wellness features. Designers are also discussing ways to make kitchens more resilient: 65 percent cite leak-detection systems and automatic shut-off valves, 62 percent cite backup power, and a little over half point to ventilation and air filtration. Julia Cancilla Social Media & News Editor Julia Cancilla is the social media & news editor at ELLE Decor, where she oversees the brand's socials and covers design, pop culture, and emerging trends. She also authors the monthly ELLE Decoroscope column. Her work has appeared in Inked magazine, House Beautiful, Marie Claire, and more. items.title: 7 Gilded Age Homes Where You Can Live Like the Astors
items.summary: In honor of   The Gilded Age  ’s fourth season, here are the period mansions-turned-hotels you can stay in right now.
items.text: Erin McGinn Above, Castle Hill Inn in Newport, Rhode Island. Gilded Age barons of industry constructed extravagant homes—year-round mansions and summer “cottages”—that were more palaces to their wealth than practical residences. Notable families like the Vanderbilts, Carnegies, and Astors once had houses dotted across New York City and throughout fashionable summer retreats like Newport, Rhode Island. Many of these elaborate structures have since fallen to the ravages of time, with the staggering costs of upkeep rendering their use as private residences all but obsolete. Yet, though some of these private homes have disappeared, our curiosity about them has only increased. Since HBO’s hit show The Gilded Age debuted, interest in visiting the era’s architectural marvels has surged, and in Newport, which is home to one of the country’s largest concentrations of Gilded Age mansions, there’s been a steady rise in visitors touring the town’s mansions specifically because of the show. Visiting the opulent, and often wildly impractical, mansions that inspired the fictional lives of The Gilded Age ’s characters has its charms, but rather than just taking a tour, why not spend the night? Up and down the East Coast, a handful of Gilded Age mansions are preserved not as museums, but as hotels—inviting curious travelers to do more than just visit and admire the history, but to sleep within the jewel boxes of their walls. Courtesy of Castle Hill Inn Castle Hill Inn Newport, Rhode Island Castle Hill Inn is a different kind of Gilded Age mansion, one that turns to timber and antiquities over marble and gilding. The home’s original owner, Alexander Agassiz, was a Harvard professor of natural sciences who made his fortune in copper mining. With his newfound wealth, Agassiz built his summer home—Castle Hill—on a relatively isolated parcel of forty acres, a fifteen minute drive away from the pomp and pageantry of the Vanderbilt’s side of town. He used the home as a summer research lab, hosting students in its many rooms and running the lab in what is today the parlor, while also entertaining a who’s who of literary luminaries, including Edith Wharton and Mark Twain. Today, Castle Hill Inn is one of the most famous places to stay in Newport, not only for its luxurious rooms, afternoon tea, and award-winning restaurant, but also for its sweeping ocean-front lawn and seaside views. Thorton Wilder lived in the turret suite—Agassiz’s former observatory and today the hotel’s most beautiful room—while writing his last book, and Grace Kelly lived in one of the beach cottages during the 1955 filming of “High Society.” Stopping by Castle Hill Inn for a drink and taking a short walk to its still in-use lighthouse remains a summer essential in Newport, but there is nothing quite like staying the night. Courtesy The Chanler at Cliff Walk Hotel Chanler Newport, Rhode Island Hotel Chanler is, unlike Castle Hill, right in the thick of Newport’s Gilded Age neighborhood, and it’s clear from its location that it was built (to use a period expression) to keep up with the Joneses. The opulent mansion was constructed in 1873 as the summer “cottage” of New York Congressman John Winthrop Chanler and his wife Margaret Astor Ward. Chanler hosted an elaborate range of guests at his summer home, including President Theodore Roosevelt and poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. The home, which Chanler called “Cliff Lawn,” was the very first mansion to be built on the Cliff Walk, now a public walkway with views of these historic homes. Over the years, the mansion went from being a private residence to a museum and later a girl’s school. It wasn’t until 2003 that it opened as the twenty-room Chanler Hotel. Today, it’s ornately decorated in various period-specific styles such as Regency, Louis XVI, Renaissance, and English Tudor. Last spring, The Chanler opened a more pared down restaurant, Remy’s Loose. Remy’s feels fit for Mr. Chanler and his guests, who we can imagine sprawling out across the chenille, fringed edged slipper chairs, and enjoying the just fussy-enough French menu. Advertisement - Continue Reading Below Courtesy of The Fifth Avenue Hotel The Fifth Avenue Hotel New York, New York The Fifth Avenue Hotel, which opened its doors in late 2023, has a multi-layered history rooted in the Gilded Age. In 1856, legendary hostess and doyenne of New York society, Charlotte Goodridge, commissioned the construction of a lavish private home and carriage house at the coveted corner of Fifth Avenue and 28th Street. Goodridge filled her mansion with treasures from around the globe and entertained lavishly. But following her death, Goodridge’s home met the same fate as much of the neighborhood and was torn down. However, rather than being replaced by a skyscraper like much of the surrounding area, Goodridge’s mansion was reborn in 1907 as a striking five story neo-Renaissance palazzo design by McKim, Mead & White, the architects behind many of the New York’s most famous early 20th century buildings including The Morgan Library and Museum, the Bowery Savings Bank, and the Metropolitan Club. More recently, a decades-long renovation overseen by Flâneur Hospitality, Martin Brudnizki Design Studio, and architect Perkins Eastman transformed the building into a 153-room hotel, with a restored limestone and brick façade, an added-in glass tower, a ballroom fit for a Goodridge party, and a European inspired restaurant, Café Carmellini. The hotel now has a Gilded Age-inspired look, complete with polished marble floors, grand arched windows, rich color palettes, and art and curiosities from around the world. Michael Worthington Hotel Bardo Savannah, Georgia Hotel Bardo may have opened in 2024, but its history extends much further back. It was built in 1888 as a private home for Lewis Kayton, a businessman from Baltimore who settled in Savannah. items.title: Next-Gen Mineral Surfaces for Your Kitchen, Bath, and More
items.summary: Éclos by Cosentino merges natural beauty and breakthrough technology.
items.text: Courtesy of House Beautiful 3 min read As a homeowner, the two things you tend to expect most from your ideal kitchen countertop are all too often in conflict: You want it to be truly beautiful, to evoke elemental, one-of-a-kind natural stone. But you also want all the resilience, innovation, and eco-friendliness that 21st-century technology can provide. Renowned sustainable-surfaces brand Cosentino has made its reputation bridging those desires, and its Éclos line is both good-looking and good for the planet, simultaneously timeless in appeal and tech-forward in performance. That’s exactly what made it a surface of choice for many of the rooms in the House Beautiful Whole Home in Charleston, South Carolina, an effort of our sister publication. Here’s what makes Éclos the next generation of surfaces: Technology Courtesy of House Beautiful The Whole Home kitchen (also shown at top) is clad in Éclos Legnd. Unlike traditional stone that is cut from a quarry and installed in discrete slabs, Éclos is manufactured from a combination of minerals fused together with a proprietary technology the company calls Inlayr—the name of which gives rise to this new category of high-tech materials: inlayered mineral surfaces. Advanced robotics allow the surfaces to be imbued with sophisticated, three-dimensional veins and patterns that echo those of precious materials pulled from the earth. The result is the unique appearance of prized stone like marble or granite, with a strength that natural stone could never achieve on its own. Durability Courtesy of House Beautiful The powder room countertop was fabricated with Éclos Wonder. So what does that mean once you actually install Éclos in your kitchen or bathroom? For one thing, far less maintenance than might be required of natural materials. Éclos is nonporous, so it never needs to be sealed, much less resealed every six months to a year as, say, you might need to do with a marble counter. And it’s as solid as a rock—wait, more solid than rock: In the kitchen, it can withstand temperatures up to 428°F without showing signs of damage such as stains or cracks. In the bathroom, a knocked-over bottle of nail polish remover is no big deal. Dings, scratches, stains... things of the past. Sustainability Courtesy of House Beautiful A guest bathroom’s double-sink countertop features Éclos Landr. One of Cosentino’s core values as a company is sustainability—the brand devotes a large portion of its research and development resources to discovering new and better ways to employ recycled materials and reduce its overall carbon footprint. In the case of Éclos, Cosentino says the development of the surface involved nearly 30,000 hours of research and testing. The result is its most advanced product yet; Éclos uses zero crystalline silica and a minimum of 50 percent recycled materials (in some products in the new line, that goes up to almost 90 percent). That’s welcome news for designers and homeowners who are committed to incorporating sustainable, socially and environmentally responsible materials and practices into their renovations and new builds. Aesthetics Courtesy of House Beautiful Éclos Wondr gracefully tops a counter in another Whole Home bathroom. Of course, when it comes to creating a space you love and will be happy living with for years, state-of-the-artness only goes so far—style and sophistication are the other half of the equation. It’s a principle Cosentino, which also created designer-beloved modern surfaces like Silestone and Dekton , has doubled down on. The Éclos line is characterized by a carefully curated selection of quietly luxurious colors and textures, each crafted to mirror the richness and tactile appeal of quarry-cut stone. The surfaces have a visual depth and luster that almost make you forget how hardworking they are. For kitchens and bathrooms—anywhere you can envision the sophistication of stone— Éclos can be key to crafting a space that is high-end but never high-maintenance. It's the future of surfaces, delivered right now. Advertisement - Continue Reading Below

items.title: Uncommon Hospitality unveils Nordic-inspired spa lodge
items.summary:
Maine-based Uncommon Hospitality has announced Fara Lodge & Nordic Spa, an intimate mountain getaway coming to Rangeley in Late 2027. […] 
 The post  Uncommon Hospitality unveils Nordic-inspired spa lodge  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Uncommon Hospitality unveils Nordic-inspired spa lodge 16 November 2026 | In Projects | By Eleanor Howard Maine-based Uncommon Hospitality has announced Fara Lodge & Nordic Spa, an intimate mountain getaway coming to Rangeley in Late 2027. Designed in partnership with Maine -based architecture firm Jocelyn O Dickson Architecture (JODA), the property will reimagine a historic escape through a contemporary lens, preserving its architectural character while introducing elevated accommodations and an expansive Nordic spa experience developed with MCD Spa Consulting. Inspired by the communal culture of Nordic saunas and the distinctive charm of the Rangeley Lakes Region, known as the “Jewel of the Maine Mountains,” Fara Lodge will offer a design-forward hospitality experience built around the natural rhythm of adventure and restoration. The property will feature a collection of guest rooms and private cottages, comprehensive spa facilities with multiple sauna and thermal experiences, a nourishing café and communal spaces, and a restored historic bar that has welcomed mountain-worn Rangeley adventurers for decades. Fara Lodge is designed to honour the landscape from every vantage point, offering guests a deeply tranquil experience through a contemporary lens. Interiors draw from Western Maine’s rugged character while introducing a more refined approach to mountain design. Original stone fireplaces and pine panelling will sit alongside oversized lanterns, vintage Swedish sofas, and a palette of oxblood, dusty blue, and deep rust, a quietly Scandinavian sensibility that feels entirely at home among the lakes and peaks of this corner of the state. The lodge will feature 10 guestrooms and two private cottages, with simple yet beautiful touches including wrap-around pine banquettes; a considered mix of fabrics by Schumacher, McLaurin & Piercy and Commune for Kufri; integrated boot warmers and built-in storage millwork; and rich teal tilework that offers an unexpected moment of colour in the otherwise neutral, relaxing rooms. “My family has been coming to Rangeley for generations, so this project carries a particular meaning. The design had to honour what longtime visitors already love about this place, its history, its character, its quietness, while creating something that feels genuinely new for those discovering it for the first time,” comments Jocelyn O Dickson, Principal of JODA. “Every material decision, from the Maine-made furniture to the art program, tells the story of this region and the people who have shaped it.” The Great Hall will function as the natural gathering place of the property: a warm, unhurried space anchored by two stone fireplaces. The all-day cafe will offer counter-service breakfast, lunch, and dinner alongside grab-and-go offerings, all inspired by Scandinavian cuisine’s emphasis on seasonality and simplicity. A bar tucked in one of the property’s most historic spaces remains as a humble nod to the lodge’s long history of well-adventured guests, its original wood floors still marked by the spikes of generations of golfers. The heart of Fara Lodge will be its destination-worthy wellness centre overlooking Saddleback Mountain, offering a range of thermal and relaxation experiences derived from the shared humanity of bathing culture. The sprawling wellness campus will feature Maine-built cedar tubs, outdoor wood-fired saunas, an indoor Finnish dry sauna, fireside lounging, a relaxation yurt, and outdoor hot and cold plunge pools. With additional communal areas including a welcoming reception area, outdoor spa deck with hot tubs and showers, and calming relaxation rooms, the experience is built to encourage exploration, both of the facilities’ restorative benefits, and of oneself. “The inspiration for this project is Rangeley itself. We fell for the property and the area years ago, enchanted by the natural beauty and endless things to do. My family now enjoys Rangeley year-round and that personal connection is a big part of why this project means so much to us,” says Nate DeLois, Co-Principal of Uncommon Hospitality. “We’ve learned that the most meaningful hospitality experiences are the ones rooted in genuine place and community, and we’re approaching Rangeley with the same spirit. We can’t wait to welcome a new generation of travellers to experience it for themselves.” Americas Lodge maine spa uncommon hospitality Related Posts 25 January 2024 Das Central welcomes new Summit Spa 24 October 2023 Envi Lodges to debut in Oman 12 October 2020 The Rusty Parrot Lodge & Spa announces details of rebuild

items.title: The Postcard Hotel to debut in Nepal with riverfront retreat
items.summary:
The Postcard Hotel is set to make its debut in Nepal with The Postcard on the Rapti River, Chitwan. Set […] 
 The post  The Postcard Hotel to debut in Nepal with riverfront retreat  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: The Postcard Hotel is set to make its debut in Nepal with The Postcard on the Rapti River, Chitwan. Set along the Rapti River, with uninterrupted views of the surrounding forests and hills, the 22-key luxury retreat adjoins the buffer zone of Chitwan National Park, one of South Asia’s most significant wildlife destinations. The opening marks the brand’s expansion into its fourth country, following India, Bhutan and Sri Lanka. The Postcard on the Rapti River has been conceived to make the surrounding landscape an integral part of the stay. Guests arrive through a Temple Court built around a stupa, an architectural introduction to a hotel thoughtfully designed to reflect its setting. The 22 generously proportioned rooms and suites, starting at 1,300ft 2 , feature private sit-outs overlooking the river or forest. On fortunate days, guests may experience the thrill of watching wildlife from the privacy of their rooms. The two-bedroom Presidential Suite, extending across 5,000ft 2 , offers space and privacy, complete with its own private pool. Dining and leisure are equally connected to the destination. Tree Tops, the hotel’s indoor-outdoor restaurant and bar, occupies an elevated deck overlooking the forest, with The Postcard’s signature anytime breakfast allowing guests to dine entirely at their own pace. As evening falls, Tribal Circle brings guests together around a bonfire for an open-air barbecue inspired by the culinary traditions of the Tharu community, indigenous to the Terai. The hotel also features a swimming pool, spa treatment rooms, a steam room and sauna, while a spacious elevated viewing deck by the pool offers sweeping views of the surrounding wilderness and opportunities for wildlife sightings. Beyond the hotel, programming includes naturalist-led jeep safaris, guided forest walks, canoe excursions along the Rapti River and birdwatching experiences. Visits to nearby Tharu villages offer an introduction to the region’s distinctive cultural heritage and the communities that have lived alongside these forests and rivers for generations. “At The Postcard, we have always believed that some of the world’s most remarkable destinations are those that remain beyond the usual travel map,” says said Kapil Chopra, Founder and CEO, The Postcard Hotel. “Our ambition is to bring these places to life through hotels that are deeply rooted in their surroundings, while allowing the destination itself to take centre stage. “What drew us to The Postcard on the Rapti River was the conviction Savanna and her father, Suraj, brought to the project. Their desire to showcase Nepal beyond its mountains, and to create something that respects the landscape, its wildlife and its people, resonated deeply with our own philosophy. This is precisely the kind of destination we want to introduce to the world – one that offers not just a beautiful place to stay, but a meaningful connection with a part of the world that deserves to be discovered.” Savanna Vaidya Basnyat, owner of The Postcard on the Rapti River, adds: “Chitwan is one of the most precious parts of that world, and sharing its beauty with the world is something I feel deeply passionate about. From the moment we discovered this beautiful bend in the river, overlooking the forest and the hills beyond, we knew we had found something truly special. We wanted to create a place that belonged to its surroundings, rather than one that simply occupied the landscape. My father has been central to bringing this vision to life, and building something so meaningful together has been an incredibly special journey.” Basnyat concludes: “For me, this project is about more than hospitality. It is about conservation tourism and finding a way for tourism and nature to coexist in harmony.” Nepal rapti river the postcard hotel Related Posts 27 September 2024 Trailborn set to debut latest hotel in Arizona 14 April 2015 Delano Hotel to debut in Dubai 19 April 2012 Firmdale to re-open their debut hotel

items.title: Gottfried Gruber and Lains Architects unveil vision for Hotel AUI
items.summary:
Gottfried Gruber and Lains Architects have reimagined the former Lärchenhof Hotel as Hotel AUI in Maranza, South Tyrol. The project […] 
 The post  Gottfried Gruber and Lains Architects unveil vision for Hotel AUI  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Gottfried Gruber and Lains Architects unveil vision for Hotel AUI 13 November 2026 | In Projects | By Eleanor Howard Gottfried Gruber and Lains Architects have reimagined the former Lärchenhof Hotel as Hotel AUI in Maranza, South Tyrol. The project involved a redesign of the building’s exterior, communal areas, part of the spa and most of its 26 rooms. While the original load-bearing structures were retained, the architects reworked the hotel’s identity and interiors to introduce a more flexible approach to hospitality. The hotel takes its new name from the South Tyrolean dialect word for ‘up’. South Tyrol-based studio Lains Architects was responsible for the interior design, collaborating with architect Gottfried Gruber on the building’s exterior and pool. “One of the central ideas behind the design of AUI was the interplay between opposites: social interaction and privacy, activity and relaxation, openness and a sense of comfort, digital and analogue,” explains Sabrina Negri, Lains Architects. “The spaces are designed to accommodate these contrasts naturally.” Green is the defining colour of the redesigned building, extending from its exterior into the interiors. The new façade unifies the previously fragmented structure, with individual balconies connected to form a continuous outer plane. Inspired by the silhouette of traditional pitched-roof houses, the design features coarsely brushed spruce wood finished with a two-layer colour glaze. Its textured surface references traditional South Tyrolean timber construction, including relief structures and coffered elements. “The façade takes its cue from the silhouette of a traditional pitched-roof house, repeated across the building,” notes Gottfried Gruber. “This reference connects the hotel to the Alpine landscape and suggests the idea that each guest can, in a sense, have their own private chalet. At the same time, each individual space remains part of a larger whole, reflecting the idea at the heart of the AUI community: Gruber also designed the new pool, positioned following an analysis of the sun’s path. Light simulations informed its placement, while the indoor-outdoor configuration creates a visual connection with the surrounding mountains. Mirrored surfaces reflect the water, sky and landscape. “The position of the new pool was determined through a careful analysis of the sun’s path,” says Gottfried Gruber. “Using light simulations throughout the day, we identified the point where the experience of the water would be at its best.” Inside, the surrounding forests inform the material palette, particularly the use of larch-inspired greens and copper tones. The ground floor has been reconfigured as an open communal space rather than a conventional hotel lobby. At its centre is a boomerang-shaped table incorporating self- check-in facilities, a traditional stube, a communal dining area and the breakfast buffet. “The first element guests encounter when entering the hotel is a long, boomerang-shaped table,” reveals Sabrina Negri, Lains Architects. “It brings together the self-check-in, the small stube, the community table and the breakfast buffet. In doing so, the traditional separation of hotel functions is dissolved: there is no dominant reception desk, nor a rigid hierarchy between host and guest.” The surrounding areas accommodate a range of functions, including a trust shop and community kitchen. Material changes help distinguish different zones, with larch flooring used in areas intended for longer stays and ceramic surfaces marking circulation routes. Green furniture accents provide further visual continuity throughout the communal spaces. The first and second floors house the redesigned rooms and apartments. Custom-made furniture maximises the available space, while the apartments incorporate compact kitchens and sofa areas that can be converted into additional sleeping accommodation. Spruce is used extensively in the interiors, complemented by fabrics and wallpapers in the hotel’s wider colour palette. “The characteristic green of AUI continues throughout these floors,” explains Michaela Greifenegg, Lains Architects. “Spruce remains the defining material, used extensively in solid wood, and its natural fragrance adds a particular sense of warmth. Carefully selected fabrics and wallpapers complete the material concept, creating comfortable spaces that invite guests to linger.” gottfried guber lains architects refurbishment renovation South Tyrol Related Posts 6 February 2024 Marin Architects designs new addition to New York’s skyline 17 October 2023 First Look: Trunk(Hotel) Sapporo 19 August 2022 GM Architects transforms Lebanese heritage house into boutique hotel

items.title: Q&A: Paragon Studio brings wellness into the guestroom
items.summary:
Having made its name in superyacht and prime residential gyms, Paragon Studio is now working with hotel operators and designers […] 
 The post  Q&A: Paragon Studio brings wellness into the guestroom  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Q&A: Paragon Studio brings wellness into the guestroom 12 November 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle Having made its name in superyacht and prime residential gyms, Paragon Studio is now working with hotel operators and designers to bring wellness into the hotel guestroom. Ahead of the launch of In-Suite at HIX, Founder Edward Thomas talks craftsmanship, carbon and why a hotel’s wellness offering shouldn’t stop in the gym. Paragon Studio began in superyachts and prime residential. What did that world teach you about luxury hospitality? Nobody puts up with an ugly object in a beautiful room for very long. On a yacht or in a luxury home, the gym is often the last space to be designed and the first one the owner judges. So, we work function first and build the form around it. Every hand-made piece has to survive a hard session, and then it has to be a feature that a designer is proud to see on the wall. Yachts also teach you control within a limited space, which is why so much of our range is storage: tree racks, wall units and the Credenza we originally built for a yacht and that now lives in homes on dry land. How does that carry over into hospitality? Hotels have the same problem, multiplied. An operator will specify stone, timber and bespoke joinery throughout, and then fill the gym with black rubber from a catalogue. Inside The Manchester Hotel in Lexington we laser-engraved the hotel’s logo into the end plates of our Diabolo Dumbbells, debossed it into the boxing pads, and matched the racks and cork yoga kit to the finishes upstairs. At the Golden Goose Arena in Milan, a curtain in the members’ lounge draws back on a wall installation we designed around the brand’s star. The brief is always the same: the gym should look as though it belongs to the building and the brand. Wellness now sits on almost every brand’s list of guest experience priorities Where is the industry getting it right? Spas, sleep programmes and personalisation. Luxury hotel groups have invested properly there. The gap is the guest who wants to train at six in the morning and finds the gym is in the basement, shared, and possibly still locked. A lot of people now travel with a routine and don’t want to drop it for four nights. Our research showed that plenty of others would simply rather not exercise in front of strangers. Hotels build wellness offerings around four disciplines (movement, recovery, nutrition, and sleep) but movement gets treated as a single, undifferentiated category (the gym) when it actually splits into three: the gym, activities and in-room wellbeing. Why have you launched In-Suite, your in-room fitness solution? One guest kept coming up in our research, and almost nobody was designing the modern traveller who doesn’t want to use the gym, but still values exercise, movement and routine. This guest profile is more likely to enjoy practicing mindful movement, such as yoga, Pilates and light mobility. These guests value privacy, space and quality and hotels have been slow to notice them while prioritising more and more upgrades in the main gym. That’s why we built an ecosystem around the product: the kit, the content and the service, so the room becomes personalised to the guest. What exactly is In-Suite? The collection is our bespoke offering: a series of kits that hotels can specify around movement, recovery and strength. Each can be supplied as a drawer insert to fit the existing joinery in the room, housed in a wooden tray, or delivered to the room to order by concierge. Recovery and movement kits are the core options, and every element of the look and feel can be specified to match the hotel’s design. Hotels can provide each room with a set. Guests choose what they’d like to do from the menu on the digital platform, which offers workouts for strength and conditioning, Pilates or recovery, each using different equipment from the kit. The platform also lets guests order specialist equipment to their room, if the hotel wants to offer that. Each kit carries a laser-etched plaque with a QR code, which links guests to their workout through the hotel’s software. For our launch at HIX Europe, we have partnered with Naturalmat to display In-Suite within the bed frame itself to show the versatility of the product, and how it can be designed within the room at concept stages of projects. Why a drawer? Because the room is already full. A drawer insert takes up no additional footprint, so it can be retrofitted into rooms that are open and trading, with no change to the layout – and no joinery modifications are required. It’s also easy to manage. Every piece has its own cut-out, so housekeeping can see, at a glance, whether anything has walked. How far can a hotel make it its own? As far as it likes. The starting point is our own web app with the full video library. The next step is light-touch branding: the app in the hotel’s colours and logo, branded intros and outros, subtitles in the languages its guests speak. Beyond that, we’ll film a bespoke library on site, in the hotel’s own rooms. Our software includes an ever-growing library of workout videos that are monitored for performance, and use the data to keep the content fresh, relevant and engaging. The hardware follows the same logic. Equipment can carry the hotel’s logo, and the trays, inserts and kit can be made in finishes outside our standard range to suit the interior. What’s the commercial case for an operator? In-Suite is a room feature a hotel can charge for, and a clear way to separate one room category from another. The video library runs on a subscription, and we look after the hardware through a servicing and maintenance package: an emergency allowance to replace anything stolen or damaged, an ongoing refurbishment programme for well-used pieces, and an annual on-site inspection. Kettlebells do occasionally leave hotels. We’d rather the operator didn’t have to think about it. Sustainability is the question every specifier now asks. What’s

items.title: Groupe GM brings personalised scent experience to hospitality
items.summary:
Groupe GM has announced an exclusive partnership with Compoz Paris, a French fragrance and wellbeing brand combining patented diffusion technology […] 
 The post  Groupe GM brings personalised scent experience to hospitality  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Groupe GM brings personalised scent experience to hospitality 10 November 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle Groupe GM has announced an exclusive partnership with Compoz Paris, a French fragrance and wellbeing brand combining patented diffusion technology with refined design. Together, the two companies are set to bring a new olfactory dimension to the hotel guest experience through an intuitive and refined approach to personalised scent. Through this partnership, Groupe GM will make Compoz Paris’ technology available to its international hospitality network across more than 80 countries, extending access to a distinctive in-room fragrance experience that moves beyond the traditional hotel signature scent and allows each guest to choose an atmosphere that suits their mood or moment. As travellers increasingly look for stays that feel more personal, immersive and attuned to their wellbeing, hotels are embracing new ways to further personalise and enrich the guest experience. By allowing guests to choose the scent atmosphere around them, Compoz Paris adds a more sensory dimension to the stay, creating moments of comfort, relaxation and escape that can be tailored to each individual. Founded by fragrance and innovation enthusiasts Aymeric Wuidart, David Lopez Bonet and Xavier Pourcines, Compoz Paris was launched in response to five years of research and development around how fragrance can be created, personalised and experienced. The brand developed patented technology enabling the real-time blending and diffusion of fragrance composition in one click, bringing together olfactory expertise, digital innovation and intuitive use. Inspired by the natural movement of scent through the air, Compoz Paris technology releases fragrance molecules without heat, water, alcohol or combustion, creating a clean and refined olfactory experience with no lingering scent once diffusion has stopped. Compoz Paris built its original olfactory repertoire around natural-origin essential oils sourced from renowned producing regions around the world, including ylang-ylang from the Comoros, jasmine from Egypt, patchouli from Indonesia, lavender from Provence or bergamot from Calabria. The brand’s collaboration with Groupe GM centres around Le Compositeur, Compoz Paris’ connected fragrance diffuser powered by patented real-time blending technology. The system works with a curated set of five fragrance capsules: Verbena & Musk, Fig & Sandalwood, Jasmine & Neroli, Incense & Spices and Amber & Chai. The experience is designed to be effortless for both guests and hotel teams. Once the set of five capsules is inserted, Le Compositeur is ready to use. Guests simply browse the available scent experiences on the integrated touchscreen and select the atmosphere they prefer. The system automatically blends the capsules to recreate and diffuse one of ten distinctive scent ambiances, from the fresh and uplifting Mist of Sun to the woody warmth and comfort of By the Fireplace or the aromatic escape of Nature Detox. Unlike conventional room fragrance systems that can leave a lingering scent in the air, Le Compositeur is designed for fragrance diffusion without remanence. Guests can enjoy the atmosphere they choose during their stay without imposing the same fragrance on the next guest, making scent a more personal and flexible part of the experience. Its plug-and-play format requires no complex set-up, making it straightforward for hotel teams to introduce into the guest room and intuitive for guests to use throughout their stay. Le Compositeur has been conceived not only as a fragrance diffusion device, but also as an interior object. Elegant, sculptural and carefully designed, it blends naturally into refined hotel interiors rather than appearing as a technical device. Designed by Alnoor Mitha de Bharat, it is available in lacquered, natural wood and leather finishes to complement different interior styles, with bespoke finishes also available for more customised projects. Le Compositeur can be used across hotel rooms and suites, spas, and meeting rooms, with optimal fragrance diffusion indicated for enclosed spaces from approximately 5 m² to 70 m². The exclusive partnership also brings together Groupe GM and Compoz Paris’ shared consideration for product design, sourcing and resource use. Groupe GM’s long-standing commitment to responsible hospitality through its Care About Earth programme aligns closely with Compoz’s sustainability-focused approach. The brand exclusively uses essential oils of natural origin and supports responsible sourcing practices designed to protect both communities and ecosystems. In addition, used Compoz capsules are recovered and processed through the company’s Natucare programme, allowing approximately 80% of materials to be reused in manufacturing while ensuring the remainder is fully recycled. “Our partnership with Compoz Paris opens a new olfactory dimension within the hotel guest experience,” says Laurent Marchand, President of Groupe GM. “By combining Compoz’s patented fragrance technology and refined French design with Groupe GM’s hospitality expertise and international network, we can offer hotels a genuinely distinctive way to personalise the in-room experience. Guests can choose the scent atmosphere that suits their mood or moment, while hotels benefit from a solution designed to integrate naturally into their guest offering.” Aymeric Wuidart, CEO of Compoz Paris, adds: “When we created Compoz Paris, our ambition was to provide each client with the scents they love, in a fully personalised and natural way. We soon understood that hospitality specialists were looking into enhancing the guest experience and wellness. Today, Groupe GM’s hospitality expertise and international reach gives us a unique opportunity to bring that vision to life providing all hotels around the world with a scent solution that is intuitive for both guests and hotel teams.” www.groupegm.com bespoke scent compoz pari

Originally designed by one of Greece’s leading architects, Periklis Sakellarios, and now reimagined by Berlin-based studio Vision Alphabet, the 60-key hotel’s architectural character has been preserved through a sensitive restoration with Casa Cook’s distinctive, understated design, and will open a further 45 rooms its second stage. The launch of Cook’s Club Kassandra marks the next evolution of the brand, introducing its first property on the Greek mainland, alongside a new creative direction. Scheduled to open in Summer 2027 among the pine-covered hills of Kriopigi on Halkidiki’s western peninsula, the adults-only property resembles a relaxed, private summer house centred around the main pool and pool bar area. The Boathouse, an open kitchen and restaurant, offers locally sourced dishes, the spa and outdoor gym are accompanied by yoga platform and the landscaped gardens provide social areas for extended relaxation. Art plays a heightened role with contemporary pieces and large murals displayed throughout the hotel, and a collaboration with Brazilian artist Luciano Cian marks the beginning of a wider series of creative partnerships, from original works and live murals to occasional artist residencies. Spanos, CEO of Domes Resorts and Chairman of Casa Collective. “These three openings in hotels we own showcase how much we believe in the soul and the character of these brands.” Remo Masala, Founder of Casa Collective and Vision Alphabet, adds: “As Casa Collective grows, we’re building on our deeper understanding of our guests to create meaningful reasons to return, with experiences that respect the individual character of each brand and destination.” casa collective Casa Cook Domes Resorts europe expansion Greece Related Posts 24 January 2025 Casa Cook to launch first mountain retreat 29 March 2023 Domes announces further Greek expansion 6 December 2021 Domes Resorts to expand internationally

items.title: Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings
items.summary:
As rising temperatures and energy costs place greater pressure on hospitality operators, Magnovent CEO Jonathan Jover explores how intelligent airflow […] 
 The post  Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings 5 November 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle As rising temperatures and energy costs place greater pressure on hospitality operators, Magnovent CEO Jonathan Jover explores how intelligent airflow and bioclimatic design can improve guest comfort while reducing energy consumption. How are changing guest expectations reshaping environmental comfort in hospitality? Rising temperatures and increasingly demanding guest expectations are making thermal comfort a strategic priority for hospitality operators. At the same time, rising energy costs are putting pressure on operating margins. The challenge is to create consistently comfortable environments without allowing energy consumption to escalate. This requires a more intelligent approach to managing temperature, airflow and insulation. What is bioclimatic architecture, and why is it so important for hotels and residences? Bioclimatic architecture considers the relationship between a building, its local climate and the people who use it. In hospitality, this means combining effective insulation, natural or mechanical ventilation and efficient heating and cooling systems to reduce reliance on air conditioning. By designing for climate from the outset, hotels can improve thermal comfort, reduce energy demand and create spaces that feel naturally comfortable while preserving their architectural identity. How can climate and airflow enhance the guest experience? Comfort is not determined by air temperature alone. Air movement influences how the body perceives heat, allowing guests to feel comfortable at higher thermostat settings. By combining air conditioning with well-designed ventilation, hotels can create a more balanced and pleasant indoor climate, while reducing energy consumption. The result is an environment that feels better, operates more efficiently and supports a more enjoyable guest experience. How do your solutions help hotels reduce energy use without compromising comfort? The key is to move beyond the assumption that lower temperatures automatically mean greater comfort. Setting air conditioning to 20°C, for example, can significantly increase energy consumption without necessarily delivering a better guest experience. By combining efficient ceiling fans with air conditioning, hotels can maintain comfort at higher thermostat settings and reduce cooling energy consumption. Based on results reported by our clients, this approach can deliver energy savings of 30–45%, depending on the building, climate and operating conditions. Our objective is to make comfort measurable, efficient and easier to manage. Can you share a hospitality project that demonstrates the impact of your approach? One Ibiza Suites is a good example of how a considered combination of building performance and airflow can transform the guest experience. By improving roof insulation and introducing ceiling fans in the lobby and restaurant, the hotel enhanced thermal comfort in key shared spaces. The combined intervention achieved a reduction in perceived temperature of approximately 4°C, demonstrating that comfort can be improved without relying exclusively on more intensive air conditioning. What’s next for Magnovent? Our next step is to help hospitality operators reduce their reliance on air conditioning, in both summer and winter, with a target of reducing energy consumption by an average of 30%. Through increasingly sophisticated control systems, we aim to manage airflow, heating and cooling as an integrated solution, helping operators maintain their desired level of perceived comfort while optimising energy use. Ultimately, we want to move the industry towards a more intelligent understanding of temperature: one in which buildings are designed and operated around how people actually experience comfort, rather than simply the number displayed on a thermostat. www.magnovent.eu air conditioning bioclimatic design climate change guest comfort magnovent Related Posts 19 September 2023 Inside FOH’s luxury hospitality solutions 22 June 2023 Madera talks timber, bespoke design and hospitality interiors 5 December 2019 Cameron Design House’s Inari chandelier designed for hospitality settings

items.title: Thompson Hotels lands in Rome
items.summary:
Hyatt has announced the opening of Thompson Rome, a 69-room hotel owned and operated by AG Group and Rossifin Group, […] 
 The post  Thompson Hotels lands in Rome  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Hyatt has announced the opening of Thompson Rome, a 69-room hotel owned and operated by AG Group and Rossifin Group, marking the brand’s debut in Italy . Set within a reimagined iconic landmark on Via delle Botteghe Oscure, Thompson Rome draws on the architectural character of its 1940s home and the layered history of Via delle Botteghe Oscure, one of Rome’s most significant streets and a landmark in post-war Italian political history. Original elements, including a sweeping marble staircase, have been carefully restored, while a sculptural wall and inlaid floor by celebrated Italian artist Gio Pomodoro, rediscovered during the renovation after decades hidden from view – have been preserved and given new prominence within the hotel. Bespoke furnishings, refined detailing and layered natural materials bring a contemporary expression to the building’s history. Thompson Rome’s 69 guestrooms and suites take cues from the character of a contemporary Roman residence, pairing warm natural materials with custom furnishings and understated details. With 19 suites, nearly one-third of the hotel’s accommodation offering, guests can choose from Junior Suites, Suites with patios or terraces, and the 104-square-metre Thompson Suite with 80-square-metre private terrace. Designed as a counterpoint to the energy of the city outside, the rooms feel residential and refined, with select accommodations offering views across Rome’s historic rooftops and landmarks. Several rooms feature balconies overlooking Via delle Botteghe Oscure, while select rooms offer private patios facing Rome’s historic buildings. Thompson Rome’s art programme, creates a dialogue between the history of the site and contemporary art. The collection brings together works by artists associated with the Scuola Romana and the Scuola di Piazza del Popolo, alongside contemporary artists whose practices reflect Rome’s longstanding cultural openness and international influences including Francesco Del Drago, Giangaetano Patanè, and Guido Strazza. Presented throughout the hotel’s public spaces and guestrooms, the artworks are an integral part of the guest experience, connecting the memory of the site with the creativity of Rome today. A rotating artist-in-residence programme will further extend Thompson Rome’s connection to the city’s creative community through exhibitions, conversations and other cultural programming. Three distinct food and beverage venues carry Thompson Rome from morning espresso and leisurely lunches through aperitivo, dinner and drinks above the city. At Lyve Restaurant, Executive Chef Fabio Fioravanti brings a contemporary Mediterranean approach to ingredients and traditions from the Italian coast and across the region. Seafood is central to the menu, with Mediterranean fish and shellfish alongside dishes that draw on bouillabaisse, rockfish broths, wild coastal herbs and rouille, reworked with a lighter touch while preserving the depth and character of the originals. The same attention extends to the pastry kitchen, where precise technique and contrasting flavours and textures shape the dessert menu. A native of Ostia, Fioravanti brings more than two decades of international experience, including time with the Alain Ducasse group and at the three-Michelin-starred Le Louis XV – Alain Ducasse at the Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo. At Lyve, that technical precision carries through a dining experience that is refined yet relaxed, with the quality of the ingredients and clarity of the cooking taking centre stage. Above the hotel, Lyve Rooftop pairs views across Rome with cocktails, Italian aperitivi and a menu designed for sharing. The Lobby Lounge offers the hotel’s most casual gathering place throughout the day, from coffee and light fare to aperitivo and cocktails. The hotel will extend the guest experience through a year-round programme shaped by Rome’s culinary, artistic and creative communities. Experiences will range from culinary workshops and guided tastings to Empire of Light, a photography-led experience from the hotel’s seventh floor that invites guests to discover Rome from above. “Rome has such a strong identity, so we wanted Thompson Rome to start with the city itself,” says Amar Lalvani, Chief Creative Officer, Hyatt Corporation and President & Creative Director, The Lifestyle Group, Hyatt . “The building, the neighbourhood, the food, the people and the way Romans live all shaped the hotel. The goal was to create a Thompson hotel that feels at home in Rome, a hotel travellers want to discover and Romans want to come back to.” architecture europe hotel design hyatt interior design italy rome thompson hotels Related Posts 14 June 2023 Thompson Hotels heading to Rome 21 February 2022 Design Hotels welcomes four new members 9 August 2021 Thompson Hotels arrives in Savannah

items.title: Minor Hotels announces first Minor Reserve Collection in Asia
items.summary:
Minor Hotels has announced the signing of a hotel management agreement with Amal Group of Companies to launch Gardens of […] 
 The post  Minor Hotels announces first Minor Reserve Collection in Asia  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Minor Hotels has announced the signing of a hotel management agreement with Amal Group of Companies to launch Gardens of Eden Resort Phuket, Minor Reserve Collection. Scheduled to open in 2031, the 310-key resort will be located in Bang Tao, Phuket, marking the first property under the new luxury collection brand in Asia. The newly built property will form the hospitality centrepiece of the broader Gardens of Eden development, a 33-acre integrated luxury living and wellness destination that will also feature Etro Residences and Gardens of Eden Residences. Gardens of Eden Resort Phuket, Minor Reserve Collection will comprise a 100-key hotel and 210 one-, two- and three-bedroom residences operated as part of the resort inventory. Wellness will be a defining element of the guest experience, centred around a dedicated facility spanning more than 5,000m 2 . Dining venues are planned to include an all-day dining restaurant, two speciality restaurants, an organic café and a lobby lounge. Designed by Martin Palleros of Tierra Design, the project will reflect the natural setting of Bang Tao while delivering the distinctive character, personalised service and elevated experiences that define the Minor Reserve Collection. “Thailand is home for Minor Hotels, so introducing the new Gardens of Eden Phuket, Minor Reserve Collection to the kingdom is a significant milestone for our company and our luxury brand strategy,” says Omar Romero, Chief Development & Luxury Officer, Minor Hotels. “Phuket continues to evolve as one of the world’s most compelling resort and wellness destinations, and we are pleased to partner with Amal Group of Companies to bring this exceptional project to life.” Alexander Chuvalov, CEO, Gardens of Eden, adds: “Gardens of Eden has been conceived as a destination where luxury living, wellness and nature come together in a meaningful way. As the project enters this next phase, we are delighted to partner with Minor Hotels to introduce the first Minor Reserve Collection property in Asia. Phuket remains one of the world’s most attractive resort markets, and we believe the combination of Minor Hotels’ luxury hospitality expertise and the strength of the Gardens of Eden vision will create a distinctive offering for both international travellers and residents.” bang tao minor hotels minor reserve collection Phuket resort thailand Related Posts 7 July 2026 Shurooq appoints Minor Hotels to manage Sharjah Collection 20 April 2026 Minor Hotels to debut Colbert Collection in London 18 March 2022 Minor Hotels to bring NH Collection to Asia in 2023

items.title: Capella to open at Dubai Peninsula in 2030
items.summary:
Capella Hotel Group has announced Capella Dubai, set to open in 2030 on the Dubai Peninsula in Dubai, United Arab […] 
 The post  Capella to open at Dubai Peninsula in 2030  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Capella Hotel Group has announced Capella Dubai, set to open in 2030 on the Dubai Peninsula in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. The 115-key hotel will include a collection of suites with private pools, culminating in a 600m 2 Capella Suite conceived as a residential-style retreat. Set along one of Jumeirah’s most desired shorelines, Capella Dubai will open within the 210-acre waterfront destination by H&H. Conceived as a first-of-its-kind, design-driven destination, the Dubai Peninsula brings together hotel brands and private residences, complemented by dining, retail, a superyacht marina, a kilometre of private beach and over two million square feet of botanical gardens. Developed by H&H and designed by Denniston , the hotel will feature five social venues from the lobby lounge and The Living Room to the signature restaurant. Above it all, the rooftop will be home to a specialty restaurant and destination bar, inviting guests to dine against the Dubai skyline. Stretching nearly 70m across the rooftop, the pool will offer a tranquil retreat above the city, alongside single and double cabanas. A family pool will also feature at beach level. Capella Wellness will offer a holistic approach to wellbeing, encompassing the Auriga Spa, a Fitness Centre and Mind Body Studio, as well as an outdoor fitness area. Inspired by the restorative rhythms of the moon, Auriga Spa will feature male and female treatment rooms, a co-ed suite and VIP suite, alongside a hammam, hydrotherapy circuit pool, two biohacking facilities and grooming services. Dedicated relaxation lounges will offer quiet spaces to pause before and after treatments. For celebrations and gatherings, Capella Dubai will offer a spacious ballroom with a pre-function lounge, complemented by two meeting rooms, a VIP Majlis and an outdoor event lawn. “As Capella grows beyond Asia Pacific into the Middle East and Europe, we are entering an important new chapter for the brand,” says Roland Fasel, President, Capella Hotel Group. “The Middle East shares our appreciation for craftsmanship, culture and exceptional service, making it a natural home for Capella. Capella has always been deliberately selective about where it goes, choosing destinations where we believe we can create something meaningful and distinctive. “At Dubai Peninsula, our partnership with H&H is the foundation for all that we are building. They share our vision for the intimate, highly personalised experience Capella is known for, one that connects guests more deeply with Dubai, its culture and its people. With the opening of Capella Dubai in 2030, we will further establish our presence in one of the region’s most compelling cities, while remaining true to the hospitality that defines Capella.” Shahab Lutfi, Chairman, H&H adds: “Dubai Peninsula is conceived as a destination with a distinct identity, bringing together some of the world’s most renowned hospitality brands, exceptional residences and a unique waterfront setting. Capella brings a different dimension to this vision through its intimate, highly personalised approach to hospitality. We see a strong alignment between Capella’s emphasis on individual experiences and sense of place and our ambition to create a destination that offers more than exceptional design and location. Capella Dubai will introduce a more intimate, service-led hospitality experience to the city’s resort landscape, adding depth and character to the overall offering. “Working alongside Denniston, we are bringing hospitality, architecture and landscape together from the outset, ensuring that each responds to the setting and contributes to a coherent vision. For us, the strength of Dubai Peninsula lies in the way its different elements come together, from its shoreline and central park to its collection of hospitality and residential offerings. Capella’s distinctive character will be an important part of that mix, shaping a destination that feels considered, cohesive and different.” capella capella dubai Denniston dubai dubai peninsula H&H Jumeirah Related Posts 27 August 2025 Mandarin Oriental to open second Dubai outpost 11 October 2024 Ennismore’s Delano lands in Dubai 9 December 2009 Dusit Princess debuts in Dubai
