items.text: Chater Paul Jordan 17 September 2026 Fifteen leading architects and designers met last week to decide the winners of Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble , which will be revealed at the Dezeen Awards 2026 party in November. The master jury took place at the One Hundred Shoreditch hotel in London and included architects Ma Yansong and Daniel Libeskind as well as interior designers Wendy Saunders and Jaime Hayon . Designers Martin Lotti and Jo Barnard , as well as architects Dominique Petit-Frère and Aziza Chaouni also joined to determine the 49 winning projects, ahead of next week’s shortlist announcements between 21-23 September. Winners announced at the Royal Opera House All this year’s winners will be announced at the Dezeen Awards 2026 party which takes place at the Royal Opera House in London on 16 November. Guests at the party will be the first to find out who has won the prestigious project of the year awards across architecture, interiors and design. Tickets are available to purchase here . Also unveiled at the ceremony will be the six winners of this year’s Designers of the Year, who have each been shortlisted and selected by Dezeen’s editorial team. The Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design. “Designers thinking more critically about context” The master jury discussed 392 shortlisted entries selected from over 4,300 projects in 91 countries around the globe. Architectural designer John Cummins joined the architecture master jury panel which comprised architects Yansong , Libeskind , Chaouni and Petit-Frère . Speaking to Dezeen, Petit-Frère observed how “this year’s projects reflect a generation of designers thinking more critically about context, materiality, technology, and the social impact of what they create”. Top image: (from left to right) John Cummins, Dominique Petit-Frère, Daniel Libeskind, Ma Yansong and Aziza Chaouni. Above: (from left to right) Wendy Saunders, Jaime Hayon, Smita Thomas, Benni Allan and Julien Sebban at the master jury day at One Hundred Shoreditch Hayon and Saunders were joined on the interiors master jury panel by Benni Allan , Julien Sebban and Bangalore-based Smita Thomas . Thomas was also struck by the depth of this year’s entries, which she saw as imbued with a sense of purpose rather than being solely aesthetic exercises. “There were a number of projects that felt more like statements of intent than displays of style,” she said. “It charged me to see design beginning to shapeshift toward strengthening human connection in a time when we need it most,” Thomas continued. Parisian designer Sebban noted the “presence of so many young and emerging studios experimenting with new materials and new ways of thinking”. “The next generation is asking better questions, not just creating better answers” Lotti and Barnard were alongside Michael Anastassiades , Min Chen and Alexie Sommer to decide the winners of the design categories. Lotti, chief design officer at sportswear brand Nike , remarked that “the strongest projects weren’t simply beautiful – they were purposeful, distinct and challenging the status quo”. “What struck me most was the range of thinking behind it. I came away feeling that the next generation is asking better questions, not just creating better answers,” he continued. (From left to right) Alexie Sommer, Min Chen, Michael Anastassiades, Jo Barnard and Martin Lotti at the master jury day in London Following the day of judging, an exclusive drinks reception and dinner took place in the One Hundred Room at One Hundred Shoreditch, where the master jury was joined by fellow 2026 judges Zandra Rhodes and Miminat Shodeinde . Designers Paul Cocksedge , Ron Arad and Sebastian Cox also joined to celebrate the day’s conclusion. Following the shortlist announcements next week, the Dezeen Awards 2026 public vote will open and readers will be asked to vote for their favourite shortlisted projects. We will announce the public vote winners on Dezeen and across our social media channels ahead of the Dezeen Awards party on 16 November. Zandra Rhodes and Paul Cocksedge joined for the celebratory dinner at One Hundred Shoreditch. Photo by Olivia Chenery Tickets for the Dezeen Awards 2026 party are on sale. The occasion is an opportunity to celebrate with fellow nominees and VIPs, connect with others from around the world and reward your team for their hard work. Studios that have been shortlisted for this year’s Dezeen Awards will be eligible to purchase discounted tickets for £249. These tickets will be released on 21 September, alongside the shortlist announcements. Subscribe to the Dezeen Awards newsletter to keep up to date with the latest announcements on the party. items.text: Chater Paul Jordan 1 June 2026 British architect Norman Foster is the latest industry leader to be announced as a member of the judging panel for Dezeen Awards 2026 . Dezeen Awards, in partnership with Trimble , is searching for the world’s best architecture, interiors and design. The search finally concludes this coming Wednesday, 3 June at 23:59 London time – there will be no extension to the deadline . Read on for more as “the most successful architect in history” joins this year’s panel. Foster to judge Dezeen Awards 2026 Foster, whose career spans nearly six decades, is renowned as one of the industry’s most prolific names. He leads international studio Foster + Partners, which he founded in 1967, and is behind some of the most notable projects in the world. The architect’s oeuvre reflects his impact as a pioneer and proponent of high-tech architecture . Norman Foster will judge Dezeen Awards 2026 Landmark projects include the HSBC Building in Hong Kong , London Stansted Airport and Apple Park, USA . In an interview with Dezeen, Foster expanded on the importance of “architecture without architects” , advocating for the lessons the industry can take from using buildings constructed with local materials and with passive design strategies. Last year, on the eve of his 90th birthday, Dezeen explored how the Manchester-born architect grew to become the most successful architect in history , speaking to former colleagues and industry peers – including Foster himself. Still highly prolific, he remains at the helm of the global architectural powerhouse as executive chairman, while also serving as president of the Norman Foster Foundation – an initiative that promotes interdisciplinary thinking and research to help new generations of architects, designers and urbanists anticipate the future. Recent projects by Foster + Partners include an art gallery wrapped in with ribbed glass facades , a supertall skyscraper in Manhattan and a museum signalled by soaring ventilation towers modelled on the wings of a falcon . Other projects include a bespoke time capsule created to mark the USA’s 250th anniversary of independence . It will be buried under the plaza at Washington Monument and is destined to be reopened on 4th July 2276 for the USA ‘s 500th Independence Day. Foster is the latest judge to be announced as part of this year’s Dezeen Awards judging panel. He will join the architecture panel alongside Daniel Libeskind , Massimiliano Fuksas and Amanda Levete as well as Malini Doshi , Dominique Petit-Frère and Annabelle Selldorf . Khalil aims to merge beauty, cultural resonance and human connection in her work, creating spaces that feel both elevated and deeply connected. Kulapat Yantrasast will join the Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture jury Joining Johnston on this year’s architecture jury is architect Yantrasast, founder of Los Angeles -based WHY Architecture . Yantrasast is known for his work on projects in the cultural realm, designing spaces that focus on the human impact of the arts. Landmark projects include an overhaul of the Michael C Rockefeller Wing at The Met , an “immersive” tent for the first Frieze Los Angeles and a museum expansion featuring a corrugated metal facade . The architect is also a board member of the Pulitzer Arts Foundation and the Noguchi Museum in New York and serves as principal architect for New Delhi’s Yuge Yugeen Bharat national museum. Ben Cross will judge this year’s architecture entries Cross, co-founder of London -based development management and advisory firm More, will join Johnston and Yantrasast on the architecture jury. At More, Cross aims to bring a design-led approach to real estate with a focus on commercial refurbishments across central London. The architect has worked across some of the UK’s most well-known commercial buildings, including No 1 Poultry , the Heal’s Building and 50 George Street. Alexie Sommer will join the Dezeen Awards 2026 design jury Sommer, a designer and communication expert who focuses on business sustainability, will judge this year’s design entries. Sommer is co-founder of Urge Collective , a climate-focused brand consultancy that helps businesses and leaders drive sustainability agendas. She also organised the Design Declares initiative, a campaign to help UK designers tackle their environmental footprint. Writing for Dezeen, Sommer argued that declaring a climate emergency is “just the beginning of the journey” . Entries close next week! There is less than one week left to enter Dezeen Awards 2026. Creating an entry is easy! Simply create an account or log in via our entry platform, answer five simple questions and upload your best project imagery. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble . Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe. Read more Dezeen Awards

November 13 A new sibling-run Brooklyn restaurant Sisters Emily Swaine and Hannah Swaine are opening their Williamsburg Italian neighborhood restaurant this month. Swaine’s is opening on Wednesday, November 18 at 577 Lorimer Street, near Metropolitan Avenue. Emily (who had been the executive chef of Forsythia, a sous chef at Maialino, and worked at Blue Hill at Stone Barns) is dishing up an evening menu of dishes including pizzettes with toppings like clams, parsley, and chile or marinara, sliced garlic, and oregano; pasta like bucatini with royal red shrimp; and roasted vegetables like charred cabbage with green tahini and pistachio. For drinks, look for natural wines and cocktails such as the fig leaf sour and dessert-sounding Nonna’s Chocolate Milk. Hannah is running the operations. Book reservations on Resy . The restaurant will start with dinner service from 5 to 11 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday. — Nadia Chaudhury A Chinatown Hong Kong cafe handover happens soon Longtime Chinatown cha chaan teng M Star set its final day of service for New Year’s Eve on Thursday, December 31, per Flushing Foodie . But don’t worry, the address is going into good hands thanks to chef Lucas Sin . The chef has been operating his hot pop-up Lok Kee this year, and he’s taking over the space to turn it into his very own Hong Kong cafe in early 2027 . Are you one of the lucky ones who snagged reservations for the select December pop-up dates? — NC Briefly shuttered Japanese omurice pop-up is back The Dearbros omurice pop-up is back open after what turns out to be a pause , starting on Monday, November 9, at 5 p.m. at its temporary location at Midtown Japanese cafe BentOn on 156 E. 45th Street, near Third Avenue. Originally, the team had opened in October and had to close nine days later because the team got overwhelmed with guests. They’re looking to open a permanent New York City location too. — NC Everyone wants to all-you-can-eat now In an about-face from the pandemic era, people are on the prowl for all-you-can-eat (AYCE) restaurants, with the Wall Street Journal reporting an over 200 percent jump in searches from last year. The outlet rounds up national options for AYCE, from Fogo de Chão to K-Pot Korean BBQ restaurants. Looks like Crown Heights Portuguese bakery Lisbonata is opening a spinoff location focused on its soft serve , Sofi , in the West Village, at 31 Carmine Street, between Bedford and Bleecker streets. Eater has reached out for more information. — NC Why a chef left a hyped art museum restaurant The New Museum’s new restaurant Oberon opened in July on the Lower East Side, by the Oberon Group (which runs places like Rhodora , June , and Rucola ) with co-executive chefs artist Julia Sherman and Ali Ghriskey. Falco started making dough at Roberta’s in Bushwick when it opened in 2008; for at least a decade, he has consulted for pizzerias […]
items.text: NYC Restaurant Openings A Pizza Czar Finally Opens His Own Brooklyn Spot Former Roberta’s pizzaiolo Anthony Falco will roll out Pizzeria the Pantheon Bar in Williamsburg next week by Melissa McCart Nov 13, 2026, 5:07 PM UTC Facebook Link Pizzeria the Pantheon Bar Melissa McCart is the lead editor of the Northeast region with more than 20 years of experience as a reporter, critic, editor, and cookbook author. Facebook Link Anthony Falco, the pizzaiolo who helped make Roberta’s a breakout pizza destination, opens Pizzeria the Pantheon Bar on Friday, November 20, at 276 Grand Street, between Roebling and Havemeyer streets, in Williamsburg. Falco started making dough at Roberta’s in Bushwick when it opened in 2008; for at least a decade, he has consulted for pizzerias around the world. Now he and his business partner, Roberta’s front-of-house alum Mateo Vivas, own the restaurant outright. The name comes from Alejandro Jodorowsky’s 1973 film The Holy Mountain , in which seekers on the road to enlightenment are distracted by a place called the Pantheon Bar. “Psychedelic influences have been a really big part of my life,” Falco tells Eater. It’s also a nod to the Pantheon in Rome, where Queen Margherita, the namesake of the margherita pizza, is buried, Grub Street reported . Pizzas will cost in the $20s range. “We don’t want people talking about the price,” Falco says. “There are no $40 pizzas.” The opening lineup includes a sour-cream-and-onion pie with Vermont creme fraiche and onions and chives from the Greenmarket. When Eater visited, Falco was developing a mushroom pizza. The dough is made with Cairnspring Mills flour from the Pacific Northwest and leavened with Falco’s 10-year-old sourdough starter, which he has carried around the world and which now lives in a temperature-controlled dough room in the rather large basement prep kitchen. Mozzarella is stretched to order, from BelGioioso curd and, occasionally, from Caputo Brothers, at a station with a hot-water dispenser set to 200, 190, and 188 degrees Fahrenheit. It will be served with a fashionably grassy olive oil from the first pressing of the season, which Falco’s cousin is shipping from Italy. “He was like, ‘Are you sure you want this? It’s a little strong for most people,’” Falco tells Eater. Focaccia at Pizzeria the Pantheon Bar. Melissa McCart Focaccia will be sold by the slice or whole, filled with items like mortadella, salami rosa, or cherry tomatoes and olives. A double induction burner will allow the restaurant to serve sides like beans and greens. Pizzas bake in a three-deck Moretti electric oven, similar to the kind Falco has installed in pizzerias from Mongolia to India. Falco is also inviting collaborators from abroad to bake with him, starting with a Turkish pizza collaboration with Defne and Emre Kasrat of Gusina in Istanbul. They will be in the kitchen on Wednesday, November 25, to launch the pie, which will stay on the menu for a month. Brent Young of the Meat Hook is smoking a rib-eye rubbed with Turkish thyme and Aleppo pepper. The beef will be shaved thin over mozzarella and onions and finished with pomegranate molasses. “It’s been their number one seller since I consulted on that space,” Falco says. The bar pours Italian-leaning wines, and Vivas plans to serve cocktails like smoked-tomato Negronis and guanciale-washed martinis, alongside sparkling waters such as Spain’s salty Vichy Catalan and Ferrarelle from Campania in 1.5-liter bottles, Grub Street reported. The room feels like a Roman pizzeria: terrazzo floors, wainscoting, caned chairs, and a long bar. The space had been a crystal shop with concrete floors and cinder blocks when Falco and Vivas found it. They spotted the for-lease sign while waiting in line for I Cavallini down the block. “I’ve been looking at spaces for 10 years,” Falco, who has lived in Williamsburg for nearly two decades, says. The centerpiece is a solid oak bar, at least 60 years old, that their builder found at a tortilla company in Bushwick; it was disassembled and rebuilt here. The first painting on the wall is of a Roman sculpture by an artist in his 90s who lives in a retirement home on Powers Street. There’s also a colored-pencil piece of a pizza slice by Australian artist Bella McCormick and a photo of Vivas’s wife’s grandparents making zeppole at New York’s Feast of San Gennaro. The kitchen is built for Falco’s workflow. He mocked up the pizza station in cardboard at home and had it designed in Detroit. A steel fabricator around the corner from his apartment built the rest. The backyard patio with a tree that frames the back of the restaurant is phase two. Pizzeria the Pantheon Bar is open Wednesday through Sunday, 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. It’s walk-in only for now. Melissa McCart Pizzeria the Pantheon Bar 276 Grand Street, Brooklyn, New York 11211, United States Link https://www.instagram.com/pantheonpizzeria/ See More : NYC Restaurant Openings

items.text: Dining Reports The Lower East Side’s Most Interesting New Restaurant Is a Love Letter to Cassava ﻿It’s already a tough reservation, but a meal at Vitor Mendes’s Iara is worth the effort by Bettina Makalintal Nov 12, 2026, 8:11 PM UTC Facebook Link The picanha con frita at Iara. Bettina Makalintal Bettina Makalintal is a senior reporter at Eater.com, covering restaurant trends and all the food you can’t escape on your TikTok FYP. Previously, she worked for Bon Appétit and VICE’s Munchies. In our Dining Reports, we share a firsthand perspective of a recent restaurant visit, covering everything from the vibe to must-get dishes. See more in the Eater app. Download the app Isn’t it refreshing when you find a restaurant that actually feels like it has a new perspective? That’s the case at Iara , which opened in October from chef Vitor Mendes, an alum of the ever-popular Theodora . Like Theodora, Iara emphasizes its use of live fire, on display through the restaurant’s open kitchen, where chefs wrangle steaks and huge slabs of fish. What truly sets Iara apart is its emphasis on Amazonian ingredients: Mendes cites a trip to Brazil after his father’s death as inspiration. Here, you’ll find the seed puxuri (also known as Brazilian nutmeg) and the fruit cupuaçu (a relative of cacao). Nothing features as prominently as cassava. The tuber appears in the form of bouncy tapioca-based bread, tapioca pearls on desserts, cassava crisps beneath delicate slices of scallop, and as tucupi, fermented cassava juice that’s employed at Iara in ceviche and martinis. (Naturally, it also decorates the dining room.) Iara is already a tough reservation, but even this early into its tenure, a meal there is worth the effort, especially for a special occasion. What to order The pão de queijo ($14), small balls of cheese bread, feel essential at a Brazilian restaurant. Made with cassava, these have a mochi-like squishiness, but the order is as much about the sauces as the bread — the inky charred-eggplant dip in particular is a standout. (Save some of it for the fries, if you get them.) The dadinho de tapioca ($16) is pricey for small bites, but they exemplify what makes Iara interesting. The tapioca is crispy and warm, and the toppings offer an exhilarating interplay of sensations. The piece of lean tuna atop is chilled. Then, the bud of jambu, an herb, offers a citric zap similar to Sichuan peppercorns. The moqueca ($48), a fish stew with a coconut broth, is comforting, especially as the weather cools. The rice that comes alongside it is grown in the Hudson Valley and topped with a trio of sauces (one spicy, one herby, and one creamy), plus a sprinkle of farofa (coarse, toasted cassava) for texture. (Think of it like what toasted rice powder adds to larb.) The toppings keep each bite of rice and stew interesting and novel. The picanha con fritas ($68) is technically yet another take on steak frites, but it’s worth a spot on the table, if just to get a taste of the live-fire cooking. Even here, the restaurant makes fun choices. The very long fries are made out of tapioca for a juxtaposition of chewy and crispy. Açaí lends a berry-like note to the ketchup on the side. The desserts are all hits, though I found the sorvete ($12) refreshing after the large meal. It’s made with cupuaçu, which has a milky and lightly tart flavor similar to soursop. That’s finished with small tapioca pearls and sweet farofa, finer this time. The moqueca at Iara. Bettina Makalintal Best for The restaurant is great for anyone who feels jaded by all the same-y restaurants on their roster and wants to try something with ingredients they’ve likely encountered less often in NYC. It’s also fun for pairs who don’t mind splitting everything and want a show with their dinner (make sure to get seats at the chef’s counter). Diners who are tired of limited gluten-free options (or ones that feel like afterthoughts) will also appreciate the range here: By virtue of the restaurant’s focus on cassava, the vast majority of the menu is gluten-free. Much of it can also be made vegan. Insider tip Your server might offer the tambaqui special, featuring half of a large Amazonian river fish that’s grilled and presented with sides, intended to serve four. The quantity is very limited each night, given that the fish is sourced directly from Brazil — if it appeals to your group, act quickly, or email the restaurant ahead of time if you know you want it. items.title: Introducing New York’s 2026 Eater Award Winners
items.summary: This year’s New York City restaurant award winners have a point of view, and they’re sticking to it. Their menus tell a story about where the chefs grew up, who trained them, and how they like to cook. Some give a familiar kind of restaurant a fresh reason to exist; others bring together ingredients you […]
items.text: Dining Out in NY Introducing New York’s 2026 Eater Award Winners The Best New Restaurant, Best New Bakery, Dish of the Year, and more by Nat Belkov , Nadia Chaudhury , Bettina Makalintal , and Melissa McCart Nov 10, 2026, 3:00 PM UTC Facebook Link A spread of dishes from Somssi. | Cole Saladino /Eater NY Facebook Link This year’s New York City restaurant award winners have a point of view, and they’re sticking to it. Their menus tell a story about where the chefs grew up, who trained them, and how they like to cook. Some give a familiar kind of restaurant a fresh reason to exist; others bring together ingredients you might not expect to share a menu. These new restaurants also gave us reasons to keep going out in a year when everything got more expensive. Not every pick here is a bargain, but they’re generous in how you’re treated, what’s on the plate, and often what you’re paying for. These restaurants make dinner feel like a good use of time and money. In New York right now, that’s everything. Without further ado, here are the 2026 selections, and don’t miss the rest of the 2026 Eater Awards , presented by Capital One. Related Check out the map of New York’s 2026 Eater Award winners — and discover special dining perks with select restaurants The Potato Potato Potato at Somssi. Cole Saladino /Eater NY Best New Restaurant: Somssi Somssi , from Ahris Kim and chef Daniel Gronert, is one of the clearest examples in New York of a restaurant that goes all-in on personal history, rather than focusing on the broader food culture of any one country or a region. Korea-born Kim, who ran operations at Atomix , lived in Indonesia and the Philippines before moving to Wisconsin with her family. Gronert, who has German roots and spent time as a pitmaster in South Carolina, cooked across restaurants in Atomix’s parent company. Those influences show up in dishes like the caviar-crowned Potato Potato Potato, a crispy-soft tater tot simulacrum nested on miso hollandaise; ox tongue grilled and glazed with tare, a kaleidoscope of textures; and pork schnitzel presented like shrimp toast (it works). With the team’s fine dining pedigree, Somssi sets a high bar for hospitality, yet it’s still casual: The room is designed to feel like a home, and the menu nods to places Kim and Gronert have lived. The bar extends that expertise. Christian Gray’s cocktails include well-made minis, which the bartenders are game to explain to curious drinkers. Sommelier (and Punch contributor) Jenny Eagleton’s list of wines and sakes leans toward lesser-known areas. The duo and their staff reward handing your night over to them, whether you’re there with a group or alone with a Kindle. Personal touches carry through the space in gloriously analog fashion. Lace curtains on the door spell out the restaurant’s name in embroidery, and handprints line the bathroom wall, left by the broader constellation of people who helped build Somssi into the singular restaurant it is today. — Nadia Chaudhury , deputy editor, Eater New York Fried boca negra at Zoli. Zoli Chef of the Year: Ned Baldwin, Zoli Chef Ned Baldwin has spent more than a decade winning over diners at Houseman in Hudson Square: His restaurant has become the kind of neighborhood fixture any chef would wish to run. Among its regulars are contemporary art center founders, Lonti Ebers and her husband, Bruce Flatt, of Amant : The couple later recruited Baldwin to open Zoli , adjacent to their gallery, after watching him steer Houseman through thick and thin. It was a smart pick. Without fine dining fussiness, Baldwin glams up pole beans with a soy-pickling, he roasts okra for skewers, and he tucks Sungolds with romano beans to make a case for ordering well beyond the fish offerings he’s known for. Still, don’t skip the surf clams with avocado and serrano or the triggerfish with leeks — or really any seafood on the menu, particularly fish Baldwin has caught himself out East. Baldwin’s strength extends to the people cooking alongside him. A generous mentor, he brought Houseman pastry chef Nicole Sheets to Zoli to offer a bigger kitchen and better tools. His restaurant has become a next step for chefs who used to work at standouts like Frenchette, Wildair, and Estela. Baldwin’s achievement here is bigger than a handful of excellent dishes: With his team and his benefactors, he has built a compelling restaurant destination that gives his team room to grow. — Melissa McCart , dining editorial manager Lamb and rib-eye samosa, Saffron Shah, firni concha, and sheer pira. The pastries from Diljān traverse Afghanistan with some Latin American influences. Cole Saladino /Eater NY Best New Bakery: Diljān With Afghan influences and some Latin American flair, Diljān gives New Yorkers a bakery with a point of view and innumerable reasons to become a regular. Ali Zaman and Mohamed Ghiasi, owners of Astoria’s Little Flower Cafe, teamed up with Bryan Ford, Honduran American baker and cookbook author, to conceptualize the bakery, now perched on a corner near Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn Heights. Their combined talent makes for some of the city’s most compelling baked goods. For the Saffron Shah, laminated pastry holds delicate saffron cream in the shape of a crescent, an important Islamic symbol. Halwa tops the sticky bun, while a swirl of samosa pastry wraps halal lamb under a dusting of powdered sugar. Don’t miss the enormous Afghan flatbread crowned with toppings such as halal beef bacon with scallions or sour cherry cream cheese. The team has also branched into pizzas topped with cheese and Afghan cumin, kofta kebabs, or beef pepperoni. Look for specials like the flan with cardamom-poached apricots and conchas stuffed with firni, a rice pudding. — NC The $32 half bird at Badaboom. Henry Hargreaves/Eater Dish of the Year: Badaboom In 2026, one marriage took the food zeitgeist by storm: a holy union between the natural wine bar and roast chicken. The once-casual dinner has been made chic and, increasin

items.summary: It’s not every day that a popular Miami restaurant expands to the West Coast, what with the narrative of California’s difficult environment for conducting business and Los Angeles’s often Byzantine rules for opening a large-scale restaurant. But Kyu’s November 9 opening in Century City, tucked behind the historic Fairmont Century Plaza at the base of a […]
items.text: LA Restaurant News Miami’s Kyu Brings Wood-Fired Cooking and Significant Buzz to Century City Kyu joins the recently relocated Birdie G’s at the expansive Century Plaza project. by Matthew Kang Nov 13, 2026, 11:20 PM UTC Facebook Link The main dining room at Kyu Los Angeles in Century City. | Kyu Restaurants Matthew Kang is a correspondent for Eater. Previously, he was the lead editor of Eater’s Southern California/Southwest region. He has covered dining, restaurants, food culture, and nightlife in Los Angeles since 2008. Sign up for his weekly newsletter, Kangtown . It’s not every day that a popular Miami restaurant expands to the West Coast, what with the narrative of California’s difficult environment for conducting business and Los Angeles’s often Byzantine rules for opening a large-scale restaurant . But Kyu’s November 9 opening in Century City, tucked behind the historic Fairmont Century Plaza at the base of a two-skyscraper luxury residential project owned by billionaire developers David and Simon Reuben , makes sense for a restaurant chain with plans to expand globally. Kyu debuted in Miami in 2016 and opened inside Las Vegas’s Fontainebleau in December 2023. With a Nobu-style menu of approachable grilled dishes and an expansive, high-design interior, Kyu brings another compelling restaurant to Century City — which had been on the wane in recent years, following the closure of Craft . Things are turning, though, as just a few weeks ago, Jeremy Fox reopened Birdie G’s at the Fairmont Century Plaza, and noteworthy restaurants Sushi Noz from New York and vibey Greek seafood specialist Estiatorio Milos are slated to open next to Kyu in 2027. At Westfield Century City mall a few blocks away, Super Peach, Casa Dani, Katsuya, and Rumi’s Kitchen have expanded the shopping center’s already impressive restaurant set. Dining room at Kyu Los Angeles. Kyu Restaurants A typical meal at Kyu might start with fire-roasted shishitos with yuzu salt, or hamachi crudo with tomatillo ponzu salsa. Expect an izakaya feel to early bites like pork gyoza with truffle ponzu or the restaurant’s signature roasted cauliflower, gently singed on the outside and served over a pale green shishito herb vinaigrette. Among the mains, smoked brisket sliced and served on the bone conjures Texas barbecue, while the Thai rice stone pot with king crab or confit duck (there’s also a vegetarian version) will feel familiar to fans of bibimbap. Two things distinguish this Kyu from the other locations: A “reserve” menu features dry-aged steaks (30-day-aged rib-eye, 45-day-aged tomahawk), plus Japanese and Australian wagyu cuts for beef aficionados. And a handy happy hour menu distinguishes itself with an LA-only Korean-style short rib taco and a pork belly bao bun (references to Kogi and Momofuku, respectively). For dessert, the cinnamon roll with chai frosting is a must-order. Kyu corporate executive chef Raheem Sealey continues to oversee food operations, while culinary director Emre Koyel will run the kitchen in Los Angeles day-to-day. General manager Harley DeMeyers was previously at Tao, San Vicente Bungalows, and Houston Hospitality, incorporating a service model where everyone will feel like a VIP . Los Angeles has long loved high-energy pan-Asian restaurants, with upscale Japanese lounges like Katana, Koi, Katsuya, and, of course, Nobu, serving raw and cooked proteins in sleek environments. Now Kyu joins those ranks, with Century City’s white-collar office worker-types ready to bounce in in for happy hours as well as swanky business dinners, dates, and more. Kyu Los Angeles will serve from 4 p.m. to 10 p.m. Tuesday to Thursday, until 11 p.m. on Friday and Saturday, closed Sundays and Mondays. Happy hour runs from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. Reservations are available here . It’s located at 10200 Constellation Boulevard, Suite 225, Los Angeles, CA 90067. items.text: Dining Out in LA Your Los Angeles Restaurant Weekend Guide: November 13 Your handy guide on where to eat from the editors at Eater LA by Eater Staff Nov 13, 2026, 8:10 PM UTC Facebook Link Tlayudas and meat on the grill at Maydan Market. | Stan Lee Dining Out in LA Your Los Angeles Restaurant Weekend Guide: November 13 Your handy guide on where to eat from the editors at Eater LA by Eater Staff Nov 13, 2026, 8:10 PM UTC Facebook Link Tlayudas and meat on the grill at Maydan Market. | Stan Lee Facebook Link Every Friday, our editors compile a trusty list of recommendations to answer the most pressing of questions: “Where should I eat?” Here are four places to check out this weekend in Los Angeles. And if you need some ideas on where to drink, here’s our list of the hottest places to get cocktails in town. This week’s recommendations focus on the 2026 Eater Awards recipients in Los Angeles. For an award-winning pie: Chainsaw in Melrose Hill Icebox pie. Oscar Mendoza Selecting Chainsaw as our best new bakery winner for the Eater Awards required some discussion. Although the pop-up-turned-cafe initially started with strict devotion to their noteworthy pies — especially the signature passionfruit lime icebox pie — Chainsaw quickly became a notable neighborhood stop for coffee and arepas, too. Still, baking is at the core of Chainsaw, and we as a team were excited by what this tiny shop on Melrose brings to Los Angeles. When you try Karla Subero Pittol’s treats, you’ll see why it’s a winner in our book. 5022 Melrose Avenue, Los Angeles, CA 90038. — Kat Thompson, audience editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest For a rising star in the Valley: Alto in Studio City Alto. Soledad Recatume Alto , the recipient of our Eater Awards Rising Star recognition, brings a stronghold for South American cooking to the Valley. Helmed by chef Esteban Klenzi and Juana Castellanos, the restaurant explores Argentine-Uruguayan wood-fired cooking in a sleek dining room right off Ventura Boulevard. Start with the chipa, a cheesy tapioca bread paired with tomato butter, before tucking into an empanada filled with braised beef, dry-aged bone-in short rib, and a pork chop roasted in kombu seaweed. 12969 Ventura Boulevard, Studio City, CA 91604. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest For California fine dining: Lielle in Beverlywood Squab with yuzu pepper, bitter greens, and beets. Andrea Jernmark Marcus Jernmark, Eater LA’s Chef of the Year , puts forth his interpretation of California cooking at Lielle and its upstairs sister restaurant, Marée . The menu at Lielle is constantly evolving as Jernmark looks to his surroundings for inspiration: Dishes such as barbecue abalone and tres leches ice cream with dried milk skin have made appearances since the restaurant opened. Although Jernmark is from Sweden, he has embedded himself in California over the last few years, studying the region’s terroir and wine with deep curiosity. The $150 menu (though the bill will likely be closer to $250 per person with beverages) is a look inside Jernmark’s mind as he experiments with ingredients, putting forward plates that are unlike any other in the city. 9575 W Pico Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90035. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest For our hyperfixation chicken: Henrietta on the border of Echo Park and Westlake Half chicken. Danielle Adams It’s been a big year for chicken , a menu standby that is often overlooked for flashier beef or pork. Still, the dish that captured Eater LA’s heart (and Dish of the Year ) is Henrietta’s roast chicken, which arrives bedded alongside a chicory Caesar with torn croutons made from Clark Street Bread. The seemingly simple dish takes three days to make, resulting in a deeply savory half chicken, kissed with dark grill marks that deepen its flavor. Nods to Zuni Cafe are apparent in the spot-on execution, but the chicken still feels entirely its own. Go to Henrietta for the chicken, but be sure to add on the tartare toast — sure to convert raw beef nonbelievers — and the tender ricotta dumplings. 343 Glendale Boulevard, Los Angeles, CA 90026. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest For tlayudas, pozole, and Thai cooking all under one roof: Maydan Market in West Adams Tlayudas and meat on the grill at Maydan Market. Stan Lee Maydan Market , a West Adams food hall of sorts anchored by D.C. import Maydan, captures the breadth of Los Angeles cooking under one roof. In the hangar-like space, which was recognized as Eater LA’s Best New Restaurant this year, Malena by Tamales Elena churns out soul-warming pozole flights, while Lugya’h by Ponchos Tlayudas smears oversized tortillas with beans before crowning them with tasajo or chorizo. At Golden Mountain Chicken, the team behind Holy Basil fries up chicken topped with crispy shallots, while Maydan offers a sit-down Lebanese dinner complete with wine and cocktails. 4301 W. Jefferson Boulevard, Los Angeles, CA 90016. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest Related The 38 Best Restaurants in Los Angeles See More : Dining Out in LA Dining Out

items.title: Downtown LA’s Semi-Hidden Whiskey Den Is Back
items.summary: Bar Jackalope, the whiskey den tucked in the back of Seven Grand, is back. After closing in July 2025, the bar will reopen on Thursday, November 19, with whiskey flights, classic cocktails, and a locker program that lets guests keep their own bottles on-site.  After its initial debut in 2014, the bar gained a devoted […]
items.text: LA Restaurant Openings Downtown LA’s Semi-Hidden Whiskey Den Is Back ﻿Bar Jackalope resurrects in the back of Seven Grand by Rebecca Roland Nov 13, 2026, 6:50 PM UTC Facebook Link Bar Jackalope. | Carvingblock Studios Rebecca Roland is the deputy editor of the Southern California/Southwest region, who covers the evolving landscape of LA’s food scene. Bar Jackalope , the whiskey den tucked in the back of Seven Grand , is back. After closing in July 2025, the bar will reopen on Thursday, November 19, with whiskey flights, classic cocktails , and a locker program that lets guests keep their own bottles on-site. After its initial debut in 2014 , the bar gained a devoted following. Adam Kloos, who took over as Seven Grand’s general manager in October 2025, says that even after Bar Jackalope’s closure, guests would come in asking about reservations. ”We still get questions all the time, and people get super bummed that it’s not open,” he says. “There’s just so much excitement behind it.” Kloos made it his personal project to revive the bar over the last few months. Bar Jackalope will reopen with a menu of six whiskey cocktails: Old Fashioned, rye Manhattan, Sazerac, sour, julep, and highball. Each highlights a different whiskey, including Heaven Hill Bottled in Bond in the Old Fashioned and Maker’s 46 in the sour. The bar will also serve a bourbon flight for $50 featuring Old Forester Seven Grand Single Barrel, a $110 Scotch-focused executive flight with Glenfiddich 18, and a $62 Japanese flight spanning bottles like Ichiro’s Malt and Grain and Iwai Tradition. “We’re leaning more heavily towards independent bottlings of Scotch and cool releases of Japanese whiskeys,” Kloos says. Eventually, bar bites will join the menu. Bar Jackalope’s membership program, which includes on-site bottle storage and priority reservations, will be available at three monthly tiers: $10 for one bottle stored, $15 for two, and $20 for three or more. The revived Bar Jackalope retains its original interior with emerald green leather chairs and glossy black leather banquettes. A sturdy wood bar grounds the room, with rows of whiskey bottles tucked in cabinets above and below. The reopening comes amid a tumultuous few years for Downtown Los Angeles, as restaurants like Rossoblu shutter while others, such as Cole’s and the Pantry Cafe , plot their resurrections. Kloos says that while Seven Grand has been lucky to retain regulars and feel the neighborhood’s support, he hopes Bar Jackalope’s return will draw even more people to the area. “I think right now is a very interesting time to do this,” Kloos says. “It’s a great time to offer some excitement where it seems like everything else is going away. This is kind of rising from the ashes.” Bar Jackalope is located at 515 W. Seventh Street #200, Los Angeles, CA 90014, at the back of Seven Grand. It will be open Thursday through Saturday evenings. Lodge Bread’s founder, two-time James Beard Award semifinalist Or Amsalam, has big plans for the bakery’s Pasadena space, with an expanded menu, baked goods that use naturally leavened dough, a daytime […]
items.text: LA Restaurant Openings Lodge Bread Brings Its Massive Cinnamon Rolls and Sourdough Loaves to Pasadena The bakery’s latest expansion offers a stacked pastry case, sandwiches, and grain bowls, plus a forthcoming pizza-pasta restaurant by Mona Holmes Nov 12, 2026, 8:00 PM UTC Facebook Link Lodge Bread. Wonho Frank Lee Mona Holmes is an editor at Eater Southern California/Southwest, a regular contributor at KCRW radio, and a 2022 James Beard Award nominee. Lodge Bread Co. , the bakery known for its oversized cinnamon rolls and sourdough loaves, opened its fourth location in Pasadena on Thursday, November 12. Lodge Bread’s founder, two-time James Beard Award semifinalist Or Amsalam, has big plans for the bakery’s Pasadena space, with an expanded menu, baked goods that use naturally leavened dough, a daytime menu of sandwiches, and expansive seating, plus an adjacent pizza-pasta restaurant called Full Proof, which will debut in early 2027. Arthur Sherman, who became Lodge Bread’s managing partner in 2021, says the former industrial building in Pasadena presented an opportunity to expand the business. After years of being limited to cooking breads, pizzas, and other items from a wood-fired oven at other locations, the team was able to install a full kitchen. “We love the bread that we make,” says Sherman. “We’re lucky to fully realize what Lodge can finally be. With a full kitchen, Pasadena is the first place we get to do that.” The Pasadena location resides on the border of Pasadena and Altadena; the duo signed the lease four months before the Eaton Fire . Dan Brunn Architecture, which also designed Funke in Beverly Hills , built out the 6,000-square-foot space that seats 75, with Full Proof’s capacity at 105. The room uses softer elements to balance the industrial design with natural wood, a white-and-blue color palette, polished concrete floors, and plaster, all surrounded by large windows to keep everything bright and open. It’s an ideal spot to hop in for a quick order, dine in, or take home ancient grain loaves , baguettes, brioche challah, morning buns, cookies (don’t skip the chocolate whoopie pie), and croissants . Breakfast burrito. Wonho Frank Lee Pastries. Wonho Frank Lee Lodge’s toast menu includes sourdough smeared with ricotta and seasonal jam, or cinnamon sugar toast crowned with cultured butter and sea salt. Breakfast sandwiches get stacked with eggs and cheese, while lunchtime sandwiches include smoked pastrami, turkey pesto, and albacore tuna. Lodge Bread Pasadena will debut new menu items, including a schnitzel pita, breakfast burrito, grain bowls, and salads. To drink, coffee, matcha, hot tea, and kombucha are available. When Full Proof opens in January 2027, it will serve pasta and pizzas in the evenings. Melrose Umbrella Co. alum David Purcell and Stanley’s Wet Goods developed the wine and non-alcoholic beverage menu. Amsalam first launched Full Proof as a pop-up in 2019 and planned for two locations before COVID-19 hit; the restaurant briefly operated out of a Beverly Hills location in 2022. Like its previous iterations, Pasadena’s Full Proof will center around sourdough pizza, though the rest of the menu is still in development. “We tried to mimic a good New York slice, but smaller,” says Amsalam. “It’s like a bread baker’s pizza.” More than a decade after first opening in Culver City, Amsalam is looking towards the future with more locations already planned for Westlake Village and Brentwood. “We just celebrated 11 years,” he says. “We imagine being able to grow it far more. Lodge Bread Pasadena is open Wednesday through Sunday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. at 1951 Lincoln Avenue, Pasadena, CA 91103. Spread of dishes. Wonho Frank Lee Lodge Bread. In the Palisades, though many residential buildings are in full rebuild, with construction crews scattered throughout […]
items.text: LA Restaurant Openings Nancy Silverton Opens LA’s Most Hopeful Restaurant in Pacific Palisades The famed chef brings Spacca Tutto to the neighborhood as it looks to rebuild after the Palisades Fire by Matthew Kang Nov 12, 2026, 6:50 PM UTC Facebook Link Spacca Tutto. | Matthew Kang Matthew Kang is a correspondent for Eater. Previously, he was the lead editor of Eater’s Southern California/Southwest region. He has covered dining, restaurants, food culture, and nightlife in Los Angeles since 2008. Sign up for his weekly newsletter, Kangtown . Altadena and its vibrant restaurant community have been well documented in the aftermath of the Eaton Fire that devastated the neighborhood; the Pacific Palisades has, so far, had less of a comeback , with fewer rebuilding permits issued to businesses. In the Palisades, though many residential buildings are in full rebuild, with construction crews scattered throughout the seaside borough, many families have opted not to return . Sign up for the Kang Town newsletter This post originally appeared in my Kang Town newsletter, where I cover all things dining in the West. Sign up here to get my latest stories. In the immediate aftermath of the Palisades Fire, LA chef, podcast host, and owner of the footwear brand Snibbs Daniel Shemtob was one of many restaurant workers who immediately mobilized to feed victims and first responders of the wildfires, partnering with World Central Kitchen to provide meals from his food truck, the Lime Truck. Having lost his own home in the fire, he purchased a new one in eastern Beverly Hills, near the border of West Hollywood. Now Shemtob has reasons to feel hopeful about the Palisades. Two new restaurants — Alphabet Bar & Grill , from nightlife group h.wood, and Nancy Silverton’s Spacca Tutto — have opened inside real estate developer Rick Caruso’s Palisades Village. The upscale shopping center, which features a yet-to-reopen Erewhon and a handful of high-end luxury boutiques , plus a still-open Blue Ribbon Sushi and Angelini Ristorante, was protected by a private firefighting force during the Palisades Fire. Shemtob told me Silverton’s arrival in particular marks a new chapter for the Palisades: “I think [Spacca Tutto] is epic for the neighborhood. I think it brings hope and gives momentum, which I think is really important to build culture.” Malibu’s less flashy but almost equally wealthy neighbor, Pacific Palisades has long been one of the best places to live in Los Angeles, if you can afford it. (For a brief time, I had access via a college friend whose parents had a house perched in the hills.) Even before the fires, the only negative: the paucity of good restaurants. You’re better off scooting over to Brentwood or Santa Monica. The Palisades wildfire destroyed over 6,800 buildings and killed 12 people, making it one of the worst natural disasters in LA history. Many restaurants were destroyed, though the mostly residential area lost more homes than commercial buildings. One of my favorite restaurants, the Reel Inn, is gone; longtime favorite Vittorio’s is rebuilding and currently operating out of a food truck; Cinque Terre West relocated to Venice. The owner of Alphabet Bar & Grill, prolific nightlife group h.wood, made its name with celebrity hangouts and recently gained some culinary mojo with its Vegas expansion of Delilah (a supper club par excellence). Alphabet boasts former Otium chef Timothy Hollingsworth, who has been on a tear lately, opening restaurants in Long Island, Washington D.C.’s Georgetown, and, soon, another 200-plus seater in Atlanta. Occupying the space that was Hank’s (named after Caruso’s late father), Alphabet plants its flag as a ritzy all-day restaurant. The menu reads like a snoozy but upscale hotel restaurant, but in reality the food is unnecessarily excellent. The grilled shrimp topped with sliced chiles packs a serious heat that made me, a notorious spice addict, sweat profusely (which I enjoyed). The Cabbage Crunch is essentially Burmese tea leaf salad without tea leaves, but with the same salty-sweet-tangy punch. Every table had an order of the chicken Caesar wrap — at “just” $21, not bad for the neighborhood. (Heck, Erewhon’s, just a few steps away, costs $18 and doesn’t come with fries on the side.) The glorious, golden brown, uniformly juicy rotisserie chicken is worthy of a Thomas Keller disciple. (Hollingsworth was chef de cuisine at the French Laundry for years.) The ambience reads Polo Lounge or Palm Steakhouse, albeit more Disneyfied. Alphabet Bar & Grill would be a superb addition to literally any neighborhood, but I’ve seen virtually zero chatter about it. Spacca Tutto, on the other hand, has been buzzed about from the start, thanks in part to a huge preview lunch that brought over a majority of the local food media (including me) in early October. Caruso showed up to explain how he basically offered the restaurant to Silverton in a handshake deal. Silverton beamed, and why not? The rather fetching, Italianate space, lined with burgundy, black, and white marble, has a baby grand piano, dark-red leather seating, and a potent air of Old World luxury. It’s actually much more beautiful and pleasant than Chi Spacca, Silverton’s steakhouse that inspired this sequel. I spoke with Silverton last week, and she said, “I never really knew it was such a tight-knit community, and they’ve been very welcoming. They say how much the Palisades needed this kind of restaurant.” Nancy Silverton and Rick Caruso at Spacca Tutto. Matthew Kang Foodwise, Spacca Tutto is unimpeachable. The highlights from a $360 follow-up lunch in which two of us over-ordered: the beefsteak tomato salad; artichoke dip with fried Ritz crackers (brilliant); Chi Spacca’s signature focaccia di recco, redolent of excellent olive oil; Dal Rae -style picanha steak smothered in bacon, scallions, and lemon zest; and a righteously loaded baked potato. The menu is more expansive, more accessible, and more available — Spacca Tutto

items.summary: When I heard that a restaurant called Skywalker Grill was opening at the new Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, I was expecting a wonderland of Star Wars-themed food and drinks (not dissimilar to the Blue Milk and Ronto Wraps served at Disneyland’s Galaxy’s Edge) in a hyperfuturistic dining room. My predictions were entirely wrong. Skywalker […]
items.text: Dining Reports Skywalker Grill Is Los Angeles’s Most Beautiful New Restaurant ﻿Curb your expectations about the food and appreciate the scenery and the Star Wars lore by Kat Thompson Nov 12, 2026, 4:30 PM UTC Facebook Link Food at Skywalker Grill in the Lucas Museum. Tom McGovern Kat Thompson is the audience editor of Eater’s Southern California/Southwest region. In our Dining Reports, we share a firsthand perspective of a recent restaurant visit, covering everything from the vibe to must-get dishes. See more in the Eater app. Download the app When I heard that a restaurant called Skywalker Grill was opening at the new Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, I was expecting a wonderland of Star Wars -themed food and drinks (not dissimilar to the Blue Milk and Ronto Wraps served at Disneyland’s Galaxy’s Edge) in a hyperfuturistic dining room. My predictions were entirely wrong. Skywalker Grill is a beautiful and modern museum restaurant with a menu that doesn’t feel as enthralling as a space opera saga between good and evil. Still, if you can manage to get a reservation and temper nerdy expectations, Skywalker Grill is worth a visit, if only to appreciate the modern architecture, stunning downtown views, and simple — but serviceable — menu. Skywalker Ranch Wagyu Burger. Tom McGovern What to order Tangles of fried calamari in a craggy batter that feels light and crisp, tossed with aromatic fried basil and sliced Fresno chiles, arrive steaming hot. For me, what made this shareable appetizer was the smoky kick of the accompanying chipotle aioli. The chopped salad is the most beautiful rendition I’ve ever seen, with jewel-toned beets, perfectly cubed cheddar cheese, fresh tomatoes, bacon, boiled eggs, corn, and chickpeas — all underneath a visually impressive sliced avocado. There’s creaminess from the avocado, crunch from the bacon bits, and a pleasing earthiness from the beets. The salad is delightfully fresh, with an acid-forward balsamic vinaigrette that ties it all together. Order pigs in a blanket for the table for snackable bites of hot dogs encased in a flaky croissant dough topped with everything bagel seasoning. The punchy mustard for dipping stands in stark contrast to the saltiness of the dog. You should get one of the meatier dishes from the menu to try Skywalker Ranch beef. I recommend the burger , which has classic backyard burger vibes thanks to toppings of grilled onions, lettuce, tomato, and a slice of cheddar cheese, all on double sesame seeded buns. The bolognese also highlights Skywalker Ranch beef in a meaty ragu over al dente gemelli pasta. Pigs in a Blanket. Tom McGovern The vibe Skywalker Grill offers a stunning view of Downtown Los Angeles from its expansive patio — optimal on a sunny Los Angeles day. The interior looks nothing like the Millennium Falcon; instead, the space oozes with warm, ambient lighting and wood tones, with swooping, futuristic architecture vaguely reminiscent of The Jetsons . Insider tip You don’t actually have to have tickets to the Lucas Museum to drop into Skywalker Grill. Instead, upon entering the museum, go straight to the elevators designated for the restaurant. Dining room. Tom McGovern The takeaway I don’t expect a museum restaurant to blow my culinary mind, and Skywalker Grill certainly does not. Although I wish the restaurant took bigger and more inventive swings when it comes to the menu, the space is gorgeous enough to make me overlook the ordinariness of the food. At this restaurant, the dishes have to be approachable and appeal to a mass audience; they’re secondary to the vibes of the space and lore of George Lucas. Maybe that’s okay. Maybe that’s the point. Regardless, I think Skywalker Grill is worth at least one visit, whether you’re a tourist in Los Angeles or want to bear witness to the prettiest new restaurant in LA. items.summary: A slew of reimagined bistros, revivals of old dining favorites, colorful cafes, and specialty pastry makers all entered the Los Angeles scene this past year and struck a chord with diners. But being a successful Los Angeles restaurant in 2026 meant far more than superlative food and service. Each introduced experiences that transcend what we […]
items.text: Dining Out in LA Introducing LA’s 2026 Eater Award Winners The Best New Restaurant, Chef of the Year, Dish of the Year, and more by Nicole Fellah , Rebecca Roland , Matthew Kang , Mona Holmes , and Hilary Pollack Nov 10, 2026, 3:00 PM UTC Facebook Link Tlayudas from Lugya’h at Maydan Market. | Stan Lee/Eater Facebook Link A slew of reimagined bistros , revivals of old dining favorites , colorful cafes, and specialty pastry makers all entered the Los Angeles scene this past year and struck a chord with diners. But being a successful Los Angeles restaurant in 2026 meant far more than superlative food and service. Each introduced experiences that transcend what we expect from a restaurant in spite of a severe economic slowdown , continuing ICE raids , and a steep decline in Los Angeles tourism . This crop of restaurants reflects the continued inventiveness of Los Angeles’s chefs and independent business owners in the face of uncertainty. In late 2025, Little Fish expanded into Melrose Hill, drawing crowds with a unique style of West Coast seafood, while Hermon’s became an envied neighborhood restaurant. Yerord Mas’s $38 sandwich kept long lines, while tasting menu prices dropped considerably. The year 2026 was also one of rebirths, with chef Ray Garcia’s Broken Spanish Comedor , chef Casey Lane’s formidable Tasting Kitchen , and the return of classic movie palaces . Those looking for inventive wine bars and cocktails found newcomers like Bar Betsy and Vandell , the latter with its clever produce-focused drinks. Of course, awarding the best of the new also becomes a bittersweet acknowledgement as longtime favorites like Taix , Crustacean , and Sky’s Gourmet Tacos shuttered in 2026. Though plenty of predictable “ Erewhonified ” restaurants debuted, refreshing bakeries like Pinecone also emerged, as did Pasadena’s cinnamon roll expert Badash Bakes . The taco scene continues to deliciously veer Northern Mexican, with styles from Tijuana and Sonora gaining influence at Echo Park’s Tijuanero by Tijuanazo and Silver Lake’s carne asada superstar, Tacos Royale . Here are the 2026 Eater Award winners, representing the best and brightest of the newcomers in Los Angeles of the past year. Visit Eater for the full list of 2026 Eater Awards , presented by Capital One. — Mona Holmes , editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest Related Check out the map of LA’s 2026 Eater Award winners — and discover special dining perks with select restaurants Alfonso Martinez. Stan Lee/Eater Tlayudas and meat on the grill at Maydan Market. Stan Lee/Eater Best New Restaurant: Maydan Market Maydan Market opened in 2025 as a collaborative restaurant space and marketplace home to a few different Los Angeles-born businesses; in essence, it functions as one super-incubator for some of the best food you can find in the city. Diners bounce around to try a pozole flight and pescadillas (sofrito-fried fish nested in supple blue corn tortillas) at Maléna, from the family behind the beloved Tamales Elena; a crisp, UFO-sized, asiento-painted tlayuda from Lugya’h, from Los Angeles legend Poncho’s Tlayudas; and chile-sauce-slicked gai tod from Golden Mountain Chicken (formerly Yhing Yhang), from the intrepid team behind Thai restaurant Holy Basil. They will certainly stop to perch at the rotating Club 104 stall, which has hosted Black-owned businesses such as Melnificent Wingz and Caribbean diasporic pop-up Rubie, as well as Palestinian home restaurant Mid East Eats. On their way out, they may circle the storefront simply named Sook to eye wines, spices, and woven goods sourced from the Levant. This is not to mention the market’s anchor restaurants: the Lebanese-influenced Maydan and Compass Rose, respectable D.C. transplants from prolific restaurateur Rose Previte, who, alongside her team, curated the market with the knockout lineup of Indigenous vendors. Maydan Market feels boldly like one whole; people rarely come for a single hyped stall. The point, in effect, is the crawl. In a year marked by ongoing, unrelenting, nationwide ICE raids targeting Black and brown immigrants, the fact that the market centers Indigenous Mexican-owned businesses, allowing their owners the space and sovereignty to reach a wider stage and audience, speaks loudly. — Nicole Fellah , dining editorial manager Marcus Jernmark. Andrea Jernmark Chef of the Year: Marcus Jernmark, Lielle and Marée Marcus Jernmark quietly landed in Los Angeles five years ago with Michelin pedigree, hosting an $800 dinner series at private homes and trying to drum up support for his own professional projects. Over time, he learned what this city was about: casual refinement, the labor of love in sourcing local ingredients, and effortless style, which he has implemented in spades at his new restaurant Lielle (and California French bistro Marée , which just opened upstairs). The results are stunning: barely cooked shrimp tangled into handmade uni pasta; fire-kissed dry-aged squab that reflects a truly joyful, energetic viewpoint. Jernmark could have shaped Lielle to be an unattainable, once-a-year dinner but instead chose a more accessible $150 prix-fixe approach — serving a menu that changes every few months to lure local diners back in to try his deceptively ambitious, inventive cooking. It’s exciting to see someone who made his career in New York, Singapore, and Stockholm embrace Los Angeles for what it is — a discerning diner’s wonderland with unparalleled food from street to tasting counter — and set a new standard. — Matthew Kang , Eater West Coast correspondent Passionfruit lime icebox pie. Shelby Moore/Eater Karla Subero Pittol. Shelby Moore/Eater Best New Bakery: Chainsaw Born as an underground dinner party operated out of Karla Subero Pittol’s Echo Park garage, Chainsaw finally got its own digs this year in the form of a lively cafe in Melrose Hill, an unquestionably gentrifying neighborhood that has become home to some of Los Angeles’s best independent restaurants. items.text: Tin Tin Dining Out in Miami The Best New Bars in Miami Where to grab a drink right now in the Magic City by Allison Ramirez Updated Jul 15, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Facebook Link Allison Ramirez is a freelance journalist with over 15 years of experience covering food and drink, travel, art, culture, and more. As a gateway between the U.S., the Caribbean, and Latin America, Miami has long been a champion of diverse flavors — rum and agave spirits mingling with notes of citrus and exotic fruits. Recently, vermouth and sherry-based drinks, along with classic Spanish cocktails and Italian spritzes, are popping up in the local scene, further shaping the city’s evolving cocktail landscape. Miami’s drinking culture really reflects its melting pot history, and this year, some iconic bars and restaurants have reopened with a refreshed look and feel, bringing back old-school favorites alongside international, travel-inspired drinks. From tiki recipes and passion fruit infusions to sparkling concoctions of all sorts, our latest cocktail map highlights the best drinks and the hottest new spots to try them, from Coral Gables to Miami Beach and everywhere in between. Sunny’s Steakhouse Sunny’s Steakhouse in Miami’s Little River has been the talk of the town (many towns, actually) since opening in October 2024. The massive space and the dishes are worth the hype, but the unspoken star is the bar, featuring cocktails like the refreshing Green Ghoul (tequila, mezcal, poblano, cucumber, lime) and the Monchito, a coconut-washed agricole rhum drink with sherry that evolved from a piña colada to a ti punch of sorts. The menu includes house cocktails, martinis, and “fine & fancy” options — the fino martini service, which comes with a sidecar, is a must. Made with gin, clarified passionfruit, and fino sherry, it’s a steal at $18 per person. Co-owner Will Thompson calls the Living Dead cocktail — a bold mix of clairin, absinthe, tabasco, passion fruit, ginger, and allspice — an unexpected hit, saying, “The ingredients are all generally too loud, but they end up balancing each other nicely to work for guests who don’t normally fit the mold of an adventurous drinker.” Loved it Want to try Booking Book a table Get there with Lyft Location 7357 NW Miami Ct, Miami, FL, 33150, US External Link Phone (305) 456-4562 Link Visit Website Michael Pisarri See more Miami’s Most Romantic Restaurants Feb 12 Miami’s Most Romantic Restaurants 14 Best Steakhouses in Miami Aug 1, 2025 14 Best Steakhouses in Miami Bar Bucce Opened last spring in Little River from the team behind Macchialina, Bar Bucce was just named a 2026 James Beard Semifinalist for “best new bar.” The bottleshop and pizzeria is big on beer and wine, but for the cocktail lovers, the drink list leans Italian just like the food menu. Try a low ABV Red Foulard made with Savoia (an all-natural orange wine aperitivo), Select Aperitivo (a Venetian bittersweet orange liqueur), and soda; or go bold with spirit-forward, aperitif-driven gin cocktails like the Signora del Lago (22% ABV) or Martini Catalano (25% ABV). Start with a caviar cone and the olives (modern and traditional include liquid olives that burst when you pop them into your mouth). items.summary: A new Mexican seafood restaurant, Mi Vecino, is opening in Circle C, courtesy of chef Amir Hajimaleki and his brother Ali Hajimaleki of Roya Hospitality Group. It’s slated to open between now and early 2027, per a release. The restaurant, Mi Vecino, will open at 5701 West Slaughter Lane, replacing another of the group’s restaurants, […]
items.text: Austin Restaurant News Fire-Grilled Mexican Seafood Is Coming to South Austin The team behind Roya and Oasthouse will open Mi Vecino, a coastal restaurant focused on raw and fire-kissed dishes by Erin Russell Oct 28, 2026, 6:47 PM UTC Facebook Link Chef Amir Hajimaleki will oversee the menu, managed by Mi Vecino’s executive chef Jose Alajandro Sanchez. Sarah Natsumi Moore/Eater Erin Russell is a journalist and an Austin native, who has been writing about food for eight years. A new Mexican seafood restaurant, Mi Vecino, is opening in Circle C, courtesy of chef Amir Hajimaleki and his brother Ali Hajimaleki of Roya Hospitality Group. It’s slated to open between now and early 2027, per a release. The restaurant, Mi Vecino, will open at 5701 West Slaughter Lane, replacing another of the group’s restaurants, Keeper’s Coastal Kitchen , which closed Saturday, October 24. Mi Vecino, which means my neighbor in Spanish, will focus on Mexican seafood dishes, both raw and fire-grilled. That means offerings like shrimp enchiladas with white mole, ceviche, oysters, and fajitas served with fresh tortillas. Drinks-wise, there will be a full bar with margaritas, ranch waters, palomas, and other cocktails. Chef Hajimaleki will oversee the menu, which will be executed by chef Jose Alajandro Sanchez. The Hajimalekis’ restaurants are mostly clustered on Slaughter Lane in South Austin. Gastropub Oasthouse Kitchen + Bar , cocktail bar Daisy Lounge , and forthcoming Mi Vecino all share a building, and the group’s first restaurant , American spot District Kitchen + Cocktails , is just down the street. Mi Vecino replaces Keeper’s Coastal Kitchen, a different Roya Hospitality Group restaurant that closed in October. Jasmin Porter Photography This is not the first time Roya Hospitality Group has reimagined one of their restaurants. Roya , Hajimalekis’ highly personal Persian restaurant in North Shoal Creek, opened this year in a space that was previously Shortie’s, the group’s foray into New England Greek-style pizza. Roya is the group’s only North Austin restaurant, and sits above a former second District Kitchen, which closed and became an event space. Given the group’s penchant for reinvention, only time will tell whether it stays an event space. Whether you’re planning a milestone birthday, hosting a corporate dinner, or gathering friends for an engagement celebration, Austin has a private dining room to suit your needs. Some are swanky and tucked into Downtown dining landmarks. Others are cozy, or perched on patios with sweeping views. All of them make an outing feel like an event, while also taking the stress out of group dining — meaning, there’s no awkward table shuffling, no shouting over the crowd, and no fighting for the check. The city’s best private dining spaces are more than just a curtain and a prix fixe menu. Many spots go beyond dinner, offering perks like custom cocktails, floral design, built-in audio and video setups, and after-hours buyouts. From iconic institutions like Fonda San Miguel, Matties, and Jeffrey’s to sleek hotspots like Eberly, La Condessa, and Bar Toti, these venues combine atmosphere with standout service and memorable menus. Here are the city’s most impressive private and semi-private dining options — spaces that strike the right balance between style and function. items.title: Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques
items.summary:
At Cotoletta in Coconut Grove, there are no decisions to make. The Miami restaurant serves only one entree: Cotoletta alla… 
 The post  Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques  appeared first on  Resy | Right This Way .
items.text: Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques — Resy | Right This Way Cotoletta 4.7 · Italian · $ Miami Book Now Published: Nov. 9, 2026 At Cotoletta in Coconut Grove, there are no decisions to make. The Miami restaurant serves only one entree: Cotoletta alla Milanese. No substitutions. No alternatives. Just a golden, pan-fried veal cutlet — and a bet that it’s all you’ll need. Until recently, making a reservation required a phone call, which only deepened the sense that this place operates on its own terms. (The good news: You can now reserve a table on Resy.) The concept debuted in Coconut Grove in the fall of 2024 and comes from 84 Magic Hospitality, a restaurant group known for a growing collection of Miami restaurants with minimalist menus ( San Lorenzo , San Marco , and the lasagna pop-up, Si Papa 3190 , are the others). Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Still, the story behind the concept stretches back further than its Miami address might suggest. Cotoletta is the creation of partners Ignacio Lopez Mancisidor and Mattia Cicognani, and former co-founder Andrea Fraquelli — who share a background in hospitality and a frustration with how transactional the industry had become. From the start, their goal at Cotoletta has been to make things simple for guests and allow them to focus on what really matters: great food and genuine connection. “Across the globe, many of the best restaurants do one item and they do it to absolute perfection,” co-founder Mattia Cicognani says. “We drew inspiration from the Italian essence of committing to one hero dish and prioritizing ingredients of the highest quality.” “Only serving one dish was a risk,” Cicognani acknowledges, “but the popularity and love for the concept has proven that it really works. Our customers learned that they love what we do and that is why they continue to come back.” Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Head chef Davide Rosselli shared the process that delivers a consistent, classic cotoletta every time. Premium veal is hand-trimmed, gently pounded to its thin-yet-tender texture, coated in fresh egg and breadcrumbs, and fried in clarified butter until it emerges with a crisp, even, golden crust. Each cutlet weighs in at roughly 20 ounces, made to be shared between two people. The result is a traditional veal Milanese that is a signature of Northern Italian craftsmanship. Everything else on the table exists to support that centerpiece. “While the process sounds simple, it’s backed by decades of Italian tradition and time-honored techniques passed down by chefs across generations,” Rosselli says. For $90, two diners share the full prix-fixe experience: two antipasti courses of bruschetta and truffle arancino to start, followed by the veal cutlet, and two sides (the only real choice you have to make here). Dessert (tiramisu or a flourless chocolate cake) can be added on for $14. “Each appetizer sets the tone for a true Italian experience, while the sides are thoughtfully chosen to complement the veal without overpowering it.” Rosselli says. “Lighter elements like crisp salads and simple pasta dishes help balance the richness of the veal, creating a well-rounded meal.” Those side options include pasta al pomodoro, zucchine fritte, insalata di rucola, or patatine fritte. Rosselli’s personal picks: the pasta in just the right portion to leave you wanting more of the main event, and the zucchine fritte offering a warm, light bite that balances out the richness of the veal. (Wondering what happens if you bring a third wheel or want to dine solo? Odd-numbered parties can add on an individual portion of bruschetta, arancino, a smaller veal cutlet, and one side for $55.) Guests return because the menu never changes, and neither does the reason to go back. “They know exactly what they are getting every single time,” Cicognani says. Cotoletta is open weekdays from 5:30 to 10 p.m. and until 10:30 p.m. on Friday. On weekends, it opens at 12:30 p.m. until 10:30 p.m. on Saturday and 9 p.m. on Sunday. Lyssa Goldberg is a Miami-based freelance writer and content strategist. She loves telling stories about food, wellness and travel, and you can find her byline in Parade, American Way, Mashable, Miami New Times, Time Out and more. Follow her on Instagram and Twitter . Follow Resy , too. items.text: The Resy Guide to Bars and Restaurants for Music Lovers in New York — Resy | Right This Way Updated: Nov. 9, 2026 As people who love restaurants, we know that when it comes to picking a spot for dinner, it’s much more than about just the food. The vibe is just as important, and music is a key player in creating it. Sometimes, the best soundtrack is the one you don’t notice, but the places on this list aren’t for those kinds of nights. These playlists are hyper specific, the sound systems are top of the line, and often they have some of the best vinyl collections in the country, and a guest DJs on weekends who comes in to spin them. These are places you go to for the music, but where us restaurant lovers won’t need to suffer because the snacks that can often lead to full meals are far more interesting than a bag of stale potato chips. You’ll be able to listen to some Japanese jazz deep cuts over an omakase, or eclectic world beats over some of the city’s silkiest hummus — with playlists and menus like these, you might not need to make it to your second destination for the night. And if you’re looking for spots with live music, we’ve got you covered here . City Photo courtesy of 56709 What was once 929, an audio haven for Canto pop, is now a moody, atmospheric spot for Japanese city pop, from the same team. You’ll also find plenty of records that include J-pop from the 90s and 2000s, plus Japanese R&B. And the theme isn’t strictly limited to the music, either. Cocktails are named after Japanese pop stars (Anri, Momoko, Ryuichi) and anime (Agumon, Usagi), and food is a fusion of Japanese and Taiwanese flavors: Think radish cakes with XO sauce, braised pork over rice, and mala-seasoned French fries. Book Now Birds map West Village Whether you’re partial to live music or listening bar vibes, Birds has you covered. On weeknights they spin selections from their enormous vinyl collection, and on weekends they host live musicians in a variety of styles like ska, jazz, and Afrobeats. Know that on Fridays and Saturdays there’s a $30 cover charge, but it’s a small price to pay for the incredible night of music that you’re in for. Book Now Boro Brine map Williamsburg The bar. Photo by Ben Hon, courtesy of Boro Brine There are two concepts at this Williamsburg restaurant, an intimate 22-seat omakase counter and a Japanese-inspired cocktail bar. Audiophiles will be satisfied at either, as music runs throughout and the sound system is top notch. The chef’s tasting consists of an ever-changing menu of multiple courses for $98 a person, whereas the bar has an à la carte menu that features inventive cocktails and bites like a chef’s take on a filet-o-fish and octopus with saag paneer. With velvet banquets and a dimly lit interior, it’s also a perfect date night spot. Book Now ALL BLUES map Tribeca Photo courtesy of All Blues Don’t be surprised if you’re asked to keep quiet at this Tribeca listening room. It’s all about the music here, so much so to that conversation is discouraged. All Blues comes from owner Yuji Fukushima, who based the concept on the places he frequented back growing up in Tokyo. He’s invested in top-tier audio equipment and carefully selects the music each evening, which can range from funk to Dizzy Gillespie. Enjoy Japanese snacks like tempura sweet potatoes and gyoza, alongside a fine whiskey or sake while you take in the sounds. Book Now Record Room map Long Island City Photo courtesy of Record Room This Long Island City bar might be a little hard to find at first, but that’s the idea. Behind a hidden door, you’ll be transported to a music filled living room of sorts, filled with comfy couches and soft lighting. All the music here is played off vinyl and there might be occasional dancing. The drinks lean classic, with riffs on espresso martinis

items.text: 29 New York Bars and Restaurants with Excellent Zero-Proof Cocktails — Resy | Right This Way Updated: Nov. 9, 2026 Somewhere around a decade ago the dreaded term “mocktail” first started to surface on menus, referring to drinks meant to offer the cocktail experience, but none of the “buzz.” At the time, unlike their alcoholic counterparts, most of these drinks were overly sweet mixes of juice and housemade sodas with elaborate garnishes. Now, however, there’s been a shift in drinking culture: Dry January, anyone? In other words, we’re drinking less, or thinking about having that second or third drink more, and beverage directors have taken note. Today’s mocktails are now as considered and thoughtfully developed as those made full-strength. Many of them also feature the new wave of non-alcoholic spirits, like Seedlip, Lyre’s, Little Saints, Amass Riverine, and Ghia. So, whether you’re abstaining from alcohol, are taking a night off, or just want to stay and linger at the bar after your glass has run dry, here are some of the best places in the city to find zero-proof cocktails. Newly added: Bar Americano, Lord’s, Overstory, and The Up & Up.
