Nothing beats staying in a hotel whose suites hold some stories — especially if they’re of the spooky variety. The same friends who roll their eyes at mentions of luxury amenities and amazing views will be wide-eyed when you tell them about the ghost you accidentally ate breakfast with, the wailings you heard on your way to the icebox, or your run-in with an uncanny Victorian woman wearing all black. Booking a room at a regular old hotel will give you a few nice photos and a comfy robe; booking a room at a haunted one will give you tales of terror to tell for the rest of your life. At these hotels, lodges, inns, and resorts around the world, the supernatural is embraced and the unsettling is celebrated. Unexplained occurrences are simply part of the experience, and those with a healthy level of morbid curiosity will find no shortage of places to explore. Here, dark lore is hidden in every nook and cranny: a quack doctor’s treatment room, geothermal soaking pools, an old-school saloon, and a clown statue collection. Look over your shoulder and you might spot a glowing orb, a sopping-wet child, or a murderous outlaw. No matter where on this list you choose to book your stay, get ready to expect the unexpected. The Lodge at Hot Lake Springs books via Airbnb. Always confirm rates and availability directly with the property before booking. The hotel’s three suites and 65 guest rooms have original floors and doors and plenty of architectural quirks. jessemiers / Atlas Obscura User 1. The Marshall House - Savannah, Georgia Savannah has long been known for its thriving ghost population, many of whom have taken up residence at the city’s oldest hotel. Established in 1851 by Mary Magdalene Marshall, the building has played many roles: a makeshift hospital during the mid-19th-century yellow fever epidemic, a Union hospital near the end of the Civil War, and a temporary home to Joel Chandler Harris, creator of Uncle Remus, during the Reconstruction era. It’s no wonder then that guests frequently report odd activity in the hotel’s period-detailed rooms and cozy library. Common occurrences include the sound of children running down the halls at night, strange figures spotted in the foyers, doorknobs rattling, and faucets turning on on their own. Many Savannah ghost tours stop outside the hotel, but nothing beats drinking spirits amongst the spirits during the nightly social hour (sometimes with live entertainment!). During the ’00s, the fifth floor — which had been destroyed in a devastating fire in 1967 — was fully restored. Jeremy Thompson / CC BY-SA 2.0 2. items.title: Eden Rock, St Barths — MBDS
items.text: St Barths Eden Rock Eden Rock St Barths is an iconic hotel located on the beautiful Caribbean island of Saint Barthélemy. Since the 1950s, Rémy de Haenen's Eden Rock has been synonymous with unique hospitality. Martin Brudnizki It has been the byword for one-of-a-kind hospitality ever since Rémy de Haenen first welcomed guests to his Eden Rock home on the ocean, during the 1950s. In 2018 the studio undertook a renovation of the public areas and a number of rooms and suites. Eden Rock St Barths has established itself as the preferred private and discreet bolt-hole of many glamourous Hollywood characters who quickly became friends of St Barths. Howard Hughes Greta Garbo Robert Mitchum Gore Vidal Baron Rothschild David & Peggy Rockfeller Princess Lee Radziwill, amongst numbers of others. Selected works

Martin Brudnizki Refined Scandinavian Elegance Swedish design permeates the space, combining leather, silk, wool, antique chairs, and custom wooden tables. items.title: Four Seasons Astir Palace, Athens — MBDS
items.text: Athens Four Seasons Astir Palace Located on the Athenian Riviera, Four Seasons Astir Palace is an icon of Grecian hospitality. A sleek waterfront lounge with views over the Saronic Gulf. Martin Brudnizki Located in the Arion wing, Pelagos features a timber panelled ceiling, which mimes the shape of a boat's hull and a marble patterned floor inspired by traditional boat sails. The hotel's strong affinity with the region's maritime heritage is reflected in the restaurant's menu, which specialises in sophisticated seafood fare. Located in the Nafsika wing, Mercato features a warm colour palette of azure-blue and ochre with marble working together with leather and brass. Banquette seating and larger tables provide opportunities for parties to dine in a communal fashion, whilst guests in small groups can dine in a more intimate setting. The restaurant opens out onto a nautical-themed terrace area, where guests can take in the breath-taking views of the Riviera all whilst sitting back in comfort on upholstered armchairs and sofas. items.title: Scarfe's Bar at the Rosewood, London — MBDS
items.text: LONDON Scarfe's Bar Nestled within the opulent environs of the Rosewood Hotel, Scarfes Bar represents a pinnacle of hotel lounge bars in the vibrant city of London. The decor is reminiscent of a sophisticated drawing room from a bygone era. Martin Brudnizki The decor is exquisitely adorned with an eclectic collection of antiques, each imbued with its own rich history. Shelf upon shelf of vintage books imbue the air with a literary resonance, while the gentle flicker of a roaring fireplace lends the space a warm, inviting glow. Adorning the walls, the impish charm of Gerald Scarfe’s playful cartoons offers a delightful contrast , adding a touch of whimsy to the otherwise stately setting. Selected works

items.title: 31 Small Living Room Decorating Ideas That Actually Work
items.text: 31 Small Living Room Decorating Ideas That Actually Work Skip to content 31 Small Living Room Decorating Ideas That Actually Work Living Room ON September 10, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content Your living room feels smaller every time you add something new to it. You’ve tried moving the sofa, swapping the rug, even painting a wall, and it still feels cramped. These small living room decorating ideas fix that, but not with more shopping. I’ve spent twelve years fixing rooms like yours, and the problem is almost never size. It’s scale, color, and clutter working against you at the same time. You’ll get practical fixes for furniture, lighting, storage, and layout- the exact adjustments I use on real projects. By the end, you’ll know exactly where to start in your own room, and what to skip entirely. Where to Start: Diagnose Your Room First Before you touch a single accessory, figure out what’s actually wrong. Most small living rooms struggle for one of six reasons, and the fix is different for each one. If Your Room Feels Focus On Crowded Furniture scale and fewer pieces Dark Lighting, mirrors, and window treatments Plain Color, artwork, pattern, and texture Cluttered Closed storage and simpler surfaces Long and narrow Clear walkways and shallow furniture Open plan Rugs and furniture-defined zones Once you know which of these is actually working against you, the ideas below get a lot easier to filter. Here’s where I’d start. Small Living Room Decorating Ideas These small living room decorating ideas cover furniture scale, color, storage, and layout- the fixes I use on residential projects to make a tight room feel considered, not crowded. 1. Choose Furniture That Fits A sofa that reads perfectly on a mood board can still be wrong for your floor plan. Before you fall for a shape, check three numbers: seat depth, arm width, and footprint against your actual walkway. In a room under 150 square feet, I look for sofas under 34 inches deep and chairs no wider than 30 inches. Comfortable seating without swallowing the path through the room is the goal, not filling floor space with something that only looked good online. 2. Soften the Room With Curves Small rooms are full of straight lines already: window frames, cabinet edges, rectangular sofas. A round coffee table (30 to 36 inches works in most layouts), a curved accent chair, or an arched floor lamp breaks that up without adding bulk. There’s a practical reason too: rounded corners are easier to navigate in a tight layout, which matters more than people expect once you’re carrying a coffee tray through it daily. 3. Make Windows the Focal Point If your room has one good window, don’t compete with it. Keep tall bookcases and floor lamps at least a foot clear of the frame, and turn seating toward the view instead of the TV. A simple café curtain or a single sheer panel lets daylight do the work a heavy treatment can’t. I’ve pulled dense drapes out of more than one small living room, and the room read twice as large by the end of the day. 4. Add One Statement Wall Mural Pick the one wall you see first walking in, and let a mural carry the room’s personality instead of a dozen small accessories. Keep the sofa, rug, and cushions in quiet, solid tones nearby, so the mural reads as the intentional focal point rather than one more pattern competing for attention. Even an 8-foot mural works better here than a busy gallery wall in a room under 200 square feet. 5. Choose One Larger Seating Piece Three small chairs plus a loveseat almost always reads as more clutter than one well-scaled

items.title: 13 Small Apartment Living Room Ideas for Better Layout
items.text: 13 Small Apartment Living Room Ideas for Better Layout Skip to content 13 Small Apartment Living Room Ideas for Better Layout Living Room ON September 10, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content Trying to fit a sofa, TV, storage, and perhaps even a workspace into one compact room can make apartment living feel like a puzzle. The challenge is not always a lack of square footage. Poor furniture placement, bulky pieces, and unused corners can make the room feel much tighter than it needs to. The most useful small apartment living room ideas start with function before decoration. I usually look at the walking path, furniture scale, and room shape before recommending anything new. With a better layout, flexible furniture, smart storage, and thoughtful decorating, even a limited living area can feel comfortable, practical, and properly put together. How Do You Plan a Small Apartment Living Room Layout? The best way to plan a small apartment living room is to measure first, decide what the room needs to do, and arrange the largest furniture before adding smaller pieces. Measure the space: Note walls, windows, door swings, alcoves, outlets, and awkward corners. Decide its jobs: Determine whether the room needs to support lounging, TV viewing, dining, working, or guests. Place the sofa first: It usually has the biggest effect on circulation and furniture placement. Protect walking routes: Keep important paths between doors and adjoining rooms unobstructed. Add smaller furniture last: Tables, storage, and decor should fit the remaining space rather than dictate the layout. A layout that works comfortably every day matters more than one that simply looks balanced in a photograph. 1. Plan the Layout Around Your Room Shape There is no single furniture arrangement that works for every small apartment. A long room behaves differently from a square room, while a studio often needs one space to perform several functions. Start by working with the existing shape instead of forcing a symmetrical arrangement. Room Shape Best Approach Usually Avoid Long and narrow Linear seating Blocking the central route Square Defined central seating Too many small chairs Open plan Furniture-based zoning Heavy dividers Irregular Flexible or modular pieces Oversized fixed furniture I would settle the basic layout before buying anything. When the room shape and furniture arrangement fight each other, even well-chosen pieces can feel wrong. 2. Keep the Main Walking Path Clear A compact living room feels crowded quickly when people have to weave around coffee tables, chairs, and side furniture. Identify the route people naturally use between the entrance, sofa, kitchen, balcony, or hallway. That path should remain visually and physically easy to follow. If a side table constantly gets bumped, it may not belong there. If an accent chair forces people to turn sideways to pass, move or remove it. One useful trick is to temporarily shift smaller furniture out of the room and live with the simplified layout for a day. It becomes much easier to see which pieces actually support daily life and which ones simply occupy floor space. 3. Choose Furniture That Fits the Space Small rooms do not require miniature furniture everywhere. In fact, several tiny pieces can make a room look busier than one properly scaled sofa. Look for furniture with: Slimmer arms Moderate seat depth Exposed legs Simple silhouettes Proportions that leave visible floor around them Measure the full seating footprint of a sofa or chair, including arms and chaise sections, before ordering. items.title: What is the Most Durable Furniture Material? - Parts And Labor Design
items.text: What is the Most Durable Furniture Material? - Parts And Labor Design Skip to content What is the Most Durable Furniture Material? Furniture ON September 21, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content A cedar Adirondack chair and a mid-century credenza can both look built to last on delivery day, and both can disappoint within a few seasons of real use. That gap between showroom impression and lived-in performance is exactly why people ask what the most durable furniture material is, and the honest answer depends on where the piece will actually sit. Outdoors, a material has to survive sun, standing water, and temperature swings before strength even matters. Indoors, what wears a piece out is closer to home: repeated loading, spills, scratches, and joints that were never tightened right in the first place. I judge furniture the way I’d judge a contractor’s work, by what’s still true after a few years of actual use, not by how solid it feels the day it’s delivered. What Actually Makes Furniture Last Durability isn’t just about finding the hardest or heaviest material. Furniture has to resist the specific stresses created by its location and how it gets used. Outdoor pieces face moisture, direct sunlight, temperature swings, corrosion, and dirt. Indoor furniture deals more with repeated loading, abrasion, spills, scratches, and everyday cleaning. Construction adds another layer on top of all of it: a strong material joined poorly still produces weak furniture. When I’m comparing pieces, I look at the same handful of things every time: Moisture resistance: Will the material swell, rot, rust, or break down when wet? UV resistance: Will prolonged sunlight weaken or discolor exposed surfaces? Structural strength: Can frames and joints handle repeated loading? Surface wear: How easily does the finish scratch, stain, or abrade? Repairability: Can damaged parts be refinished, tightened, or replaced? Maintenance: What does the material actually need to keep performing? The material matters, but joints, coatings, fasteners, and construction quality usually decide how well the finished piece ages. Which Materials Last Longest Outdoors Outdoor furniture has a harder job than anything sitting in a climate-controlled room. A material that performs beautifully in a living room can deteriorate quickly once it meets standing water, strong sun, or repeated freeze-thaw cycles. That’s why I judge outdoor durability by weather resistance first and strength second. 1. HDPE for Low-Maintenance Outdoor Furniture High-density polyethylene, or HDPE, is worth considering when low maintenance matters more than having a natural wood surface. It doesn’t have the rot problem that comes with untreated wood, or the rust problem that comes with unprotected steel. Product quality still varies a lot here, so don’t assume every recycled-plastic piece behaves the same. POLYWOOD says its HDPE lumber blends UV inhibitors and pigments all the way through the material, not just on the surface, which is the detail that actually protects against fading. For an exposed patio or a rainy climate, a well-made HDPE piece is one of the first options I’d put on a shortlist. 2. Powder-Coated Aluminum for Patios Aluminum pairs useful structural strength with relatively low weight, which makes tables and chairs much easier to reposition than heavy steel pieces. More importantly, outdoors, aluminum naturally forms a protective oxide layer that resists corrosion, and powder coating adds another layer of protection on top of that. items.title: Sofa Dimensions Guide: Standard Sizes Explained - Parts And Labor Design
items.text: Sofa Dimensions Guide: Standard Sizes Explained - Parts And Labor Design Skip to content Sofa Dimensions Guide: Standard Sizes Explained Furniture ON September 21, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content A sofa can look perfectly proportioned online and still feel too large, too deep, or oddly small once it lands in your living room. The style is almost never the problem. The sofa dimensions on the listing are the part everyone skims past. I size a sofa by answering three separate questions before I let anyone near fabric swatches: will it fit the space, will it feel right to sit in, and can it actually get through the front door? Work through those in order, and most of the expensive sizing mistakes disappear before you ever place an order. How to Read Sofa Dimensions on a Listing Most listings show a string like 84″ W x 38″D x 34″H. That tells you the sofa is 84 inches wide, 38 inches deep, and 34 inches tall, measured at the outside edges of the frame. Those three numbers describe the footprint. They do not tell you how much of that footprint you can actually sit in, which is why inside seat width is the measurement I check first on every listing. Measurement What It Means Why It Matters Overall width Outside edge of one arm to the other Determines wall space and scale Overall depth Frontmost point to the back of the frame Shows how far it projects into the room Overall height Floor to the highest point Matters near windows and shelves Inside seat width Usable space between the arms The real measure of seating capacity Seat depth Front of seat to back cushion Upright versus relaxed sitting Seat height Floor to top of seat cushion Ease of sitting and standing Arm width Width of each arm How much width is not usable seating Two sofas can carry nearly the same overall width and still seat differently: IKEA UPPLAND three-seat sofa : 88 1/4 inches wide, with 68 1/8 inches of seat width. IKEA KIVIK sofa : 89 3/4 inches wide, with 70 7/8 inches of seat width. The KIVIK’s slimmer arms hand you roughly two and a half more inches of usable seat for almost the same wall space. For sectionals, add chaise depth, return length, and module size to that list. One overall width number cannot describe a shape with more than one side. Standard Sofa Widths by Seating Capacity There is no regulated width behind the words loveseat, three-seat sofa, or sectional. They are shopping categories, not size standards, and the range inside each one is wider than most people expect. 1. Loveseat Dimensions Plan on roughly 55 to 72 inches wide for a compact two-seat sofa, though smaller and larger versions exist. Loveseat widths vary noticeably across IKEA’s range: FINNALA : 55 1/2 inches wide. MORABO : Approximately 65 3/8 inches wide. That is just over 16 inches of difference between pieces sold under the same seating label. In a small room, compare outside width against seat width before anything else. Slim arms hand you more usable seating without adding an inch to the footprint, and in a tight apartment layout , that trade often matters more than a few extra inches of overall width. 2. Three-Seat Sofa Dimensions Three-seat sofas usually land somewhere between the low 70s and upper 90s in inches, and the label alone will not tell you which end you are getting. Current IKEA specifications put the SÖDERHAMN three-seat section at 73 1/4 inches wide and the SLATORP at nearly 97 inches, close to a twenty-inch spread inside the same seating category. Do not judge seating capacity by cushion count either. A bench-seat sofa without three individual cushions

items.title: How to Build Cabinet Doors: Slab to Shaker - Parts And Labor Design
items.text: How to Build Cabinet Doors: Slab to Shaker - Parts And Labor Design Skip to content How to Build Cabinet Doors: Slab to Shaker DIY & Renovate ON September 22, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content A run of ten matching Shaker doors isn’t a hard project; it’s a repeatable one, deciding whether your kitchen looks finished or slightly off. Rate this an intermediate build: a full day of shop time for your first door, and $150 to $400 in materials for a typical kitchen’s worth of doors once your setup is locked in. Cabinet doors look simple until several of them hang in one straight run, where a small difference in stile width or hinge position throws off the gaps on both sides. That is why how to build cabinet doors is less about turning four boards into a rectangle than about controlling dimensions from the first cut through installation. I prefer to settle the door style, hinge type, and finished dimensions before buying or milling the stock. Then I make one complete sample. If that door hangs correctly, the same setup can be repeated without carrying a small mistake across the entire kitchen. Cost Note: Figures below are my own project estimates, not a formal price survey. Actual costs vary by region, wood species, and hinge choice. Price out your own hinges and lumber before committing to a full kitchen’s worth of doors. Difficulty 3/5, intermediate joinery and a repeatable setup Time About a full day for your first door, 20 to 30 minutes per door after that Cost $8 to $20 in materials per door, plus $8 to $15 per door for quality concealed hinges Tools Needed Table saw or router table, miter saw or crosscut sled, clamps, calipers, hinge boring jig or forstner bit Skill Required Intermediate Those numbers assume you already own basic shop tools. If you need to buy a router table or a full set of matched cutters just for this one project, add that cost before you decide it’s worth doing yourself. Choose the Right Door Method The best construction method depends on four practical things: the tools available, the finish you want, the number of doors being made, and your comfort with woodworking joints. Method Difficulty Main Tools Best Finish Best For Plywood slab Beginner Saw and drill Paint or veneer Utility and modern cabinets Applied Shaker trim Beginner Saw and nailer or clamps Paint Budget updates Dado and dowel frame Intermediate Table saw or router Paint or stain Traditional Shaker doors Cope and stick frame Intermediate Router table and matched bits Paint or stain Repeated kitchen batches Raised panel Advanced Router table and specialty cutters Paint or stain Traditional cabinetry A slab door removes most joinery from the job. An applied Shaker door creates the framed look by attaching trim to a flat panel. Traditional frame and panel construction takes more setup but gives the rails, stiles, and center panel separate structural roles. For a full set of Shaker doors, I prefer a repeatable frame and panel method over the fanciest joint I can pull off just because it looks more impressive. That decision gets easier once you know whether you’re chasing a richer cabinet finish or just trying to make the fronts you already have look sharper. Plan and Measure Before Cutting The measurement stage determines whether the finished door belongs on the cabinet you’re building it for. Start by identifying the door configuration: Full overlay: The door covers most of the cabinet face. Partial overlay: Part of the face frame remains visible. Inset: The door sits inside the cabinet opening rather than over it. Full overlay tends to

items.title: 15 Gallery Wall Layout Ideas for Any Wall - Parts And Labor Design
items.text: 15 Gallery Wall Layout Ideas for Any Wall - Parts And Labor Design Skip to content 15 Gallery Wall Layout Ideas for Any Wall DIY & Renovate ON September 18, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content A group of framed photos can look completely right on the floor and surprisingly wrong once it reaches the wall. Usually, the artwork is not the problem. The proportions between the pieces are. Good gallery wall layout ideas account for the shape of the wall, the furniture below it, frame sizes, and the amount of space the whole arrangement needs. I’d sort out those relationships before buying another print or making the first hole. A gallery wall can be structured, loose, symmetrical, or deliberately mixed. What matters is having enough order that the collection reads as one arrangement rather than several unrelated frames sharing the same wall. How to Plan a Gallery Wall Layout Start with the wall you actually have rather than a layout saved from another room. Measure the usable width and height, then note anything that reduces that area, including windows, doors, switches, sconces, furniture, or nearby shelving. Next , gather the artwork you already own. Separate larger pieces from smaller ones and note which frames are vertical, horizontal, or square. That inventory usually makes the right layout easier to see. Matching dimensions lend themselves to grids. Mixed artwork gives you more flexibility with organic or anchor-based arrangements. A narrow section of wall may call for a vertical stack. I’d make those decisions before shopping. The right fix is arranging meaningful pieces well, not buying filler because a template has six empty spaces. Gallery Wall Layout Ideas That Work I usually pay less attention to what’s popular and more to what the wall, furniture, and artwork are already telling me. A layout that works beautifully over a long sofa can feel completely wrong on a narrow wall, so I’d choose the arrangement by proportion first and style second. These layouts solve different room conditions without forcing the same formula onto every wall. 1. Classic Symmetrical Grid Use equal-size frames arranged in clean rows and columns with matching gaps. This works especially well above consoles, in dining rooms, or beside built-ins. I usually repeat the frame finish and mat size because small differences show quickly in a grid. Keep every horizontal and vertical line carefully aligned. 2. Balanced Asymmetrical Group Start with two larger works placed apart, then fill around them with smaller frames. The edges do not need to match, but the overall group should still feel balanced. Spread dark frames and strong colors across both sides. I use this when mixed-size art needs order without looking too formal. 3. Organic Salon Group Mix portrait and landscape frames around a loose visual center. Keep the gaps fairly close so separate pieces still read as one collection. I like a few shared edges to give the eye subtle structure. Larger works can anchor the group while smaller pieces fill the surrounding spaces. 4. Anchor and Fill Layout Choose the largest or strongest work first, then place smaller frames around it. The main piece can sit slightly off-center instead of directly in the middle. Before marking the wall, match the hardware to each frame , especially when the pieces differ in weight or use different hangers. I balance its visual weight with several smaller works on the opposite side. This works especially well when one frame is much larger than the rest. 5. Single Horizontal Row Arrange three to seven frames along one shar

items.title: Otium — Studio UNLTD
items.text: Otium Otium presented a unique and challenging opportunity: create a ground-up restaurant on a new bridge in the heart of the economic and cultural center of Downtown Los Angeles. Chef Hollingsworth’s vision was to transport the guests from this concrete metropolis to Napa Valley via his point of view and exploration of familiar comfort dishes, working with locally sourced ingredients and maintaining a strong connection to nature. The resulting design dovetails and supports this concept from the moment you spy the 170 seat restaurant through the 100 year old olive trees of the Broad Museum plaza or perched over Hope St. like tree house in one’s backyard. PROJECT SUMMARY LOCATION Los Angeles, CA YEAR 2015 CLIENT Chef Tim Hollingsworth | Sprout LA SIZE 5,996 sq. ft. interior | 875 sq. ft. exterior “Many of Otium’s decorative elements, including tables, chairs, ceramics, and light fixtures were designed by local artisans, contributing to the ‘perfectly imperfect’ handmade charm of the space.” Elizabeth G. Dunn Surface Magazine There is a strong connectivity from the restaurant to nature visually through a large curtain wall of glass, literally through a towering mural by graphic artists Sagmeister & Walsh of NYC, and texturally through the rich material palette of walnut, hickory and ipe woods, ochre & charcoal tile, soapstone, decomposed granite, steel and copper. The elegant rusticity of the outdoor seating area stands in stark contrast to its more austere neighbors.

items.title: Bestia — Studio UNLTD
items.text: Bestia The concept for Bestia juxtaposes decorative contemporary elements against a raw, industrial space dripping with character. This approach pays homage to sophisticated modern-day Italian spaces, which often integrate contemporary interiors into centuries-old structures. Strong, traditional building materials such as tile, steel, marble, and wood also provide pops of festive color. PROJECT SUMMARY LOCATION Los Angeles, CA YEAR 2012 CLIENT Chefs Ori Menasche & Genevieve Gergis SIZE 2,933 sq. ft. interior | 400 sq. ft. exterior “The emphasis on sustainable ingredients and products can be found not only on the menu but in the design of the space as well. Contemporary elements were sourced from local artisans, who rely on reclaimed materials to create the unique elements found within Bestia, from the light fixtures to the stools and tables.” Dayana Sabatin The Momentum Distinctive booths, engineered and built by District Millworks, feature seats that appear to defy gravity. photography by Nicole Franzen A raw-copper bar top provides a canvas that will be ever-changing throughout its lifetime and reflects the craft of creating artisanal cocktails.

items.title: ORO CIPRIANI - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design
items.text: ORO CIPRIANI - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design ORO Venezia, Italy Tihany Design created the four distinctive spaces which combine to form the refined new restaurant at Venice’s most celebrated hotel. As one of the city’s most desirable alfresco dining areas, the expansive terrace of Oro provides open views to the serene Rio di San Giorgio. Inside, a warm and sophisticated Enoteca is located at the entrance. Influenced by the palazzos of Venice, the main dining room is elegant and luxurious yet contemporary and current. The room is centered with a domed gold leaf ceiling from which a magnificent, custom-made Murano glass chandelier hangs. Traditional Venetian terrazzo graces the floor in modern colors and lines. ___________________ RESTAURANT Michelin Rated ___________________ CLIENT Belmond ﻿visit website﻿ Photo Eric Laignel Previous SAUSKA TOKAJ WINERY Next THE BEVERLY HILLS HOTEL NEW YORK 135 West 27th Street New York, NY 10001 t. +1 212 366 5544 LEGAL privacy policy cookie policy copyright © Tihany Design

items.title: THE BEVERLY HILLS HOTEL - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design
items.text: THE BEVERLY HILLS HOTEL - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design THE BEVERLY HILLS HOTEL Beverly Hills, CA, United States Tihany Design led the restoration of The Dorchester Collection’s esteemed Beverly Hills Hotel on the occasion of its 100 year anniversary. A beacon of Hollywood luxury and international praise, The Beverly Hills Hotel has conveyed an iconic design aesthetic and welcoming ambience since its inception. The restoration began with the hotel lobby where Tihany Design, committed to protecting the hotel’s venerable heritage, preserved the iconic banana leaf motif with the installation of a new, banana leaf floor medallion crafted of limestone. The floors were replaced with hand tufted, wall to wall carpeting, accented with custom design area rugs. Ceruse oak wall panels are cladded in cream leather and new lighting fixtures, including a stunning centerpiece chandelier, provide a welcoming glow to the hotel’s entrance. ___________________ HOTEL GUEST ROOMS & SUITE PUBLIC SPACES RESTAURANT BAR POOL ___________________ CLIENT, OPERATOR Dorchester Collection visit website﻿ Photo Eric Laignel, Niall Clutton Previous ORO CIPRIANI Next THE OBEROI NEW YORK 135 West 27th Street New York, NY 10001 t. +1 212 366 5544 LEGAL privacy policy cookie policy copyright © Tihany Design

items.title: THE OBEROI - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design
items.text: THE OBEROI - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design THE OBEROI New Delhi, India The Oberoi New Delhi has served as the city’s social centerpiece since it opened in 1965. After over 50 years, the brand’s flagship underwent a complete interior redesign, led by Tihany Design. The lobby lounge is contemporary and comfortable with furniture inspired by the design of Edwin Lutyens, New Delhi’s celebrated architect of the early 1900s. Lutyens inspiration can be found throughout the hotel, particularly in respect to proportion and in furniture and lighting design details. The Club Bar, just off the entrance corridor, is an intimate bar and cigar lounge. The 46-seat Indian restaurant Omya is contemporary and sophisticated. On the ninth floor, the hotel’s Chinese restaurant Baochuan. With the renovation, The Oberoi’s guest rooms and suites received a significant increase in size. Each of the four room types is designed to feel residential and luxurious while staying true to the location. ___________________ HOTEL GUEST ROOMS & SUITE PUBLIC SPACES RESTAURANT BAR ___________________ CLIENT, OPERATOR The Oberoi Group visit website﻿ Photo Amit Mehra Previous THE BEVERLY HILLS HOTEL Next THE WESTIN CHOSUN NEW YORK 135 West 27th Street New York, NY 10001 t. +1 212 366 5544 LEGAL privacy policy cookie policy copyright © Tihany Design

items.text: THE WESTIN CHOSUN - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design THE WESTIN CHOSUN Seoul, South Korea The luxury hotel is a source of national pride as the symbol of Korean hospitality, since 1914. Tihany Design redesigned the first floor public spaces, comprised of the hotel Lobby, Reception, Business Center, Circle Lounge; restaurant design for Ninth Gate Grille, Payard Patisserie, Aria Restaurant and the Vecchia e Nuovo café. On the second floor, elegant and luxurious, Meeting Rooms, the Banquet Reservation area, Wedding Preview showroom and consulting areas. Located on the second floor, an eco luxury gym and fitness center provide a new focal point for guests with bold stripes of red backlit glass inset on dark wenge columns. The third level evokes complete serenity and renewal, enhanced by the panoramic views of the Ninth Gate Garden upon entering the ivory and wood slatted wall Spa reception area. ___________________ HOTEL PUBLIC SPACES RESTAURANT BAR SPA & FITNESS EVENT SPACES ___________________ CLIENT The Westin Josun Seoul ___________________ OPERATOR Marriott Visit website Photo Nacasa & Partners Previous THE OBEROI Next MAISON DE LA CATEGORIE NEW YORK 135 West 27th Street New York, NY 10001 t. +1 212 366 5544 LEGAL privacy policy cookie policy copyright © Tihany Design

items.title: MAISON DE LA CATEGORIE - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design
items.text: MAISON DE LA CATEGORIE - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design MAISON DE LA CATEGORIE Seoul, South Korea Located in the heart of Cheongdam-dong, Seoul’s upscale shopping neighborhood, Maison de la Categorie is a sophisticated, contemporary French Brasserie, loosely inspired by the Viennese Secession period. The main dining room charms guests with a stunning, inlaid marble floor, bespoke furnishings handcrafted in Italy, and remarkable service stations that dual function as refrigerated displays for luscious cakes and pastries. Strung across the double-height ceiling of the dining room is a custom, hand blown glass sculpture resembling a pearl necklace that creates dynamic reflections of light throughout the space. Connecting the dining room with the mezzanine is an extraordinary stairway adorned with nickel plated steel railings that display geometric patterns. The walls of the restaurant showcase additional details in the form of meticulous, mother of pearl inlays. ___________________ RESTAURANT Michelin rated ___________________ CLIENT Desang Hospitality visit website﻿ Photo Inchul Kim,Sun Namgoog Previous THE WESTIN CHOSUN Next DINNER BY HESTON BLUMENTHAL NEW YORK 135 West 27th Street New York, NY 10001 t. +1 212 366 5544 LEGAL privacy policy cookie policy copyright © Tihany Design

items.title: DINNER BY HESTON BLUMENTHAL - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design
items.text: DINNER BY HESTON BLUMENTHAL - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design DINNER BY HESTON BLUMENTHAL London, United Kingdom Inspired by Chef Blumenthal’s deep interest and knowledge of 16th century cookery and his use of local ingredients, the design is a contemporary British Brasserie concept; an innovative illustration which influences the senses, yet remains true to British culinary and design traditions. Rich, natural materials such as wood, leather and iron – historical elements at the root of 16th century British style - are utilized in modern ways. In the main dining room, floor to ceiling glass walls provide guests with a glimpse of the kitchen and more significantly, an unusual, one-of-a-kind large scale pulley mechanism. This contemporary chrome and steel contraption is modeled after the 16th century pulley system designed for the British Royal Court’s kitchens. As guests enter the bar area, 16th century British culinary recipes, sourced from rare antique cookbooks, are displayed along the wall behind a one-way mirror. ___________________ RESTAURANT Michelin Rated CHEF Helston Blumenthal ___________________ CLIENT Mandarin Oriental visit website Photo Eric Laignel, George Apotolidis Previous MAISON DE LA CATEGORIE Next VERANDA NEW YORK 135 West 27th Street New York, NY 10001 t. +1 212 366 5544 LEGAL privacy policy cookie policy copyright © Tihany Design

items.title: VERANDA - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design
items.text: VERANDA - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design VERANDA Kuwait Veranda sits on the upper level of Harvey Nichols’ first store in the country. Occupying a 10,000 square foot space, Veranda’s scale and spacious layout echoes the grand scope of The Avenues experience while conveying a sense of intimacy and the serene. Catering to Kuwait’s cosmopolitan clientele with an exquisite “slow food” concept, the restaurant is designed to offer shoppers a relaxing respite in an elegantly modern atmosphere. A dramatic, sculptural “canyon” of polished, stainless steel, sets the tone for a strong and transformative arrival experience. Light wood beams buttress an all-encompassing white ceiling composed of curvaceous layers. These undulating forms – whose lightness hints at a sky hovering above – ultimately bend into layered, white walls that frame the dining area. The restaurant features artwork by Bram Tihany in the form of monumental, photographic murals depicting topiary sculptures of fashion accessories including stilettos, hand bags and sunglasses. ___________________ RESTAURANT ___________________ CLIENT Harvey Nichols Kuwait ﻿ Photo Eric Laignel Previous DINNER BY HESTON BLUMENTHAL Next AT.MOSPHERE NEW YORK 135 West 27th Street New York, NY 10001 t. +1 212 366 5544 LEGAL privacy policy cookie policy copyright © Tihany Design

items.title: AT.MOSPHERE - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design
items.text: AT.MOSPHERE - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design AT.MOSPHERE Dubai, United Arab Emirates Located on the 122nd floor of the world renowned Burj Khalifa Tower, it features its design around a hushed palette of rich materials paired with bespoke original features. The intimate restaurant is chic and luxurious, created by calm shades of amethyst and cocoa in sumptuous textures. Hand-polished wood panels clad the walls and arch up across the ceiling, leading the eye to floor-to-ceiling windows, while the bold architectural forms of the wood walls and ceilings evoke an intimate vault-like feeling. Across from the restaurant a separate doorway leads to the equally alluring bar and lounge. In place of the traditional bar design is a round “conversation table” anchored by a glass-enclosed back bar room. The bar and its surroundings rest on a marble-clad, elevated platform overlooking the sunken and lushly textured VIP lounge furnishings, where each seat affords an incomparable view. ___________________ RESTAURANT ___________________ CLIENT Emaar ﻿ visit website Photo Eric Laignel Previous VERANDA Next THE SPRINGS NEW YORK 135 West 27th Street New York, NY 10001 t. +1 212 366 5544 LEGAL privacy policy cookie policy copyright © Tihany Design

WRIGHTCREST CULVER CITY, CA WRIGHTCREST CULVER CITY, CA photography by Laure Joliet We worked closely with their design-forward clients to brighten and refresh this classic California mid-century ranch, located minutes away from the creative hub of downtown Culver City, home to film studios & boutique tech startups alike. The single-level home is nestled in the charming hillside of Blair Hills neighborhood with spectacular views of downtown LA and surrounded by lush landscaping framed from the living spaces within. The homeowners, both prominent in the creative, tech start-up world, are also avid art collectors. Their modern collection became a driving force for the design of the home, along with the intent to brighten and open up the previously dark, compartmentalized spaces. Light walnut wood ceilings were added along with polished warm grey concrete floors, with new windows that maintained the classic architectural form. The interior design departs from a purely mid-century aesthetic, with warm, hand-hewn touches in the millwork and furniture selections. Lighting design from Lindsey Adelman, Apparatus, and Rich Brilliant Willing bring a more contemporary touch to the project, and complement the curation of the fine art collection as sculptures in their own right. With a bright, sun-drenched palette and a layout that spills onto the pool deck, and expansive views of Los Angeles beyond, the home is both a comfortable retreat, as well as a sun-filled gallery to highlight the homeowner’s collection and lifestyle. While embracing the existing detailing, adding a warm and bright palette of interior finishes, and curating a selection of art and lighting, we created a unique balance of organic and composed design within this verdant hillside retreat. CASA CODY PALM SPRINGS, CA, 2021 CASA CODY PALM SPRINGS, CA, 2021 photography by Lance Gerber & Josh Cho Inspired by coastal Spain, we composed a rich palette of color & texture to complement the existing historical character of Casa Cody. Casa Cody is the oldest operating hotel in Palm Springs, founded in the 1920s by Hollywood pioneer Harriet Cody, cousin to the legendary Buffalo Bill. The project blends historic preservation with fresh and modern colors, textures and patterns, honoring its Spanish Colonial Revival heritage and adobe hacienda architecture with a new lens. Quiet and secluded yet just steps from Palm Springs’ center, Casa Cody is a romantic respite with 29 rooms including three free-standing accommodations across well-manicured grounds, situated in front of the rising backdrop of the San Jacinto Mountains under the open skies of the California desert. Casa Cody is a designated Class I Historic Site, Palm Springs’ highest level of historic preservation protection. In the early 1900s, Harriet and Harold Bryant Cody came by wagon from Hollywood to Palm Springs where they settled on land that was to become Casa Cody and built a home. With warm coral velvet, textured blue-green accents, and otomi-patterned pillows, the rooms are imbued with depth to enliven the existing plaster interior. Each room features richly colored zellige tile and deep blue millwork in the bathrooms and bar areas, reflecting the Mediterranean influence in a modern design. We custom designed upholstered elements and cabinetry in the space for an inviting, residential feel. Dark wood tones balance the rich pops of color, creating a classic yet modern aesthetic that is unlike any other in Palm Springs, as unique as the vibrant history of the property. With multiple courtyards and spacious lawns against a serene mountain backdrop, Casa Cody is a sanctuary within the creative bustle of downtown Palm Springs. VICTORIA VENICE, CA, 2020 VICTORIA VENICE, CA, 2020 PHOTOGRAPHY BY LAURE JOLIET Inspired by the long history of artists seeking a creative retreat in our local Venice Beach community, we had the pleasure of partnering with clients who share deep roots in the arts, and were looking to create an inspired compound of their own. The relationship began with the exploration of various potential project sites, with the consideration of both new construction and renovation projects. The goal was to find the perfect combination of open area and urban energy, to create a strong balance between interior and exterior spaces. The site that was ultimately selected was an oversized Venice lot that provided the flexibility to design a home with a unique program including accessory spaces for art, yoga, and meditation, without sacrificing ample exterior living space. Early precedents were taken from Hacienda style architecture and modern ‘family compound’ layouts, with an emphasis on an interior layout that would unfold into the gardens, bringing light and air into the living spaces. Laced together by limestone and vein-cut travertine finishes that carry from the exterior of the buildings and hardscape to interior architectural moments, custom steel windows frame each view between spaces with thoughtful intention. Upon entry through the front gates, the property is perceived as a contained sanctuary within surrounding courtyard walls, with meandering gardens connected by architectural cornerstones and passageways. All landscaping including select specimen trees – two large olives and one exceptionally large jacaranda – is by LA-based Terremoto, softening the built environment. The warm white tones and textures of the architecture provide a clean canvas to highlight the lush garden design. Custom crafted millwork throughout the home in bleached oak and an indigo-ebony finish are paired with an unexpected yet classic consideration of interior finishes and fixtures. The simplicity in architectural form is elevated through careful detailing to ensure that the intended composition of the home is kept intact through all material transitions. A variety of Apparatus Studio fixtures serve not only as functional lighting sources but also sculptural design elements. Interior plaster finishes in warm whites, subtle blush tones, and bolder turquoise bring an additional layer of warmth and unexpected vibrancy to the home, playing off the verdant landscape that together create the feeling of a lush retreat within the property walls. With this composition of handcrafted built-in elements, and a palette of materials defined by rich natural texture, we created a unique environment imbued with aspects of Wabi-Sabi to foster the daily creativity of our like-minded clients. items.title: Pistolero Ranch • Clayton Korte
items.text: Pistolero Ranch Tarpley, Texas Pistolero Ranch is a refined yet practical family retreat nestled within a stunning 4,000-acre expanse in the Texas Hill Country, bordering a pristine nature preserve. Thoughtfully designed to support intergenerational enjoyment of the outdoors, the residence offers a modern interpretation of a classic ranch, seamlessly blending comfort, durability, and environmental sensitivity. Occupying 7,086 square feet, the home is strategically sited to embrace expansive views of the rolling terrain, with a particular emphasis on the dramatic valley to the south. Its placement and orientation optimize passive solar gain and natural ventilation, underscoring a commitment to sustainability. The architectural palette draws inspiration from the rugged landscape, employing resilient, regionally appropriate materials that will endure and evolve gracefully over time. The exterior combines native Texas limestone with a German smear mortar finish, standing-seam copper panels that will develop a rich patina, and weathered Accoya siding in sheltered areas—each element chosen for its longevity, low maintenance, and ability to reflect the site’s earthy tones and textures. Inside, the home balances rustic character with contemporary refinement. Limestone and concrete floors offer thermal mass, enhancing energy efficiency, while wide-plank white oak, veneer plaster walls and ceilings, and exposed timber structures add layers of warmth and tactile richness. Stone accents echo the geology of the surrounding hills, reinforcing a sense of place. The layout supports both privacy and togetherness, with a generous primary suite, three additional bedrooms for guests or children, and essential service spaces including a garage and carport. Expansive covered porches and deep overhangs promote year-round outdoor living, providing shelter from the elements while fostering a strong connection to the land. Cross-ventilation, ample shade, and thoughtfully placed operable windows reduce reliance on mechanical systems and encourage natural comfort. At the heart of the retreat, a large pool offers a communal space for recreation and relaxation. Pistolero Ranch exemplifies a deep respect for its environment through its integration of sustainable design strategies, contextual materials, and a site-responsive layout. It is both a sanctuary and a celebration of the enduring beauty of the Texas Hill Country—crafted to age gracefully and remain firmly rooted in its extraordinary setting. items.title: Viana Amenity Center • Clayton Korte
items.text: Viana Amenity Center Texas Hill Country A place where modern comfort meets timeless design, the Viana Amenity Center fosters community, connection, and relaxation in the heart of the Texas Hill Country. Located just 30 miles west of San Antonio, the center anchors a new bedroom community designed for families of all ages seeking a relaxed, ranch-inspired lifestyle. Defined by its connection to nature and abundant outdoor spaces, the development reflects a deep commitment to healthy living and intentional design. Rooted in the philosophy of healthy living by design, the amenity center seamlessly integrates architecture and landscape, offering panoramic Hill Country vistas and spaces that feel both grounded and inspiring. Constructed with natural, honest materials—limestone, concrete, and wood—the architecture expresses a vernacular, utilitarian language that reflects the warmth and simplicity of the region. The design plays with contrast and texture: solid masonry walls provide a sense of permanence and shelter, while light wood cladding brings warmth and refinement to the pavilions. Expansive glass openings blur the boundary between indoors and out, allowing gathering spaces to flow effortlessly onto shaded porches and sunlit terraces, reinforcing the connection to the surrounding landscape. The center is organized around a primary pavilion, flanked by an open-air porch on one side and a grand terrace leading to a naturally shaped resort-style pool on the other. A generous courtyard and a more intimate gathering pavilion with an outdoor fireplace provide a warm welcome as guests arrive, offering both communal and contemplative spaces nestled within the landscape. A large playground stretches just beyond the pool, offering space for families to play and unwind. The conditioned event space offers a cozy indoor setting for gatherings of up to 20 people, while generous outdoor gathering areas provide shaded patios and open-air seating amid native plantings. A well-appointed restroom facility accommodates events of up to 200 guests, ensuring comfort and convenience for all. Whether relaxing poolside, staying active in the fitness center, or hosting a celebration in the event lounge, the Viana Amenity Center invites residents to slow down, connect, and enjoy life in harmony with nature—a true expression of Hill Country charm and community-focused design. items.title: Cosmic Saltillo • Clayton Korte
items.text: Cosmic Saltillo Austin, Texas | Adaptive Reuse Located in a highly developed part of East Austin, two warehouse buildings long abandoned are now a thriving morning-to-night restaurant and bar. The buildings were constructed in the early 1900s and used by Texas Company, or Texaco, to hold petroleum products delivered by railcars and dispensed in trucks throughout Austin. Today, they are the second location of a city favorite: Cosmic Coffee & Beer. As a rare remnant of the industrial past of the area, it is a spot full of history and graffiti added over the course of the last century. It is a landscape-focused hospitality space where city-dwellers and visitors alike can connect in a laid-back atmosphere surrounded by nature and art. Following its ethos of sustainability, the project breathes new life into the two front-gabled warehouses and activates the spaces between as seating areas and gardens. Upon entry, signatures of the Cosmic brand come into focus: water features, fig ivy climbing steel trellises, and custom signage. The shells of two long abandoned Texaco warehouse buildings were painstakingly preserved and converted into new uses, right down to the graffiti, along with three towering elm trees and a collection of crumbling brick walls used to create intimate, vine-shrouded seating areas separate from the main courtyard. The salvaged buildings required stabilization prior to the renovation and have been entirely transformed, retaining their corrugated steel siding, wood-framed windows, and metal roofing. Anything that could be was salvaged, including the buildings’ concrete slabs, which were jackhammered out and repurposed as massive, asymmetrical pavers for the entry. Additional materials throughout the site are durable and honest, meant to weather and patina with time. The west building houses a coffee and spirit bar with a lounge area, while the east building introduces a new taqueria. Nestled between buildings is the garden; it is the heart of the property with a covered deck and open patio, as well as a koi pond immersed in vegetation. At night, the curved form of the deck and string lighting evoke starry elements of Cosmic’s brand. A stairway at the entry leads to a second-level bar for private events and more intimate setting. The historic warehouse buildings retain their corrugated steel siding, wood-framed windows, and metal roofing. A new 30-foot tower provides access to the second-level balcony, showcasing a custom mural. Cosmic provides a sustainable backyard retreat including gardens that feature native and adaptive species, multiple biological ponds and water features. The landscape team has restored an acre of broken asphalt into a verdant green space featuring a certified wildlife habitat, a rainwater catchment and irrigation system, an ecological pond (a custom fountain was built from a salvaged pipe and a gravel crusher), an on-site dedicated and intensive composting program, and a large herb and vegetable garden that will drive seasonal cocktail offerings. items.title: Certon Creek Farm • Clayton Korte
items.text: Certon Creek Farm Levering, Michigan | Renovation Overlooking the rolling landscapes of Levering, Michigan, Certon Creek Farm has remained in the same family for generations, with roots tracing back to the 1800s. The existing farmhouse, built in the early 1900s, stands as a testament to this rich history. Last year, a new chapter began when our clients acquired the property, envisioning a transformation of the existing home into a sustainable primary residence—a retreat for the couple with ample space to welcome their visiting adult children. The renovation and expansion of the wood-shingle farmhouse will bring it to a total of 2,973 square feet transforming the interiors into contemporary spaces and expanding the residence with a carefully integrated new primary suite. Additionally, a new 1,453-square-foot farm equipment barn will support the farm’s evolving needs. Spanning 120 breathtaking acres, the farm is a blend of open fields, dense woodlands, and the gently meandering Certon Creek. Benefiting from the land’s natural contours and abundant sunlight, ten acres of Marquette Cold Hardy Grape vines are flourishing on the property and harvested annually for local winemakers. Apple and plum trees among a variety of other species that round out the crops on the working farm. The surrounding wilderness is home to a diverse array of native wildlife, further enriching the sense of place. Materiality plays a crucial role in maintaining architectural continuity. Weathering steel, cedar shingles, native stone, and blackened steel are intentionally left unfinished, allowing them to develop a natural patina over time. Inside, warm wood-paneled interiors with steel accents create a tactile, grounded aesthetic that honors the farm’s heritage. Minimalistic finishes will enhance the refined, layered interiors. Thoughtfully curated furnishings and art will create tranquil, inviting spaces that align with the home’s meticulous detailing. Sustainability is at the forefront of this project. Given Michigan’s harsh winters, high-performance glazing and advanced building science techniques will ensure optimal energy efficiency. A ground-mounted photovoltaic array will provide solar power, allowing the home to operate largely off-grid while minimizing its environmental impact. items.title: Windsor Residence • Clayton Korte
items.text: Windsor Residence Austin, Texas | Renovation Located in the hilly West Austin Tarrytown neighborhood, the Windsor Residence renovation embraces the artistic and adventurous spirit of the artist who owns the home. Originally built in the early twentieth century, the one-story brick house is transformed with the addition of two modern boxes and entirely new interiors. The additions, which expand the kitchen area and add a studio library, are small blue boxes inserted into the white brick facades. Interiors are playful and inspired by client’s travels and collection of colorful artworks. Design moves are refined yet don’t take themselves too seriously, letting subtle and bold colorways and textures work together throughout the home. The interiors of the home embrace a contemporary expression that builds on the intimacy of the original design. The primary living area is now expanded with the new studio and library space where custom wood shelving and floor-to-ceiling windows looking out on to the garden. The primary living space opens up on to the new light-filled dining room and adjacent kitchen where a lighter palette of earth tones in greys complements the wavy pink hues marking the floor tiles and the rose quartz countertops. A curved zellige-tiled hood above the stove, copper sink, and custom millwork are just a few of the elevated details in this highly functional and delightful kitchen. The primary living area is now expanded with the new studio and library space where custom wood shelving and floor-to-ceiling windows looking out on to the garden. The primary living space opens up on to the new light-filled dining room and adjacent kitchen where a lighter palette of earth tones in greys complements the wavy pink hues marking the floor tiles and the rose quartz countertops. A curved zellige-tiled hood above the stove, copper sink, and custom millwork are just a few of the elevated details in this highly functional and delightful kitchen. The lighter colors of the kitchen and living area transition into darker and richer palettes in the more private areas of the home where deep greens and blues take over. In the primary suite, lush green terrazzo tiles and a light green plaster-like finish on the walls wrap the room in ethereal feeling as the changing natural light, from a curved wall reaching up to a new skylight, creates a dance of colors and textures in the room. The terrazzo floors flow through the bedroom to the primary bath finished in forest green zellige tile and a darker green plaster-like paint. A freestanding hammered-copper tub sits near a window providing a bright warm contrast to the cool emerald surroundings. The richness and layering of the interiors extend into the yard, where terraces with built-in planters overflowing with native and drought-tolerant plants create a series of inviting spaces between the residence and the new terracotta block carport. items.title: Patience Ranch • Clayton Korte
items.text: Patience Ranch Georgetown, Texas Located in the rolling hills of Central Texas and surrounded by more than 350 acres of prairie grasses, spring wildflowers, live oaks, red oaks, and cypress trees, Patience Ranch is a place for our client’s family to gather and enjoy the outdoors. The ranch property comprises a main house, four lakeside cabins, a pavilion building, a party barn with a pool, and a lookout pavilion. The buildings are sited so that the people in the main house may enjoy privacy while those in the gathering spaces and cabins can convene in closer proximity to one another. A nearby spring-fed pond, with several access points, is available for swimming, canoeing, and fishing. The idyllic scene, completed with cattle and horses, is perfect for the relaxed ranch life. The refined yet practical architecture and interior design of all buildings marries elegance with authenticity of place. Native and natural materials will weather and get better with age. Limestone walls with deeply set windows, concrete, weathered wood, and metal roofing are just some of the elements that unify the buildings. The outdoors flows easily into the indoors, as the materials are pulled inside and transform to become more polished. The resulting warm, inviting spaces are fundamentally interwoven with the ranch outside. Outdoor circulation and curated views of planted and restored meadow grasslands ensure a deep connection to landscape at all times. The main house is sited along the water’s edge and steps down to meet it. Roughly L-shaped in plan, the long bar of the residence establishes the design ethos of the ranch with a generous entry breezeway framing the view to the lake beyond. The predominately open living, dining, and kitchen areas stretch to the east as the residence unfolds from these welcoming gathering areas to the more intimate spaces of the primary suite. Guest suites and a gym are positioned on the opposite side of the breezeway, closer to the water’s edge. Light vertical wood panels clad much of the exterior of the residence, while transitions in the zones of the home are marked by open or screen breezeways and thick limestone walls. This rhythm of light wood and glazing with pauses of thick, heavy masonry grounds the residence, creating a peaceful interior experience. Interiors are defined by generous spaces where walls meet lofted ceilings with clerestory windows emphasizing the transition of the materials from the outside in with views of the tree canopy and sky beyond. The party barn is the focal point and primary gathering area for the guests of Patience Ranch. Like the main house, the spaces are expansive and welcoming, perfectly planned for hosting both small and large gatherings of family and friends. The architectural language of the main residence continues here with the exterior seamlessly folding into the interiors. Thick limestone walls and light, weathered wood contrast darker ebonized wood of the kitchen, bar, and game areas situated along the northern side of the building, while the expansive living and seating areas look out on to views of the pool and hills beyond through a series of panoramic windows. Four lakeside cabins ensure guests can enjoy the party barn and larger property for extended stays. These buildings, like the main house and party barn, emphasize an easy flow from the exterior to interior. Views and deep shaded porches ensure the lake always feels close by. While the wood cladding adds warmth to simple, yet refined design. A small limestone perch, the lookout pavilion sits lightly overlooking the hills providing respite for those seeking more seclusion and moments to appreciate the landscape. With its inherent generosity and elegance, Patience Ranch brings family and friends together in an idyllic retreat surrounded by trees, grasses, and water. items.title: Lariat Springs Residence • Clayton Korte
items.text: Lariat Springs Residence New Braunfels, Texas Nestled into a steep hillside overlooking the Texas Hill Country, Lariat Springs Residence enjoys expansive views from its clandestine perch. The residence sits within the landscape along a cliff’s edge disturbing little of its surroundings and largely blending into the colors and textures of the limestone outcroppings dotted with oak and juniper trees. Connections to the outdoors and the experience of being part of the landscape define the design of the home which flows easily from the exterior to interior. Stepping down from the covered carport, an open-air seating and dining area welcomes our clients and their guests. Two stacked stone walls extend from the entry steps through the court grounding the building into the hillside and framing a dramatic view of the sky and landscape beyond. Native plants hang from a large oculus cut into the ceiling hinting at the planted roof above and further connecting the space to the environment and sky. The building stretches from either side of this entry court with the primary living area to the west side and the more intimate wing to the east. All of the spaces in the home enjoy floor-to-ceiling windows looking out onto the lush protected gardens next to the cliffside and the hills beyond. The proximity of the limestone walls emphasizes the home’s feeling of being part of the hillside and its stealth position in the larger property. Warm wood, black steel, and stone spill from the exterior to the interiors where areas such as the kitchen are finished in finer veined stone. Yet even from the polished interiors, the exploration and joy of being outdoors still calls. Below the primary living area is a grotto, or outdoor living area with a full functioning kitchen and built in seating, for enjoying the plunge pools and spa. Beyond the grotto, property steps down to a large ledge where a small waterfall and creek will cascade over the stones. Numerous existing pathways will be cleaned up and maintained for future hiking and exploring the property. items.title: Leona Botanical Cafe & Bar • Clayton Korte
items.text: Leona Botanical Cafe & Bar Sunset Valley, Texas Home to the newest locations of Austin favorites Veracruz All Natural and Dee Dee, Leona Botanical Cafe & Bar introduces a third place—a spot away from the home and the workplace, where people can gather, relax, and refuel—to the small municipality of Sunset Valley tucked into larger South Austin. Leona is inspired by the welcoming, layered experiences of international food markets and has an approachable character that invites guests to spend time outside immersed in its gardens filled with native plants. Glass, steel, and wood are the predominate materials, lending simplicity to the design and allowing the buildings to blend into the landscape as they patina over time. Located immediately off of busy Brodie Lane, visitors enter the five-acre site that unfolds into a meadow-like green space with a tapestry of colorful, drought-tolerant plants. A circular entry portal opens up to this central node where the cafe, pavilion, and eateries are placed on the periphery. The organic forms of both the portal and site plan are important elements for the Leona identity, as they embody a connection to the environment essential to the experience of place at the cafe and bar. Informal and formal seating areas enhance the tranquil outdoor atmosphere allowing guests to relax, eat, and drink in a variety of settings. The buildings are light structures that blur the boundaries between the interior and exterior. The cafe sets the casual tone for the site and is a metal and glass box surrounded by a generous porch, which comprises more than two-thirds of the square footage of the building. The porch speaks directly to a smaller pavilion across the meadow where live music and more outdoor seating are positioned under the steel trellis framework. The design of the three nearby eateries reinforces this relaxing atmosphere. The black steel and grey ash-colored wood let these small buildings sit quietly under the trees with the trellis structure harboring more vegetation to protect the built-in seating and planters. The interior of the cafe highlights honest materials and works seamlessly with the characteristics of the architecture, creating a cohesive design experience and a strong indoor-outdoor connection. Black terra-cotta tile lays ground to a transportive, rustic interior. The same stucco finish that wraps the exterior continues inward to envelop the walls and banquettes. Raw stoneware tile defines the bar and cleverly placed lighting creates a sense of daylight deep in the heart of the cafe. Touches of weathered wood add warmth, and a sculptural ceiling element, hanging as a central feature above the bar, adds a sense of whimsey to the space. Soft interior lights continue the twinkle effect of the garden and its lights during evening and nighttime hours. items.title: Pullman Market • Clayton Korte
items.text: Pullman Market San Antonio, Texas | Adaptive Reuse Within the historic Samuels Glass building, the new Pullman Market offers a symphony of sensory delights that invite visitors to embark on a journey of discovery with the rich foodways and bounty of Texas. The building’s original materials show history and patina and provide a stunning contrast to the new elements. The result is a tactile experience that is both captivating and engaging. Visitors are drawn into the market’s vibrant atmosphere by way of light-filled patios created by infill between structural elements that connect to the rest of Pearl’s bustling pedestrian experience. By preserving the building’s existing structure and shell, the project not only eliminated tons of waste from local landfills, but also added to the historic and cultural fabric of its context. Within, a rich tapestry of distinctly Texan textures, flavors, and aromas tantalize visitors in a uniquely designed space that showcases the processes of bakers, butchers, baristas, chefs, and fishmongers. The scent of freshly baked bread, the sound of artisans at work, and the sight of chefs preparing so many mouth-watering dishes—these are the sensory experiences that await at Pullman Market.Varied materials, graphics, lighting, architecture, and branding converge to create distinct moments throughout that celebrate Texas’ expansive, bountiful nature. The market is a sensory feast, a celebration of the state’s rich cultural heritage, and a testament to the power of adaptive reuse and preservation. At Pullman Market, all visitors can reconnect with the state’s land, people, and culinary traditions. items.title: Double B Ranch Cabins • Clayton Korte
items.text: Double B Ranch Cabins Texas Hill Country Spanning 555 acres, the Double B Ranch is located in the heart of the Texas Hill Country in Fredericksburg, and is home to a number of rare, historically-significant, restored antique barns. These centuries-old barns—some pre-revolutionary—were strategically acquired from unique national collections of salvageable barns and represent some of the most sought-after examples of early functional barn architecture. Each barn was reconstructed by hand by a team of specialist craftsmen, blacksmiths, stone masons, and artisans strategically concealing 21st-century materials and technology into the walls while keeping the character of the original structures intact. The ranch has two primary nodes of buildings located in relatively close proximity to one another. The Homestead is situated in the center of the property, close to the southern entry, and to the north is a second group of buildings where the Lodge is the focal point. It is surrounded by guest accommodations including three cabins and two car ports. The Homestead and Lodge have both been carefully renovated, scrubbing spaces of their former cliché Texas ranch tendencies and infusing them with a modern sophistication reflective of the personalities of the owners and their deep affinity for the rugged landscape of the area. Each cabin includes an authentic stacked log central room that acts a primary guest suite with a seating area adjacent to a stone fireplace. A slender kitchenette and bunk suite are situated in an addition clad in wood bark shingles. The log construction is exposed on the exterior and interior of the buildings, setting the tone for simplicity and durability carried through in the limestone, custom millwork, and concrete finishes. Connections to the outdoors and natural light are provided with new windows, glazed doors, and a skylight running the length of the connection between the log and conventionally framed structures. The design of each cabin emphasizes simple forms with contrasting rough and smooth textures that stitch the buildings together into the landscape. The broad porches of the Lodge look out over a circular stock-tank pool flanked by the Merritt Cabin and Comanche Cabin with the Log Cabin situated closer to the eastern meadow. Like the Lodge, the cabins seamlessly weave authentic materials together with the new clean lines that characterize the contemporary uses. All three buildings welcome guests with expansive porches protected by broad overhangs. The ethos of beautiful and functional materials is also visible in the new carports. The weathering-steel pipe structure is clad in corrugated perforated-steel panels offer a light touch on the landscape. items.title: Sixth Street • Clayton Korte
items.text: Sixth Street Austin, Texas | Adaptive Reuse As one of Austin’s most iconic destinations, Sixth Street represents Austin’s past, present, and future. It began as Pecan Street quickly becoming a gathering place and hub of commerce for settlers and immigrants who opened the city’s first dry good stores, saloons, sporting houses, and hotels before becoming an epicenter of the city’s music and entertainment scene. Locally loved, and at times forgotten, the area has a dynamic history of many of Austin’s notable firsts in music, events, and business. Stevie Ray Vaughan’s Triple Threat Revue, Muddy Waters, and B.B. King all performed their first local shows on Sixth Street; South by Southwest launched here; and Texas’s beloved H-E-B grocery store opened its first Austin store on Sixth Street. Today, the blocks stretching from Congress Avenue east to Interstate 35 make up one of the only remaining cohesive examples of the city’s late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century architectural heritage. The Sixth Street project sensitively renovates 29 buildings, approximately 200,000 total square feet, located in a six-block area bound by Brazos Street to the west and Interstate 35 to the east. All of these blocks are part of the Historic Sixth Street District established by the National Register of Historic Places in 1975, and many of the individual buildings are recognized as Recorded Texas Historic Landmarks and City of Austin Historic Landmarks. The buildings are a mix of architectural expressions with high-style Victorian Era buildings featuring elaborate metal cornices and brickwork alongside modest one-story brick buildings that maintain the historic scale of the street. Prominent examples of the important history of the street include 520 East Sixth Street or the Carrington-Lyons Building, formerly the E.H. Carrington Store—which was established in 1872 and was one of the first Black-owned businesses on the street. The project celebrates the street’s historic character-defining elements while introducing new designs to support a more culturally rich set of businesses to complement the street. Cleaning, repairing, and restoring historic brick, stone, and metal details will maintain the scale and texture of the urban area. Contemporary design—introducing new storefronts, broad areas of glazing, new awnings, new windows and shutters, and fresh paint—is inspired by historic photographs and on-site analysis of existing materials. This work to revitalize the streetscape and bring people to the area imagines a new destination bustling by day and night, with local shops, live music, homegrown eateries, outdoor bars, and provocative art galleries. It aims to create a vibrant day-to-night community where all are welcome—ensuring 6th Street’s ongoing and essential contribution to Austin’s culture and identity.
